title: PSI: A Benchmark for Human Interpretation and Response in Traffic Interactions
central_claim: The PSI dataset enables pedestrian intention prediction with dynamically annotated crossing intentions and textual reasoning from human annotators, demonstrating that incorporating human-like reasoning improves prediction performance.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'PSI supports standardized tasks and evaluation protocols across multiple dimensions, including pedestrian intention prediction' and Table 2 shows eP2P+disagr.+rsn achieves 63.09% accuracy (best) vs. 59.04% for PIE baseline on PSI intent prediction.
mre_config: Train LSTM/Transformer intent prediction baseline on PSI-1.0 dataset with 15-frame observed bounding box sequences, predict crossing intent at frame 16. Expected ~58% accuracy (paper baseline). Train/val/test split: 75%/5%/20% across 110 videos.
agent_task: Reproduce pedestrian intent prediction baseline on PSI dataset: (1) Request dataset access from http://pedestriandataset.situated-intent.net and download PSI-1.0/2.0 videos and annotations, (2) Clone https://github.com/PSI-Intention2022/PSI-Intent-Prediction, (3) Process videos with split_clips_to_frames.py and create database with database/create_database(), (4) Train LSTM or Transformer baseline model with python main.py using train.py, (5) Evaluate on test split and verify accuracy ~58% (binary crossing intent prediction, 15 frames input, predict frame 16). Environment: Python 3.8, PyTorch 1.10.0, CUDA 11.1.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repos PSI-Intention2022/PSI-Intent-Prediction, PSI-Dataset, PSI-Trajectory-Prediction, PSI-DriverDecision-Prediction contain full training/evaluation code with train.py, test.py, models/, database/ directories. README shows complete pipeline: generate database, split clips to frames, run python main.py.

dataset_available.evidence: Dataset homepage (situated-intent.net/pedestrian_dataset) shows 'REQUEST ACCESS' button requiring registration/approval. Dataset not freely downloadable. Paper checklist claims HuggingFace hosting but HF search for 'PSI', 'Pedestrian Situated Intent', 'situated-intent', 'PSI IUPUI CSRC pedestrian' found no matching repository.

weights_available.evidence: GitHub repos PSI-Intention2022/PSI-Intent-Prediction, PSI-Trajectory-Prediction, PSI-DriverDecision-Prediction contain only training code, no model checkpoints. eP2P model weights not released in any PSI-Intention2022 organization repository. README files show no pretrained model links.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: PSI is a custom author-created dataset for pedestrian intention prediction. Not a widely recognized public ML benchmark like MNIST, COCO, or KITTI. Contains 110-196 custom annotated driving videos with proprietary cognitive annotations.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified: Paper does not report GPU hours. LSTM/Transformer baseline trained on 110 training videos (~15 frames per sample). Estimated 2-4 hours on single A100 for comparable small-scale sequence model. Converted to ~8 H100-hours assuming H100 is 1.0x and A100 is 0.32x equivalent. Actual compute may vary by implementation details and batch size.
abstract: Accurately modeling pedestrian intention and understanding driver decision-making processes are critical for the development of safe and socially aware autonomous driving systems. We introduce PSI, a benchmark dataset that captures the dynamic evolution of pedestrian crossing intentions from the driver's perspective, enriched with human textual explanations that reflect the reasoning behind intention estimation and driving decision making. These annotations offer a unique foundation for developing and benchmarking models that combine predictive performance with interpretable and human-aligned reasoning. PSI supports standardized tasks and evaluation protocols across multiple dimensions, including pedestrian intention prediction, driver decision modeling, reasoning generation, and trajectory forecasting and more. By enabling causal and interpretable evaluation, PSI advances research toward autonomous systems that can reason, act, and explain in alignment with human cognitive processes.

title: Better NTK Conditioning: A Free Lunch from (ReLU) Nonlinear Activation in Wide Neural Networks
central_claim: ReLU activation functions improve NTK conditioning (smaller condition number) and feature separation in wide neural networks, with deeper networks amplifying these effects and leading to faster gradient descent convergence.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'nonlinear activations...demonstrate their specific effects on wide neural networks: (a) better feature separation...and (b) better NTK conditioning, i.e., a smaller condition number of neural tangent kernel (NTK)'. Section 5 and Figure 3 show deeper ReLU networks converge faster than shallower ones across MNIST, f-MNIST, and LibriSpeech datasets.
mre_config: Compute NTK condition number for ReLU networks at depths L=1 to L=5 on MNIST (or synthetic 5D Gaussian data) using the released condition_num.py code. Verify that (1) NTK condition number decreases with depth, and (2) minimum gradient angle increases with depth (better separation). Use 2-3 random seeds and report average results.
agent_task: Clone https://github.com/like-hui/condition_num_ntk and run: (1) condition_num.py with --dataset MNIST to compute NTK condition numbers for depths L=1 to L=5, and (2) min_angle.py with --dataset MNIST to compute minimum gradient angles. Use 2-3 random seeds (edit seeds list in code or re-run with different PYTHONHASHSEED). Verify that NTK condition number monotonically decreases with depth and that minimum gradient angle monotonically increases with depth, matching the paper's Figure 2 results. For faster MRE, reduce batch_size to 256 and limit to first 5000 training samples.

dataset: MNIST via torchvision.datasets (standard), synthetic 5D Gaussian generated in-code

code_available.evidence: Verified repository https://github.com/like-hui/condition_num_ntk by author Like Hui (co-author) contains condition_num.py (NTK condition number), min_angle.py (gradient angles), and nn_train.py (training curves). README confirms these reproduce Figures 2(a), 2(b), and 3 of the paper arXiv:2305.08813. Code uses PyTorch, functorch, and torchvision. GitHub repo search was rate-limited; Hugging Face search returned no results. Author GitHub profile (chaoyue-liu, like-hui) was checked; only like-hui/condition_num_ntk contains paper-relevant code.

dataset_available.evidence: Code uses standard benchmarks (MNIST, CIFAR10, SVHN, FashionMNIST) available via torchvision.datasets with download=True, plus synthetic data (5D Gaussian, 2000 samples) generated on-the-fly in code. LibriSpeech requires custom file not in repo.

weights_available.evidence: This is an empirical analysis paper on NTK conditioning; no pretrained model weights are needed. All experiments compute NTK at random initialization and train networks from scratch. No checkpoint files are released or needed for the MRE.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: MRE can use MNIST (standard benchmark via torchvision.datasets.MNIST) or synthetic data (5D Gaussian generated in code). Both are publicly accessible; MNIST is a widely recognized ML benchmark.

h100_estimate_basis: Paper reports each A-100 run took 4-10 hours for full NTK condition number computation. The MRE uses smaller scale (depths 1-5 only, 2-3 seeds, reduced batch size). Estimated ~3 H100-hours using A100-to-H100 conversion (0.32x). Engineering/debugging time for functorch NTK computation setup is additional. Synthetic dataset avoids LibriSpeech custom data dependency.
abstract: Nonlinear activation functions are widely recognized for enhancing the expressivity of neural networks, which is the primary reason for their widespread implementation. In this work, we focus on ReLU activation and reveal a novel and intriguing property of nonlinear activations. By comparing enabling and disabling the nonlinear activations in the neural network, we demonstrate their specific effects on wide neural networks: (a) better feature separation, i.e., a larger angle separation for similar data in the feature space of model gradient, and (b) better NTK conditioning, i.e., a smaller condition number of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Furthermore, we show that the network depth (i.e., with more nonlinear activation operations) further amplifies these effects; in addition, in the infinite-width-then-depth limit, all data are equally separated with a fixed angle in the model gradient feature space, regardless of how similar they are originally in the input space. Note that, without the nonlinear activation, i.e., in a linear neural network, the data separation remains the same as for the original inputs and NTK condition number is equivalent to the Gram matrix, regardless of the network depth. Due to the close connection between NTK condition number and convergence theories, our results imply that nonlinear activation helps to improve the worst-case convergence rates of gradient based methods.

title: Can Class-Priors Help Single-Positive Multi-Label Learning?
central_claim: The proposed Crisp (Class-pRiors Induced Single-Positive multi-label learning) framework estimates class-priors and derives an unbiased risk estimator that achieves superior performance over existing SPMLL approaches on benchmark datasets.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'a class-priors estimator is introduced, which could estimate the class-priors that are theoretically guaranteed to converge to the ground-truth class-priors... Experimental results on ten MLL benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of our method.' Table 1 (mAP): Crisp achieves 89.931% on VOC, 74.913% on COCO, 50.045% on NUS, and 22.150% on CUB - the best among all comparing methods.
mre_config: Train Crisp on the Yeast MLL dataset (2417 samples, 14 classes) with single-positive label annotation using a simple MLP classifier with 10 epochs, measuring ranking loss and average precision. The MRE tests the core claim by comparing Crisp against baseline SPMLL methods (AN, AN-LS) using the derived unbiased risk estimator with class-prior estimation.
agent_task: Reproduce the Crisp method's core contribution: (1) Implement the class-prior estimator using threshold-based optimization as described in Algorithm 1; (2) Implement the unbiased risk estimator from Eq. (13); (3) Train on Yeast dataset with single-positive labels (randomly select one positive label per sample); (4) Evaluate using ranking loss and average precision; (5) Compare against simple baselines like Assume-Negative (AN). Datasets can be obtained from standard MLL repositories. The algorithm requires warm-up with AN, then alternating class-prior estimation and model optimization. Hyperparameters: δ=0.01, τ=0.01, λ=1, 10 epochs, Adam optimizer.

Multiple search queries across GitHub code search, repository search, and HuggingFace with variations of paper title, method name, acronym, and author names all failed to locate an official implementation.

These are well-known benchmark datasets in multi-label learning literature (Zhang et al. review, MLL community), publicly available and widely used. VOC, COCO, NUS, CUB are also standard computer vision benchmarks.

VOC, COCO, NUS, CUB are standard computer vision benchmarks. These are not custom or author-created datasets.

For Yeast (2417 samples, 14 classes) with 10 epochs and a simple MLP classifier, this is a small-scale experiment. Note: Without official code, substantial engineering time for algorithm implementation from scratch is additional and not included.
abstract: Single-positive multi-label learning (SPMLL) is a typical weakly supervised multi-label learning problem, where each training example is annotated with only one positive label. Existing SPMLL methods typically assign pseudo-labels to unannotated labels with the assumption that prior probabilities of all classes are identical. However, the class-prior of each category may differ significantly in real-world scenarios, which makes the predictive model not perform as well as expected due to the unrealistic assumption on real-world application. To alleviate this issue, a novel framework named {\proposed}, i.e., Class-pRiors Induced Single-Positive multi-label learning, is proposed. Specifically, a class-priors estimator is introduced, which could estimate the class-priors that are theoretically guaranteed to converge to the ground-truth class-priors. In addition, based on the estimated class-priors, an unbiased risk estimator for classification is derived, and the corresponding risk minimizer could be guaranteed to approximately converge to the optimal risk minimizer on fully supervised data. Experimental results on ten MLL benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of our method over existing SPMLL approaches.

title: Multidimensional Bayesian Utility Maximization: Tight Approximations to Welfare
central_claim: In the multidimensional i.i.d. unit-demand setting with n buyers and m items, the gap between optimal utility and optimal social welfare is Θ(1 + log(n/m)): a (1-1/e)-approximation when m ≥ n and an O(log(n/m))-approximation when n > m.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'We give a (1-1/e)-approximation when there are more items than buyers, and a Θ(log(n/m))-approximation when there are more buyers than items, and we prove that this bound is tight in both n and m.' Theorem 1 (constantapx) and Theorem 2 (logapx) provide the main approximation guarantees.
mre_config: This is a pure theory paper with no empirical component. The 'MRE' would be a mathematical verification of the theorems, not an experiment. No code, data, or compute is required.
agent_task: This paper is pure mechanism design theory with no empirical content. There is nothing to reproduce computationally. The main results are Theorems proving approximation bounds for the Favorites mechanism variants. No code, data, or compute is required.

code_available.evidence: No code repository found. Searched GitHub with queries: 'Multidimensional Bayesian Utility Maximization', 'MBUM', 'Kira Goldner Taylor Lundy', 'Favorites Mechanism', 'regfave', 'logfave', 'Hartline Roughgarden utility maximization', '2402.12340'. No relevant public repositories exist. This is a pure theory paper - all results are proved mathematically with no experimental validation.

dataset_available.evidence: No datasets are used in this paper. The paper contains only mathematical proofs and theoretical analysis of mechanism design algorithms. The approximation bounds are proven analytically, not validated empirically.

weights_available.evidence: No model weights or checkpoints exist. This is not a machine learning paper - it is mechanism design theory with no trained models.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: No datasets are used. This is a theoretical computer science paper with mathematical proofs only.

h100_estimate_basis: This is a theoretical mechanism design paper with only mathematical proofs. No compute is needed as there are no experiments, simulations, or model training. Verification of the paper's claims requires mathematical proof verification, not computational reproduction.
abstract: We initiate the study of multidimensional Bayesian utility maximization, focusing on the unit-demand setting where values are i.i.d. across both items and buyers. The seminal result of Hartline and Roughgarden '08 studies simple, information-robust mechanisms that maximize utility for $n$ i.i.d. agents and $m$ identical items via an approximation to social welfare as an upper bound, and they prove this gap between optimal utility and social welfare is $Θ(1+\log{n/m})$ in this setting. We extend these results to the multidimensional setting. To do so, we develop simple, prior-independent, approximately-optimal mechanisms, targeting the simplest benchmark of optimal welfare. We give a $(1- 1/e)$-approximation when there are more items than buyers, and a $Θ(\log{n/m})$-approximation when there are more buyers than items, and we prove that this bound is tight in both $n$ and $m$ by reducing the i.i.d. unit-demand setting to the identical items setting. Finally, we include an extensive discussion section on why Bayesian utility maximization is a promising research direction. In particular, we characterize complexities in this setting that defy our intuition from the welfare and revenue literature, and motivate why coming up with a better benchmark than welfare is a hard problem itself.

title: Optimistic Query Routing in Clustering-based Approximate Maximum Inner Product Search
central_claim: The Optimist router achieves the same recall as state-of-the-art routers (NormalizedMean) while probing up to 50% fewer data points in clustering-based approximate maximum inner product search.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'reaches the same accuracy as state-of-the-art routers by probing up to 50% fewer points on benchmark datasets without compromising efficiency.' Table 2 shows 54% savings on Music at 95% recall.
mre_config: Compare Optimist vs NormalizedMean routers on the Music dataset (1M points, 100 dimensions) using spherical KMeans clustering (C=1024 shards). Measure top-100 recall vs volume of points probed. Optimist parameters: delta=0.8, rank=2.
agent_task: Reproduce the MRE by: 1) Download the Music dataset (music-100.hdf5) from https://hf.co/datasets/artificial-memory-lab/ann-datasets. 2) Clone https://github.com/Artificial-Memory-Lab/optimist-router. 3) Build the Rust project with 'cargo build --release'. 4) Create a minimal YAML config to compare Optimist(delta=0.8, rank=2) vs NormalizedMean on Music using spherical KMeans with 1024 clusters. 5) Run the experiment and plot recall vs percentage of points probed. 6) Verify that Optimist achieves >=95% recall with ~50% fewer points probed than NormalizedMean.

code_available.evidence: Full Rust implementation verified at https://github.com/Artificial-Memory-Lab/optimist-router. Contains src/library/routing/optimist_router.rs (Optimist router), src/library/routing/normalized_mean_router.rs (baseline), src/experiment/executor.rs (experiment runner), and YAML configs in experiments/2405.12207/configs/ including main_results_spherical_kmeans.yaml for the MRE configuration.

dataset_available.evidence: All 6 datasets verified on Hugging Face at https://hf.co/datasets/artificial-memory-lab/ann-datasets. Music dataset (music-100.hdf5, 644MB) is one of the paper's benchmark datasets. README.md in the GitHub repo provides direct download links for all datasets.

weights_available.evidence: No model weights needed. This paper proposes a router algorithm (Optimist), not a model with parameters. The algorithm operates on data structures built during indexing (cluster centroids, covariance sketches). No pre-trained checkpoints exist because the method builds its representations during indexing on the target dataset.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: The datasets are ANN benchmark datasets (DeepImage, GloVe, Music, NQ, MsMarco, Text2Image) created for approximate nearest neighbor search research. They are not standard ML benchmarks like MNIST, CIFAR-10, or ImageNet. However, they are publicly released on Hugging Face and commonly used in ANN literature.

h100_estimate_basis: The paper states experiments run on a commercial laptop. For the Music dataset (1M x 100), KMeans clustering with 1024 clusters takes ~10-20 minutes. Router scoring is fast (<1ms per query). No GPU training needed. Estimated 2 H100-hours for a single complete MRE run (clustering + evaluation on all queries).
abstract: Clustering-based nearest neighbor search is an effective method in which points are partitioned into geometric shards to form an index, with only a few shards searched during query processing to find a set of top-$k$ vectors. Even though the search efficacy is heavily influenced by the algorithm that identifies the shards to probe, it has received little attention in the literature. This work bridges that gap by studying routing in clustering-based maximum inner product search. We unpack existing routers and notice the surprising contribution of optimism. We then take a page from the sequential decision making literature and formalize that insight following the principle of ``optimism in the face of uncertainty.'' In particular, we present a framework that incorporates the moments of the distribution of inner products within each shard to estimate the maximum inner product. We then present an instance of our algorithm that uses only the first two moments to reach the same accuracy as state-of-the-art routers such as ScaNN by probing up to $50\%$ fewer points on benchmark datasets. Our algorithm is also space-efficient: we design a sketch of the second moment whose size is independent of the number of points and requires $\mathcal{O}(1)$ vectors per shard.

title: Robust Hyperbolic Learning with Curvature-Aware Optimization
central_claim: Riemannian AdamW optimizer improves hyperbolic generalization ability and reduces overfitting compared to standard Riemannian Adam, with a novel curvature-aware optimization schema enabling stable curvature learning.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'our paper presents a derivation for Riemannian AdamW that helps increase hyperbolic generalization ability. Using this along with our curvature-aware learning schema for Riemannian Optimizers enables the combination of curvature and non-trivialized hyperbolic parameter learning.' Table 5 (EEG ablation) shows HyperMAtt + RAdamW achieves 74.12% on MI vs 68.53% with RAdam; Table 7 (graph ablation H3) achieves 78.3% on PubMed with RAdamW + learnable curvature + tangent scaling.
mre_config: Graph node classification on PubMed using hyperbolic GCN with Riemannian AdamW optimizer, learnable curvature, and tangent-based manifold mapping (H3 configuration from Table 7). Train for 200 epochs with the hyperbolic GCN layer, learnable curvature K, and the proposed RAdamW optimization. Target metric: node classification accuracy (expected ~78.3%). The baseline (without RAdamW or with trivialized parametrization) achieves lower accuracy (76.6-77.1%).
agent_task: Reproduce the paper's core empirical claim using graph node classification on PubMed. Steps: 1) Install geoopt/geoopt for base Riemannian optimization, 2) Implement Riemannian AdamW using weighted Lorentz centroid formulation (Section 3.3) and tangent-based manifold mapping algorithm (Algorithm 1), 3) Implement hyperbolic GCN layer with learnable curvature K on the Lorentz manifold, 4) Train on PubMed using RAdamW with curvature-aware staggered update schema and tanh distance rescaling, 5) Evaluate node classification accuracy and verify ~78% is achieved vs lower baseline without RAdamW or with trivialized curvature.

Tree verification confirmed only 1 file (README.md) with 1 commit; no releases published. The Riemannian AdamW and curvature-aware optimization schema are NOT in geoopt/geoopt (base RiemannianAdam only). Search queries for full title, arXiv ID 2405.13979, acronym, and related hyperbolic terms returned no alternative implementations.

The paper also uses CUB-200-2011, Cars-196, SOP (metric learning), CIFAR-10/100 (image classification), and MI/SSVEP/ERN (EEG) - all standard public benchmarks.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: PubMed citation network is a widely recognized standard benchmark for graph node classification, part of the Cornell/PubMed/Cora benchmark suite used extensively in GNN research.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified: Paper reports EEG GPU timings (e.g., 0.077s/epoch) showing 42x speedup but does not report total GPU-hours for graph experiments. For PubMed node classification with single hyperbolic GCN layer (H3 config), 200 epochs on single GPU estimated at 0.1-0.5 H100-hours (hyperbolic operations add overhead). Conservative estimate: 2 H100-hours to account for implementation and debugging. Engineering time to re-implement Riemannian AdamW from paper equations is additional and not included in compute estimate.
abstract: Hyperbolic deep learning has become a growing research direction in computer vision due to the unique properties afforded by the alternate embedding space. The negative curvature and exponentially growing distance metric provide a natural framework for capturing hierarchical relationships between datapoints and allowing for finer separability between their embeddings. However, current hyperbolic learning approaches are still prone to overfitting, computationally expensive, and prone to instability, especially when attempting to learn the manifold curvature to adapt to tasks and different datasets. To address these issues, our paper presents a derivation for Riemannian AdamW that helps increase hyperbolic generalization ability. For improved stability, we introduce a novel fine-tunable hyperbolic scaling approach to constrain hyperbolic embeddings and reduce approximation errors. Using this along with our curvature-aware learning schema for Riemannian Optimizers enables the combination of curvature and non-trivialized hyperbolic parameter learning. Our approach demonstrates consistent performance improvements across Computer Vision, EEG classification, and hierarchical metric learning tasks while greatly reducing runtime.

title: Cross-Domain Graph Data Scaling: A Showcase with Diffusion Models
central_claim: UniAug demonstrates cross-domain graph data scaling by pre-training a discrete diffusion model on thousands of graphs, achieving consistent performance improvements on downstream node classification, link prediction, and graph classification tasks through adaptive graph structure augmentation via guided generation.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'we propose UniAug, a universal graph structure augmentor built on a diffusion model...By leveraging the pre-trained diffusion model for structure augmentation, we consistently achieve performance improvements across various downstream tasks in a plug-and-play manner.' Table 3 (Link prediction Cora): GCN MRR=30.26 → UniAug MRR=35.36. Table 1 (Graph classification): UniAug achieves best average rank (1.11) across 9 datasets.
mre_config: Link prediction on Cora dataset: `python link_pred.py --config config/link_pred/cora.yaml --seed 0 --thres 0.999 --augment t`. Dataset: Cora (2,708 nodes, standard benchmark). Metric: MRR. Expected: MRR ~35.36 (±7.88) vs baseline GCN MRR=30.26 (±4.80). Uses provided pre-trained checkpoint for structure augmentation.

Only downstream evaluation on Cora dataset is needed: GCN with link prediction head on 2,708 nodes for training. Based on config/link_pred/cora.yaml (epochs=10000, batch_size=1024) and Cora's small size (2,708 nodes), estimated ~1 H100-hour for the MRE. The paper's Table 4 shows training amounts in 10^-3 PF-days but pre-training is not needed for MRE since checkpoint is provided. Engineering/debugging time additional and not included.
abstract: Models for natural language and images benefit from data scaling behavior: the more data fed into the model, the better they perform. This 'better with more' phenomenon enables the effectiveness of large-scale pre-training on vast amounts of data. However, current graph pre-training methods struggle to scale up data due to heterogeneity across graphs. To achieve effective data scaling, we aim to develop a general model that is able to capture diverse data patterns of graphs and can be utilized to adaptively help the downstream tasks. To this end, we propose UniAug, a universal graph structure augmentor built on a diffusion model. We first pre-train a discrete diffusion model on thousands of graphs across domains to learn the graph structural patterns. In the downstream phase, we provide adaptive enhancement by conducting graph structure augmentation with the help of the pre-trained diffusion model via guided generation. By leveraging the pre-trained diffusion model for structure augmentation, we consistently achieve performance improvements across various downstream tasks in a plug-and-play manner. To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first demonstration of a data-scaling graph structure augmentor on graphs across domains.

title: DeltaPhi: Physical States Residual Learning for Neural Operators in Data-Limited PDE Solving
central_claim: DeltaPhi transforms PDE solving from learning direct input-output mappings to learning residuals between similar physical states, providing implicit data augmentation that consistently improves neural operator performance (10-50% relative gains) in data-limited scenarios across diverse PDEs and architectures.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'To address this challenge, we propose DeltaPhi, a novel learning framework that transforms the PDE solving task from learning direct input-output mappings to learning the residuals between similar physical states.' Table 1 shows NORM (DeltaPhi) achieving 1.35e-4 relative error on Heat Transfer with 100 training samples vs 2.70e-4 for direct learning (50% improvement).
mre_config: HeatTransfer irregular domain PDE experiment: NORM (DeltaPhi) with modes=128, width=64, batch_size=10, 100 training samples, 2000 epochs, learning rate 0.01. Dataset downloadable from Google Drive. Metric: relative L2 error.
agent_task: Reproduce the HeatTransfer experiment from DeltaPhi paper: 1) Download HeatTransfer dataset from https://drive.google.com/file/d/1U9cWx7AZzmzF268SDOyRdubLaSEKNAtx/view and extract to datasets/HeatTransfer/. 2) Run HeatTransfer/norm_DeltaPhi.py with the default configuration (100 training samples, 2000 epochs). 3) Verify that the relative L2 error on test set is approximately 1.35e-4, demonstrating the 50% improvement over direct learning baseline (2.70e-4).

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo yuexihang/DeltaPhi contains complete training code for HeatTransfer experiment with norm_DeltaPhi.py implementing the residual learning framework, including model architecture (NORM_net_rag), data loading (rag_utils.get_rag_dataloader), and training loop. Code is runnable after downloading dataset from provided Google Drive link.

The dataset includes HeatTransfer.mat and LBO basis files (lbe_ev_input.mat, lbe_ev_output.mat). This is the same dataset used in the NORM paper (chen2023learning) which the authors reference as the basis for their experiments.

The README.md states 'Codes for additional simulation cases will be released later' indicating incomplete release. No checkpoints, model files, or trained weights found after inspecting the repository tree.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: HeatTransfer is a custom irregular-domain PDE dataset originally from the NORM paper (chen2023learning), not a standard ML benchmark like MNIST or ImageNet. The dataset consists of 3D heat transfer simulations on triangular meshes with 7199 nodes, with 100 training and 100 test samples.

h100_estimate_basis: Training on single RTX 4090 with batch_size=10, 100 training samples, 2000 epochs takes approximately 1-2 hours. RTX 4090 is roughly 0.7x H100 SXM for FP16, so ~2 RTX 4090-hours * 0.7 ≈ 1.4 H100-hours, rounded to 2 H100-hours for engineering margin. This is based on the paper stating experiments run on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 device.
abstract: The limited availability of high-quality training data poses a major obstacle in data-driven PDE solving, where expensive data collection and resolution constraints severely impact the ability of neural operator networks to learn and generalize the underlying physical system. To address this challenge, we propose DeltaPhi, a novel learning framework that transforms the PDE solving task from learning direct input-output mappings to learning the residuals between similar physical states, a fundamentally different approach to neural operator learning. This reformulation provides implicit data augmentation by exploiting the inherent stability of physical systems where closer initial states lead to closer evolution trajectories. DeltaPhi is architecture-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated with existing neural operators to enhance their performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent and significant improvements across diverse physical systems including regular and irregular domains, different neural architectures, multiple training data amount, and cross-resolution scenarios, confirming its effectiveness as a general enhancement for neural operators in data-limited PDE solving.

title: GC4NC: A Benchmark Framework for Graph Condensation on Node Classification with New Insights
central_claim: graph reduction for GNNs
claim_evidence: GraphSlim provides 15+ graph reduction methods and 15+ GNN models for evaluation
mre_config: 15+ methods, 8 datasets (Cora, CiteSeer, PubMed, Reddit, Flickr, ogbn-arxiv, ogbn-products, yelp)
agent_task: extract_mre

h100_estimate_basis: Full evaluation requires running 15+ reduction methods on 8 datasets with 15+ GNN models. Each method needs 50+ epochs of training per dataset per architecture. Estimate assumes ~10 GPU-hours per (method, dataset) combination on H100, totaling approximately 10 * 15 * 8 = 1200 hours minimum, with additional architecture cross-validation (15 models) adding ~500 hours, and dataset preprocessing adding overhead. Conservative estimate rounds up to ~2000 hours (equivalent to ~83 days of continuous H100 execution), with upper bound of ~8760 hours (1 GPU year) accounting for hyperparameter tuning and multiple seeds.
abstract: Graph condensation (GC) is an emerging technique designed to learn a significantly smaller graph that retains the essential information of the original graph. This condensed graph has shown promise in accelerating graph neural networks while preserving performance comparable to those achieved with the original, larger graphs. Additionally, this technique facilitates downstream applications like neural architecture search and deepens our understanding of redundancies in large graphs. Despite the rapid development of GC methods, particularly for node classification, a unified evaluation framework is still lacking to systematically compare different GC methods or clarify key design choices for improving their effectiveness. To bridge these gaps, we introduce \textbf{GC4NC}, a comprehensive framework for evaluating diverse GC methods on node classification across multiple dimensions including performance, efficiency, privacy preservation, denoising ability, NAS effectiveness, and transferability. Our systematic evaluation offers novel insights into how condensed graphs behave and the critical design choices that drive their success. These findings pave the way for future advancements in GC methods, enhancing both performance and expanding their real-world applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/Emory-Melody/GraphSlim/tree/main/benchmark.

title: StarTrail: Concentric Ring Sequence Parallelism for Efficient Near-Infinite-Context Transformer Model Training
central_claim: StarTrail concentric ring sequence parallelism improves distributed Transformer training throughput by reducing P2P communication volume through sub-ring division, achieving up to 77.12% improvement on GPT-style models and 114.33% on DiT models.

mre_config: Smallest MRE: 8-GPU distributed training comparison of Ring Attention vs StarTrail on GPT-3B model (12 heads, 16 layers, hidden dim 4096) with 128K sequence length, batch size 1, bfloat16 precision. Metric: throughput in tokens/second. Should show StarTrail achieving higher throughput than Ring Attention baseline.

Use random/synthetic input tokens. Report throughput ratio to confirm the paper's claim of improvement.

The NeurIPS checklist explicitly states: 'Our code is not currently available publicly, but we will prepare for open-source if accepted.' OpenReview supplement status is 'missing'. Per paper: 'During training, both models use bfloat16 precision and a batch size of 1 to accommodate longer input sequences.' No custom dataset required - MRE benchmark uses synthetic token sequences to measure training throughput.

abstract: Training Transformer models on long sequences in a distributed setting poses significant challenges in terms of efficiency and scalability. Current methods are either constrained by the number of attention heads or excessive communication overheads. To address this problem, we propose StarTrail, a multi-dimensional concentric distributed training system for long sequences, fostering an efficient communication paradigm and providing additional tuning flexibility for communication arrangements. Specifically, StarTrail introduces an extra parallel dimension and divides the peer-to-peer communication into sub-rings to substantially reduce communication volume and avoid bandwidth bottlenecks. Through comprehensive experiments across diverse hardware environments and on both Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computer Vision (CV) tasks, we demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses state-of-the-art methods that support Long sequence lengths, achieving performance improvements of up to 77.12% on GPT-style models and up to 114.33% on DiT (Diffusion Transformer) models without affecting the computations results.

title: Distributionally Robust Performative Optimization
central_claim: The distributionally robust performative optimization (DRPO) framework with the repeated robust risk minimization algorithm significantly outperforms non-robust baselines and AMKL on out-of-sample performance in performative prediction tasks.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'Extensive numerical experiments in strategic classification, revenue management, and portfolio optimization demonstrate significant performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines.' Figure 1 shows box plots of 50 independent trials where robust models (type-1 and type-2 Wasserstein) outperform both the non-robust baseline and AMKL in out-of-sample classification accuracy.
mre_config: Strategic classification with logistic regression on a class-balanced subset of the Give Me Some Credit Kaggle dataset. Setup: 200 training samples, ~3600 test samples, 40 iterations, robust parameter rho=0.1. Metric: out-of-sample classification accuracy. Comparison: robust (Wasserstein type-1 and type-2), non-robust baseline, and AMKL. Algorithm: Repeated robust risk minimization solving Tikhonov regularized logistic regression at each iteration.
agent_task: Reproduce the strategic classification experiment from Figure 1. 1) Download the Give Me Some Credit dataset from Kaggle (https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/GiveMeSomeCredit/data). 2) Create a class-balanced subset of 200 training samples and ~3600 test samples. 3) Implement the strategic classification setting: individuals linearly modify their features with x'_S = x_S - epsilon * theta_S where epsilon>0 is a sensitivity parameter. 4) Implement the repeated robust risk minimization algorithm: at each iteration t, solve the Tikhonov regularized logistic regression min_theta E_hatP(theta_t)[log(1+exp(-x*theta*y))] + rho*L*||(theta,1)||_2^2 for rho=0.1, L=1 (logistic loss Lipschitz constant), using the updated distribution at each step. 5) Run 40 iterations comparing robust type-1 Wasserstein, robust type-2 Wasserstein, non-robust baseline, and AMKL. 6) Report out-of-sample classification accuracy across 50 independent trials. Verify that robust methods outperform non-robust baseline as shown in Figure 1.

The paper's NeurIPS checklist states 'The code is available upon request.' No public code repository, no bundled OpenReview supplement, and no HuggingFace model repo verified.

Kaggle competition page verified accessible at https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/GiveMeSomeCredit/data. While the exact subset and data splits used in the paper are not released, the underlying dataset is publicly available.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: The Give Me Some Credit dataset is a well-known Kaggle competition dataset from 2011 that has been widely used as a standard credit scoring benchmark in machine learning and performative prediction literature (Perdomo et al. 2020 introduced it as the default dataset for performative prediction).

For the MRE (logistic regression, 200 training samples, 40 iterations, 50 trials), this is a small-scale CPU-based optimization problem. Rough estimate: ~2 H100-hours equivalent on CPU. abstract: In performative stochastic optimization, decisions can influence the distribution of random parameters, rendering the data-generating process itself decision-dependent. In practice, decision-makers rarely have access to the true distribution map and must instead rely on imperfect surrogate models, which can lead to severely suboptimal solutions under misspecification. Data scarcity or costly collection further exacerbates these challenges in real-world settings. To address these challenges, we propose a distributionally robust framework for performative optimization that explicitly accounts for ambiguity in the decision-dependent distribution. Our framework introduces three modeling paradigms that capture a broad range of applications in machine learning and decision-making under uncertainty. This latter setting has not previously been explored in the performative optimization literature. To tackle the intractability of the resulting nonconvex objectives, we develop an iterative algorithm named repeated robust risk minimization, which alternates between solving a decision-independent distributionally robust optimization problem and updating the ambiguity set based on the previous decision. This decoupling ensures computational tractability at each iteration while enhancing robustness to model uncertainty. We provide reformulations compatible with off-the-shelf solvers and establish theoretical guarantees on convergence and suboptimality. Extensive numerical experiments in strategic classification, revenue management, and portfolio optimization demonstrate significant …

title: Convex Approximation of Two-Layer ReLU Networks for Hidden State Differential Privacy
central_claim: The paper demonstrates that noisy cyclic mini-batch gradient descent (NoisyCGD) applied to a stochastic convex approximation of two-layer ReLU networks achieves privacy-utility trade-offs comparable to DP-SGD applied to 2-layer ReLU networks for hidden state differential privacy.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'We demonstrate that it is possible to privately train convex problems with privacy-utility trade-offs comparable to those of 2-layer ReLU networks trained with DP stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD).' Table 1 shows MNIST results: DP-SGD + Convex Approximation achieves 93.1±0.1% at ε=1.33 vs DP-SGD + ReLU at 91.7±0.1%.
mre_config: MNIST 10-class classification comparing NoisyCGD + convex approximation vs DP-SGD + 2-layer ReLU. Run Conv_relus_MNIST.py with parameters: beta=0.01, lr=0.00031, sigma=5.0, batch_size=1024, P=100 (or use scripts/run_mnist_5.sh for σ=5.0). Compare test accuracy to Table 1 baseline of ~93% at ε=1.33 (δ=10⁻⁵). Dataset: MNIST via torchvision. Training: 400 epochs, cross-entropy loss.

This trains the convex model for 400 epochs. Report test accuracy at ε=1.33 (δ=10⁻⁵). The baseline to match from Table 1 is ~93.1% (±0.1). Compare against DP-SGD + ReLU baseline (~91.7%). The central claim is that convex approximation + NoisyCGD should match or exceed DP-SGD + ReLU accuracy.

Based on comparable MNIST DP-SGD experiments, 400 epochs on 60k samples with batch size 1024 would require ~59 batches per epoch = ~23,600 total steps. Estimated ~2 H100-hours for a single MRE run. Paper reports experiments on 8 RTX 3090 GPUs for ~3 days for full hyperparameter tuning (multiple runs), but the basic MRE single run is much cheaper.
abstract: The hidden state threat model of differential privacy (DP) assumes that the adversary has access only to the final trained machine learning (ML) model, without seeing intermediate states during training. However, the current privacy analyses under this model are restricted to convex optimization problems, reducing their applicability to multi-layer neural networks, which are essential in modern deep learning applications. Notably, the most successful applications of the hidden state privacy analyses in classification tasks have only been for logistic regression models. We demonstrate that it is possible to privately train convex problems with privacy-utility trade-offs comparable to those of 2-layer ReLU networks trained with DP stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD). This is achieved through a stochastic approximation of a dual formulation of the ReLU minimization problem, resulting in a strongly convex problem. This enables the use of existing hidden state privacy analyses and provides accurate privacy bounds also for the noisy cyclic mini-batch gradient descent (NoisyCGD) method with fixed disjoint mini-batches. Empirical results on benchmark classification tasks demonstrate that NoisyCGD can achieve privacy-utility trade-offs on par with DP-SGD applied to 2-layer ReLU networks.

title: Adv-SSL: Adversarial Self-Supervised Representation Learning with Theoretical Guarantees
central_claim: Adv-SSL (Adversarial Self-Supervised Representation Learning) achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10 (93.01% linear probe, 90.97% k-NN), CIFAR-100 (68.94% linear probe, 58.50% k-NN), and Tiny ImageNet (50.21% linear probe, 37.40% k-NN), outperforming existing SSL methods through an unbiased mini-max optimization approach.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'Our approach not only outperforms the existing methods across multiple benchmark datasets but is also supported by comprehensive end-to-end theoretical guarantees.' Table 1 in the paper shows CIFAR-10 Linear 93.01%, CIFAR-100 Linear 68.94%, and Tiny ImageNet Linear 50.21% for Adv-SSL, substantially exceeding Barlow Twins baselines.
mre_config: Train Adv-SSL on CIFAR-10 for 1000 epochs using ResNet-18 encoder (embedding size 512), linear probe evaluation. Command: `python -m train --dataset cifar10`. Expected result: ~93% top-1 accuracy with linear classifier. Tolerance: ±2% to account for variance.

(3) Evaluate with linear probe: `python -m test --dataset cifar10 --fname=<checkpoint_path> --clf=sgd`. (4) Verify top-1 accuracy reaches ~93% (±2%). Note: No pretrained checkpoints provided; full 1000-epoch training from scratch is required.

abstract: Learning transferable data representations from abundant unlabeled data remains a central challenge in machine learning. Although numerous self-supervised learning methods have been proposed to address this challenge, a significant class of these approaches aligns the covariance or correlation matrix with the identity matrix. Despite impressive performance across various downstream tasks, these methods often suffer from biased sample risk, leading to substantial optimization shifts in mini-batch settings and complicating theoretical analysis. In this paper, we introduce a novel \underline{\bf Adv}ersarial \underline{\bf S}elf-\underline{\bf S}upervised Representation \underline{\bf L}earning (Adv-SSL) for unbiased transfer learning with no additional cost compared to its biased counterparts. Our approach not only outperforms the existing methods across multiple benchmark datasets but is also supported by comprehensive end-to-end theoretical guarantees. Our analysis reveals that the minimax optimization in Adv-SSL encourages representations to form well-separated clusters in the embedding space, provided there is sufficient upstream unlabeled data. As a result, our method achieves strong classification performance even with limited downstream labels, shedding new light on few-shot learning.

title: Unifying Symbolic Music Arrangement: Track-Aware Reconstruction and Structured Tokenization

abstract: We present a unified framework for automatic multitrack music arrangement that enables a single pre-trained symbolic music model to handle diverse arrangement scenarios, including reinterpretation, simplification, and additive generation. At its core is a segment-level reconstruction objective operating on token-level disentangled content and style, allowing for flexible any-to-any instrumentation transformations at inference time. To support track-wise modeling, we introduce REMI-z, a structured tokenization scheme for multitrack symbolic music that enhances modeling efficiency and effectiveness for both arrangement tasks and unconditional generation. Our method outperforms task-specific state-of-the-art models on representative tasks in different arrangement scenarios -- band arrangement, piano reduction, and drum arrangement, in both objective metrics and perceptual evaluations. Taken together, our framework demonstrates strong generality and suggests broader applicability in symbolic music-to-music transformation.

title: Linguini: A benchmark for language-agnostic linguistic reasoning

abstract: We propose a new benchmark to measure a language model's linguistic reasoning skills without relying on pre-existing language-specific knowledge. The test covers 894 questions grouped in 160 problems across 75 (mostly) extremely low-resource languages, extracted from the International Linguistic Olympiad corpus. To attain high accuracy on this benchmark, models don't need previous knowledge of the tested language, as all the information needed to solve the linguistic puzzle is presented in the context. We find that, while all analyzed models rank below 25% accuracy, there is a significant gap between open and closed models, with the best-performing proprietary model at 24.05% and the best-performing open model at 8.84%.

title: TopER: Topological Embeddings in Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Graph embeddings play a critical role in graph representation learning, allowing machine learning models to explore and interpret graph-structured data. However, existing methods often rely on opaque, high-dimensional embeddings, limiting interpretability and practical visualization. In this work, we introduce Topological Evolution Rate (TopER), a novel, low-dimensional embedding approach grounded in topological data analysis. TopER simplifies a key topological approach, Persistent Homology, by calculating the evolution rate of graph substructures, resulting in intuitive and interpretable visualizations of graph data. This approach not only enhances the exploration of graph datasets but also delivers competitive performance in graph clustering and classification tasks. Our TopER-based models achieve or surpass state-of-the-art results across molecular, biological, and social network datasets in tasks such as classification, clustering, and visualization.

abstract: Watermarking has emerged as a crucial method to distinguish AI-generated text from human-created text. Current watermarking approaches often lack formal optimality guarantees or address the scheme and detector design separately. In this paper, we introduce a novel, unified theoretical framework for watermarking Large Language Models (LLMs) that jointly optimizes both the watermarking scheme and detector. Our approach aims to maximize detection performance while maintaining control over the worst-case false positive rate (FPR) and distortion on text quality. We derive closed-form optimal solutions for this joint design and characterize the fundamental trade-off between watermark detectability and distortion. Notably, we reveal that the optimal watermarking schemes should be adaptive to the LLM's generative distribution. Building on our theoretical insights, we propose a distortion-free, distribution-adaptive watermarking algorithm (DAWA) that leverages a surrogate model for model-agnosticism and efficiency. Experiments on Llama2-13B and Mistral-8$\times$7B models confirm the effectiveness of our approach, particularly at ultra-low FPRs. Our code is available at https://github.com/yepengliu/DAWA.

title: Simplicity Prevails: Rethinking Negative Preference Optimization for LLM Unlearning
central_claim: SimNPO removes the reference model from NPO-based unlearning, simplifying the optimization and eliminating reference model bias that undermines NPO effectiveness on varying-difficulty forget data
claim_evidence: The WMDP implementation in GA.py shows SimNPO computes loss purely from current model output: log sigmoid applied to beta * current_forget_loss without any reference model term. In contrast, NPO_FT computes neg_log_ratios = current_forget_loss - ref_forget_loss using a frozen reference model. The TOFU forget.yaml configures simnpo_grad_diff with ref_policy='fine_tuned', but the core SimNPO equation in the WMDP model card shows: -2/beta * log sigma(-beta/|y|*log pi_theta(y|x) - gamma), which uses only current model probabilities. The paper's Mixture of Markov Chains analysis supports why removing reference model dependence improves robustness.
mre_config: 7B parameter causal LMs (Llama-2-7b-chat for TOFU, zephyr-7b-beta for WMDP, Mistral-7B variants) fine-tuned then unlearned with SimNPO against forget data subsets while retaining remaining data

Total including hyperparameter sweeps and eval: ~15 H100-hours.
abstract: This work studies the problem of large language model (LLM) unlearning, aiming to remove unwanted data influences (e.g., copyrighted or harmful content) while preserving model utility. Despite the increasing demand for unlearning, a technically-grounded optimization framework is lacking. Gradient ascent (GA)-type methods, though widely used, are suboptimal as they reverse the learning process without controlling optimization divergence (i.e., deviation from the pre-trained state), leading to risks of over-forgetting and potential model collapse. Negative preference optimization (NPO) has been proposed to address this issue and is considered one of the state-of-the-art LLM unlearning approaches. In this work, we revisit NPO and identify another critical issue: reference model bias. This bias arises from using the reference model (i.e., the model prior to unlearning) to evaluate the unlearning success, which can compromise NPO's effectiveness. Specifically, it leads to (a) uneven allocation of optimization power across forget data with varying difficulty levels and (b) ineffective gradient weight smoothing during the early stages of unlearning optimization. To overcome these challenges, we propose a simple yet effective unlearning optimization framework, called SimNPO, showing that `simplicity' in removing the reliance on a reference model (through the lens of simple preference optimization) benefits unlearning. We provide deeper insights into SimNPO's advantages through an analysis based on mixtures of Markov chains. Extensive experiments further validate SimNPO's efficacy …

title: Learning Orthogonal Multi-Index Models: A Fine-Grained Information Exponent Analysis
central_claim: Online SGD can learn orthogonal multi-index models with sample complexity O(d P^{L-1}) by leveraging both second-order and higher-order Hermite terms, improving over vanilla information exponent analysis which gives O(d^{L-1}).
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'In this work, we show that by considering both second- and higher-order terms, we can first learn the relevant space using the second-order terms, and then the exact directions using the higher-order terms, and the overall sample and complexity of online SGD is O(d P^{L-1}).' The simulation section (Appendix) provides empirical validation with P=5 and varying d to show linear d-scaling.
mre_config: Train a two-layer network with width m = O(P^2) on synthetic Gaussian data N(0, I_d) with target function f_*(x) = sum_{k=1}^P phi(v_k* · x) where phi = h_2 + h_4 (Hermite polynomials) and {v_k*} are orthonormal. Use online spherical SGD with learning rate eta ~ c/d. Track correlation of each neuron with ground truth directions over training. MRE: P=5, d in {50, 100, 200, 500}, m ~ 25, early stopping when max_k v_{p,k}^2 >= 0.95. Verify that correlations converge and that convergence time scales linearly with d.
agent_task: Reproduce the core simulation demonstrating that online SGD learns orthogonal multi-index models with linear d-scaling. Steps: (1) Generate synthetic data x ~ N(0, I_d) for d in {50, 100, 200}; (2) Initialize P=5 orthonormal ground truth directions v_k*; (3) Define target function f_*(x) = sum_{k=1}^5 (h_2(v_k*·x) + h_4(v_k*·x)) using normalized Hermite polynomials h_2(x)=x^2-1 and h_4(x)=x^4-6x^2+3; (4) Initialize m=O(P^2)=25 neurons with symmetric initialization (v_i ~ Unif(S^{d-1}), v_{i+P} = -v_i); (5) Train with online spherical SGD: v_{t+1} = normalize(v_t + eta * f_*(x_t) * grad_phi(v_t·x_t)), with phi' as derivative, eta ~ c/d for small constant c; (6) Track correlation c_{p,i} = |<v_i, e_p>| over training steps; (7) Verify neurons converge to ground truth directions (max correlation >= 0.95) and that iteration count required scales linearly with d. Paper states experiments ran to completion in less than one day on laptop without GPU.

abstract: The information exponent ([BAGJ21]) and its extensions -- which are equivalent to the lowest degree in the Hermite expansion of the link function (after a potential label transform) for Gaussian single-index models -- have played an important role in predicting the sample complexity of online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in various learning tasks. In this work, we demonstrate that, for multi-index models, focusing solely on the lowest degree can miss key structural details of the model and result in suboptimal rates. Specifically, we consider the task of learning target functions of form $f_*(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{k=1}^{P} φ(\mathbf{v}_k^* \cdot \mathbf{x})$, where $P \ll d$, the ground-truth directions $\{ \mathbf{v}_k^* \}_{k=1}^P$ are orthonormal, and the information exponent of $φ$ is $L$. Based on the theory of information exponent, when $L = 2$, only the relevant subspace (not the exact directions) can be recovered due to the rotational invariance of the second-order terms, and when $L > 2$, recovering the directions using online SGD require $\tilde{O}(P d^{L-1})$ samples. In this work, we show that by considering both second- and higher-order terms, we can first learn the relevant space using the second-order terms, and then the exact directions using the higher-order terms, and the overall sample and complexity of online SGD is $\tilde{O}( d P^{L-1} )$.

abstract: Time series data is prevalent across numerous fields, necessitating the development of robust and accurate forecasting models. Capturing patterns both within and between temporal and multivariate components is crucial for reliable predictions. We introduce xLSTM-Mixer, a model designed to effectively integrate temporal sequences, joint time-variate information, and multiple perspectives for robust forecasting. Our approach begins with a linear forecast shared across variates, which is then refined by xLSTM blocks. They serve as key elements for modeling the complex dynamics of challenging time series data. xLSTM-Mixer ultimately reconciles two distinct views to produce the final forecast. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate its superior long-term forecasting performance compared to recent state-of-the-art methods while requiring very little memory. A thorough model analysis provides further insights into its key components and confirms its robustness and effectiveness. This work contributes to the resurgence of recurrent models in forecasting by combining them, for the first time, with mixing architectures.

title: Small Singular Values Matter: A Random Matrix Analysis of Transformer Models
central_claim: Small singular values (decile 1) in transformer weight matrices contain more important information than larger bulk singular values, as measured by perplexity increase when deciles are removed.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'zeroing out the singular values that deviate from RMT raises language-model perplexity far more than removing values from the bulk, and after fine-tuning the smallest decile can be the third most influential part of the spectrum.' Figure 5 (NeurIPS_plot5.pdf): Perplexity increase when removing singular value deciles from Pythia and Llama, showing decile 1 is more important than larger deciles for non-square matrices.
mre_config: Pythia-410m-deduped on WikiText: Load model from HuggingFace (EleutherAI/pythia-410m-deduped), compute SVD on one non-square weight matrix (e.g., Up-Projection or Down-Projection), group singular values into 10 deciles, remove decile 1 (smallest 10%), reconstruct matrix, measure perplexity increase on WikiText test split, verify that removing decile 1 causes larger perplexity increase than removing mid-range deciles (e.g., deciles 3-6).
agent_task: Reproduce a minimal version of Figure 5 (NeurIPS_plot5.pdf): (1) Load EleutherAI/pythia-410m-deduped from HuggingFace. (2) Select one non-square weight matrix type (Up-Projection or Down-Projection) from a middle layer (e.g., layer 10). (3) Compute SVD of the weight matrix to obtain singular values and vectors. (4) Group rank-ordered singular values into 10 equal-size deciles (decile 1 = smallest 10%). (5) Zero out decile 1, reconstruct the weight matrix using original singular vectors, and replace the layer weight. (6) Compute perplexity on WikiText test split using the modified model. (7) Verify that perplexity increases more when removing decile 1 than when removing deciles 3-6 (e.g., ΔPPL_decile1 > ΔPPL_decile5). (8) Compare magnitude to paper's Figure 5 which shows decile 1 is the second most important decile for Down-Projection matrix.
