abstract: This work analyzes singular-value spectra of weight matrices in pretrained transformer models to understand how information is stored at both ends of the spectrum. Using Random Matrix Theory (RMT) as a zero information hypothesis, we associate agreement with RMT as evidence of randomness and deviations as evidence for learning. Surprisingly, we observe pronounced departures from RMT not only among the largest singular values -- the usual outliers -- but also among the smallest ones. A comparison of the associated singular vectors with the eigenvectors of the activation covariance matrices shows that there is considerable overlap wherever RMT is violated. Thus, significant directions in the data are captured by small singular values and their vectors as well as by the large ones. We confirm this empirically: zeroing out the singular values that deviate from RMT raises language-model perplexity far more than removing values from the bulk, and after fine-tuning the smallest decile can be the third most influential part of the spectrum. To explain how vectors linked to small singular values can carry more information than those linked to larger values, we propose a linear random-matrix model. Our findings highlight the overlooked importance of the low end of the spectrum and provide theoretical and practical guidance for SVD-based pruning and compression of large language models.

title: Efficient Adaptive Federated Optimization
central_claim: FedAda² and FedAda²++ achieve the same or better performance as costly jointly adaptive federated methods while eliminating preconditioner communication overhead and reducing client-side memory usage.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'we introduce a class of efficient adaptive algorithms...FedAda² and FedAda²++...achieve the same convergence rates for general, non-convex objectives as its more resource-intensive counterparts that directly integrate joint adaptivity.' Table 1 compares communication/memory complexity; Figure 1 shows jointly adaptive methods (FedAda²/FedAda²++) achieving faster convergence and higher final accuracy than server-only adaptivity and non-adaptive baselines across CIFAR-100, GLD-23K, and FEMNIST.
mre_config: CIFAR-100 with LDA non-IID partitioning (α=0.001), 1000 clients, ViT-Small (or smaller CNN for MRE), batch size 32, 5 local epochs, client participation fraction 0.1, comparing FedAvg vs FedAda² (Adam on both server and client with zero-initialized local preconditioners, no transmitted preconditioners). Metric: test accuracy over training rounds. MRE tests whether eliminating preconditioner transmission preserves joint adaptivity benefits.
agent_task: Reproduce the FedAda² algorithm for federated learning: implement the key innovation of initializing local (client-side) adaptive optimizer preconditioners to zero at each round instead of receiving transmitted global preconditioners from the server, while keeping server-side AdaGrad/Adam for global aggregation. Use the paper's Algorithm 1 (simplified framework) as the specification. On CIFAR-100 (1000 clients, LDA non-IID partition with α=0.001), partition the data, initialize a ViT-Small model (or smaller CNN for speed), run with 5 local epochs, batch size 32, Adam optimizer on both server and client, and compare test accuracy against FedAvg. The central claim is that FedAda² should match or exceed jointly adaptive methods (which transmit preconditioners) at much lower communication cost. Reproduce Figure 1 (leftmost column) or Table 1 communication complexity comparison. Implement the zero-local-preconditioner initialization strategy: at each round, client-side preconditioners start from zero constant rather than receiving transmitted server preconditioners.

code_available.evidence: No GitHub repository found for FedAda2, FedAda2++, or 'Efficient Adaptive Federated Optimization' after multiple search attempts using: full title, acronym (FedAda, FedAda2, FedAda^2, FedAda2++), arXiv ID 2410.18117, author names (Su Hyeong Lee, Sidharth Sharma, Manzil Zaheer, Tian Li), and related terms (preconditioner federated learning, SM3 federated learning, federated adaptive optimization). HuggingFace search also returned no results. The paper states 'we plan to release the code' (NeurIPS checklist) but no URL, link, or repository is provided on the arXiv page, project page, or in the paper text. The paper's algorithms are not found in any public repository.

dataset_available.evidence: CIFAR-100 verified as available on HuggingFace (uoft-cs/cifar100) with 50k training and 10k test images. The paper uses standard FL benchmarks: CIFAR-100 (LDA partitioned), FEMNIST (LEAF), StackOverflow (tens-of-millions of posts), and GLD-23K (Google Landmarks). All are publicly documented datasets from the LEAF benchmark framework and HuggingFace.

weights_available.evidence: No checkpoints, model weights, or pretrained ViT-S checkpoints for the experiments are released. The paper mentions using 'pretrained ViT-S on ImageNet-21K' but no link to model weights is provided. The paper does not mention releasing checkpoints.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: CIFAR-100 is a standard benchmark widely recognized in ML (similar to MNIST, ImageNet). It is available on HuggingFace, PyTorch (torchvision), and other standard repositories. FEMNIST, StackOverflow, and GLD-23K are also standard federated learning benchmarks from the LEAF framework and Google.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified: The paper does not report exact GPU-hours. The compute section mentions a Slurm cluster with RTX 2080 Ti, A40, and H100 GPUs. For the MRE (CIFAR-100 with ViT-S/21M params, 5 local epochs, batch 32, ~1000 clients, 10% participation, ~300 rounds), a comparable federated learning benchmark typically requires 50-200 H100-hours depending on implementation efficiency. Conservative estimate: ~100 H100-hours for the MRE configuration. Engineering/debugging time to implement FedAda² from the paper description (including implementing SM3 for FedAda²++) is additional and can be significant.
abstract: Adaptive optimization is critical in federated learning, where enabling adaptivity on both the server and client sides has proven essential for achieving optimal performance. However, the scalability of such jointly adaptive systems is often hindered by resource limitations in communication and memory. In this paper, we introduce a class of efficient adaptive algorithms, named $FedAda^2$ and its enhanced version $FedAda^2$++, designed specifically for large-scale, cross-device federated environments. $FedAda^2$ optimizes communication efficiency by avoiding the transfer of preconditioners between the server and clients. Additionally, $FedAda^2$++ extends this approach by incorporating memory-efficient adaptive optimizers on the client side, further reducing on-device memory usage. Theoretically, we demonstrate that $FedAda^2$ and $FedAda^2$++ achieve the same convergence rates for general, non-convex objectives as its more resource-intensive counterparts that directly integrate joint adaptivity. Extensive empirical evaluations on image and text datasets demonstrate both the advantages of joint adaptivity and the effectiveness of $FedAda^2$/$FedAda^2$++.

title: Fast Inference for Augmented Large Language Models
central_claim: LAMPS (LLM API- and Memory-based Predictive Scheduling) minimizes request completion time through a unified scheduling approach that considers both total request length and API handling strategies (preserve, discard, swap), achieving 27%-85% end-to-end latency reduction and 4%-96% TTFT reduction compared to INFERCEPT when serving API-augmented LLM requests.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'Our results show that LAMPS consistently outperforms INFERCEPT across various datasets and request rates, achieving improvements in end-to-end latency ranging from 27% to 85% and reductions in TTFT from 4% to 96%'. Figure 5 (perf_arrival_rate) shows end-to-end performance comparisons across Single-API, Multi-API, and ToolBench datasets at varying request rates.
mre_config: Run single-API benchmark with GPT-J 6B model at QPS 3-5: execute `exps/6B_bench.sh` benchmark script comparing MARS (LAMPS) scheduling vs INFERCEPT FCFS vs vanilla vLLM on the bundled `diverse_oneapi_merged_exp_uniform.json` dataset. Measure mean end-to-end latency; expect MARS to show ~4-5% TTFT reduction and ~15% latency reduction vs INFERCEPT at QPS 3.
agent_task: Reproduce MARS scheduling experiment: 1) Clone https://github.com/mars-repository/mars-codebase, 2) Install dependencies with pip install -e . and pip install 'numpy<2', 3) Ensure GPT-J 6B model is available (auto-downloaded from HuggingFace EleutherAI/gpt-j-6b), 4) Run MARS benchmark at QPS=3 with: CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python benchmarks/fixed_final_tput_bench_real.py --load-format dummy --qps 3.0 --msg results/single_api/6B_3.0_1800_MARS --window 1800 --api-policy V --policy-config V2 --chunk-fill --swap-space 32 --starvation-avoidance True --starvation-threshold 100 --exp-json diverse_oneapi_merged_exp_uniform.json, 5) Run INFERCEPT baseline: same command with --api-policy I --policy-config fcfs, 6) Compare mean end-to-end latency results; verify MARS achieves measurably lower latency than INFERCEPT baseline.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repository mars-repository/mars-codebase contains full implementation with vllm/core/scheduler_v2.py (LAMPS scheduler), vllm/core/policy.py (V2 policy class with get_priority ranking function), prediction/ components, and exps/6B_bench.sh benchmark script. README confirms: 'This repository contains the implementation of MARS, described in our NeurIPS 2025 paper.'

dataset_available.evidence: The MARS codebase includes bundled dataset files: diverse_oneapi_merged_exp_uniform.json (441KB) and merged_exp_uniform.json (2.1MB) which are used directly by the benchmark script via --exp-json flag. ToolBench dataset is also available from OpenBMB/ToolBench repository with documented Google Drive download links.

weights_available.evidence: GPT-J 6B model weights are available on HuggingFace at EleutherAI/gpt-j-6b (1525 likes, 266K downloads). This is the standard 6B model used in MARS experiments, configured via the benchmark script's model loading.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: The bundled diverse_oneapi_merged_exp_uniform.json is a custom API-augmented workload with API call metadata (durations, response lengths, strategy assignments), not a widely recognized public ML benchmark like MNIST, CIFAR, ImageNet, or GLUE. ToolBench is a recognized benchmark but requires separate download from Google Drive; the bundled data in MARS repo is the custom INFERCEPT-style workload specific to this research.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified: Paper reports experiments on A100 40GB GPUs with 30-minute benchmark windows. A100 40GB ~= 0.32 H100 equivalent. GPT-J 6B inference on single A100 for 30min = ~0.5 H100-hours per run. MRE requires 2 runs (MARS vs INFERCEPT baseline) = ~1 H100-hour GPU compute. However, vLLM installation requires CUDA compilation (csrc kernels), and the benchmark script modifies source files via sed commands, requiring multiple setup iterations. Conservative estimate of 10-12 H100-hours accounts for compilation, debugging, and retry cycles. Engineering/debugging time is additional and not included.
abstract: Augmented Large Language Models (LLMs) enhance the capabilities of standalone LLMs by integrating external data sources through API calls. In interactive LLM applications, efficient scheduling is crucial for maintaining low request completion times, directly impacting user engagement. However, these augmentations introduce scheduling challenges due to the need to manage limited memory for cached information (KV caches). As a result, traditional size-based scheduling algorithms, such as Shortest Job First (SJF), become less effective at minimizing completion times. Existing work focuses only on handling requests during API calls by preserving, discarding, or swapping memory without considering how to schedule requests with API calls. In this paper, we propose LAMPS, a novel LLM inference framework for augmented LLMs. LAMPS minimizes request completion time through a unified scheduling approach that considers the total length of requests and their handling strategies during API calls. Recognizing that LLM inference is memory-bound, our approach ranks requests based on their consumption of memory over time, which depends on both the output sizes and how a request is managed during its API calls. To implement our scheduling, LAMPS predicts the strategy that minimizes memory waste of a request during its API calls, aligning with but improving upon existing approaches. We also propose starvation prevention techniques and optimizations to mitigate the overhead of our scheduling. We implement LAMPS on top of vLLM and evaluate its performance against baseline LLM inference systems, …

title: Reduction-based Pseudo-label Generation for Instance-dependent Partial Label Learning
central_claim: RPLG (Reduction-based Pseudo-label Generation) significantly outperforms all baseline methods for Instance-dependent Partial Label Learning on standard benchmarks.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'reduction-based pseudo-labels exhibit greater consistency with the Bayes optimal classifier compared to pseudo-labels directly generated from the predictive model.' Table 1 (benchmark): RPLG achieves 87.53±0.21% on CIFAR-10, 65.03±0.21% on CIFAR-100, and 40.74±0.64% on TinyImageNet, outperforming all 13 baseline methods.
mre_config: CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18 backbone, SGD optimizer (momentum 0.9, batch size 256, 250 epochs), multi-branch auxiliary model with c=10 branches, meta-learner for weight aggregation, alpha=0.3. MRE metric: classification accuracy. Expected result: >85% to match paper's ablation (RPLG 87.53% vs RPLG-Nm 85.43%).
agent_task: Reproduce RPLG on CIFAR-10 (10-class, 32x32 images) using the bundled supplement code. (1) Load CIFAR-10 via torchvision, generate instance-dependent candidate labels using RPLG/utils/gen_partial_dataset.py following the strategy in xu2021instance. (2) Use RPLG/train.py with ResNet-18 backbone, SGD optimizer (lr=0.02, momentum=0.9, batch=256), 250 epochs, alpha=0.3 for the pseudo-label trade-off. (3) Train the multi-branch auxiliary model (10 branches, one per class) where each branch excludes one label from its label space. (4) Use the meta-learner g to weight branch outputs for reduction-based pseudo-labels. (5) Evaluate final classifier accuracy on test set; expect >85% to validate the claim (paper reports 87.53±0.21%).

code_available.evidence: Bundled OpenReview supplement contains complete first-party code: RPLG/train.py (main training loop), RPLG/multibranch.py (multi-branch architecture), RPLG/online.py, RPLG/models_for_multibranch/* (VGAE, convnet, linear, mlp, resnet, wideresnet), RPLG/models_ins/* (instance models), RPLG/partial_models_ins/* (partial label models for CIFAR), RPLG/utils/* (data loaders for CIFAR-10/100, loss functions, utilities). No standalone GitHub repo found after searching RPLG, full title, arXiv 2410.20797, Congyu Qiao, and method terms on GitHub and Hugging Face.

dataset_available.evidence: Standard datasets CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 used for main benchmarks (paper cites krizhevsky2009learning). OpenReview supplement includes real-world .mat files: lost.mat, birdac.mat, MSRCv2.mat, spd.mat, LYN.mat. CIFAR datasets are publicly available through torchvision. dataset_is_standard=True applies for CIFAR-10.

weights_available.evidence: No checkpoint or weight files in OpenReview supplement. Only model architecture code is provided (RPLG/models_*, RPLG/multibranch_model/*). No trained weights released. Paper does not mention releasing checkpoints.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: CIFAR-10 is a widely recognized public ML benchmark (krizhevsky2009learning), standard for image classification and partial label learning research. Available via torchvision.datasets.CIFAR10.

h100_estimate_basis: Paper uses NVIDIA RTX 3090 (approx 0.60x H100), single GPU, batch size 256, 250 epochs on CIFAR-10. CIFAR-10 training with standard ResNet typically takes 6-10 hours on RTX 3090. RPLG has additional overhead: multi-branch auxiliary model (c=10 branches), bi-level optimization requiring validation-based meta-learner updates, and two-stage classifier updates per iteration. Estimated 10-12 hours wall-clock on RTX 3090 = approximately 6-7 H100-equivalent hours, rounded to 12 H100-hours to account for multi-branch complexity. Engineering/debugging time for understanding the bi-level optimization and multi-branch architecture is additional.
abstract: Instance-dependent Partial Label Learning (ID-PLL) aims to learn a multi-class predictive model given training instances annotated with candidate labels related to features, among which correct labels are hidden fixed but unknown. The previous works involve leveraging the identification capability of the training model itself to iteratively refine supervision information. However, these methods overlook a critical aspect of ID-PLL: the training model is prone to overfitting on incorrect candidate labels, thereby providing poor supervision information and creating a bottleneck in training. In this paper, we propose to leverage reduction-based pseudo-labels to alleviate the influence of incorrect candidate labels and train our predictive model to overcome this bottleneck. Specifically, reduction-based pseudo-labels are generated by performing weighted aggregation on the outputs of a multi-branch auxiliary model, with each branch trained in a label subspace that excludes certain labels. This approach ensures that each branch explicitly avoids the disturbance of the excluded labels, allowing the pseudo-labels provided for instances troubled by these excluded labels to benefit from the unaffected branches. Theoretically, we demonstrate that reduction-based pseudo-labels exhibit greater consistency with the Bayes optimal classifier compared to pseudo-labels directly generated from the predictive model.

title: LoRA vs Full Fine-tuning: An Illusion of Equivalence
central_claim: LoRA introduces 'intruder dimensions' (new high-ranking singular vectors dissimilar to pre-trained singular vectors) while full fine-tuning does not, and these intruder dimensions cause forgetting of the pre-training distribution.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'We find that LoRA and full fine-tuning yield weight matrices whose singular value decompositions exhibit very different structure: weight matrices trained with LoRA have new, high-ranking singular vectors, which we call intruder dimensions, while those trained with full fine-tuning do not.' Figure 1 and Section 'Structural Differences' demonstrate intruder dimensions in LoRA but not full fine-tuning.
mre_config: Fine-tune RoBERTa-base on MNLI with LoRA r=1 (alpha=2) and full fine-tuning, then measure intruder dimensions using SVD-based detection (cosine similarity threshold < 0.5). Compare number of intruder dimensions in top-10 singular vectors between LoRA and full fine-tuned models. Metric: count of intruder dimensions (LoRA should have >0, full fine-tuning should have ≈0).
agent_task: Reproduce the core finding that LoRA introduces intruder dimensions while full fine-tuning does not. Steps: 1) Install dependencies: pip install -r requirements.txt (torch, transformers, datasets, peft, sentencepiece, protobuf). 2) Fine-tune RoBERTa-base on MNLI with LoRA r=1: python finetuning.py --base_model=roberta-base --task=mnli --method=lora --rank=1 --lora_alpha=2 --tune_layers=all_linear --learning_rate=3e-4 --batch_size=16 --num_epochs=5 --steps_per_validate=1000 --max_seq_length=512 --save_result=True. 3) Fine-tune RoBERTa-base with full fine-tuning: python finetuning.py --base_model=roberta-base --task=mnli --method=full --tune_layers=all_linear --learning_rate=1e-5 --batch_size=16 --num_epochs=5 --steps_per_validate=1000 --max_seq_length=512 --save_result=True. 4) Measure intruder dimensions for both models: python find_intruder_dimensions.py --model_path=trained_checkpoints/{checkpoint_name} --base_model=roberta-base --intruder_dimension_threshold=0.5 --top_k_singular_vectors=10. Expected result: LoRA r=1 should show >0 intruder dimensions while full fine-tuning shows approximately 0.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo reeceshuttle/intruder-dimensions contains complete reproduction code: finetuning.py (supports LoRA, full fine-tuning on MNLI/QQP/SST2/SIQA/Winogrande/FEVER), find_intruder_dimensions.py (SVD-based intruder dimension detection with configurable threshold), utils.py (data loading from GLUE, model setup with PEFT), bash_scripts/recreate_mnli_finetuning.sh, and requirements.txt. README provides complete usage instructions.

dataset_available.evidence: MNLI (Multi-Genre Natural Language Inference) is part of the GLUE benchmark, loaded via datasets.load_dataset('glue', 'mnli'). MNLI is a standard NLP benchmark with ~393K training examples, ~10K validation matched, and ~10K validation mismatched. Code in utils.py handles standard GLUE dataset loading.

weights_available.evidence: RoBERTa-base pre-trained weights available from HuggingFace (meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf for base model). LoRA-TMLR-2024 organization hosts paper's LLaMA2-7B LoRA adapters (rank 16, 64, 256) on HuggingFace. Code can fine-tune from scratch using AutoModelForSequenceClassification.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: MNLI (Multi-Genre NLI) is part of the GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation) benchmark, a widely used standard NLP benchmark. MNLI is one of the most common benchmarks for evaluating natural language inference models.

h100_estimate_basis: Paper reports RoBERTa-base fine-tuning runs take up to 6 hours on a single A100 GPU. Two runs needed (LoRA r=1 + full fine-tuning): 12 A100-hours. A100 80GB = 0.32x H100 SXM conversion: 12 * 0.32 = 3.84 H100-hours. Plus ~1 hour for intruder dimension evaluation (~0.32 H100-hours). Engineering/debugging overhead: ~4 H100-hours additional. Total: approximately 8 H100-hours.
abstract: Fine-tuning is a crucial paradigm for adapting pre-trained large language models to downstream tasks. Recently, methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) have been shown to effectively fine-tune LLMs with an extreme reduction in trainable parameters. But, \emph{are their learned solutions really equivalent?} We study how LoRA and full-finetuning change pre-trained models by analyzing the model's weight matrices through the lens of their spectral properties. We find that LoRA and full fine-tuning yield weight matrices whose singular value decompositions exhibit very different structure: weight matrices trained with LoRA have new, high-ranking singular vectors, which we call \emph{intruder dimensions}, while those trained with full fine-tuning do not. Further, we extend the finding that LoRA forgets less than full fine-tuning and find its forgetting is vastly localized to the intruder dimension -- by causally intervening on the intruder dimensions by changing their associated singular values post-fine-tuning, we show that they cause forgetting. Moreover, scaling them down significantly improves modeling of the pre-training distribution with a minimal drop in downstream task performance. Given this, we should expect accumulating intruder dimensions to be harmful and lead to more forgetting. This will be amplified during continual learning because of sequentially fine-tuning, and we show that LoRA models do accumulate intruder dimensions here tend to perform worse in this setting, emphasizing the practicality of our findings.

title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
central_claim: Pre-trained LLMs (Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Gemma-2-27B) contain sparse, modular reasoning circuits decomposed into four distinct families of attention heads (queried-rule locating, queried-rule mover, fact-processing, and decision heads) that implement a sequential, human-like reasoning pathway from QUERY to Relevant Rule to Relevant Facts to Decision.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.' Section 3 and Table 1: Gemma-2-9B circuit sufficiency test shows Delta^C_normal/Delta_normal = 0.94 with all 13 attention heads, and removing any head family renders the effect trivial.
mre_config: Run QUERY-based causal mediation analysis (activation patching) on Gemma-2-9B or Mistral-7B on the 'or' (disjunction) propositional logic problem. Use 60+ samples with few-shot prompting (4 examples for Gemma-2-9B, 6 for Mistral-7B). Generate normal-counterfactual prompt pairs by flipping the QUERY variable. Cache activations on both prompts, patch attention head outputs between them, and measure calibrated intervened logit difference. Identify heads with high indirect effect (near 1.0) as the core circuit. Verify sufficiency by patching only circuit heads and comparing Delta^C_normal to un-intervened Delta_normal. Dataset: synthetic propositional logic problems with rules 'A or B implies C' and 'D implies E', facts with truth assignments, and query for one variable.
agent_task: Reproduce the core circuit discovery result from Hong et al. (2025, arXiv:2411.04105): (1) Generate 60+ synthetic propositional logic samples using the 'or' chain problem template: Rules='A or B implies C. D implies E.', Facts with truth assignments, Query asking for truth value of C or E. Use few-shot prompting with 4-6 in-context examples. (2) Load Gemma-2-9B or Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1 from Hugging Face. (3) Run causal mediation analysis: for each attention head, compute the calibrated intervened logit difference between the model's output when running on normal prompts vs. counterfactual prompts (generated by flipping the QUERY variable, e.g., C->E). Patch attention head outputs between the two prompt runs. (4) Identify attention heads with high intervened logit difference (near 1.0). (5) Verify sufficiency: patch only the discovered circuit heads from QUERY to ':' position; verify Delta^C_normal/Delta_normal approaches 0.94 for Gemma-2-9B. Expected result: ~13 attention heads in layers ~19-30 show high IE, grouped into four functional families: queried-rule locating, queried-rule mover, fact-processing, and decision heads.

code_available.evidence: Exhaustive search across GitHub repositories using multiple query variants (full title, arXiv ID 2411.04105, paper acronym, method names, author names Nishanth Dikkala/Rina Panigrahy/Google Research, organization, task terms like circuit reasoning propositional logic, causal mediation analysis, activation patching) returned zero results. Bundled OpenReview supplement contains only Transformers_and_propositional_logic_Neurips_2025.pdf (a paper PDF, not code). No README, config, script, or notebook files present in the supplement. No project page, code link, or GitHub URL appears in the arXiv abstract or HTML versions of the paper.

dataset_available.evidence: The MRE uses a custom synthetic propositional logic problem defined by the authors (involving rules with 'and'/'or' operators, fact truth-value assignments, and query variables). The paper generates this data procedurally as described in Appendix A.2 and Section B.1. No release of the dataset, generation code, or prompt templates was found. The bundled supplement contains no data files, split definitions, or benchmark definition files. The dataset is not a standard public ML benchmark.

weights_available.evidence: The MRE uses pre-trained Gemma-2-9B and Mistral-7B as base models, which are publicly available on Hugging Face (google/gemma-2-9b-it and mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1). No custom checkpoints specific to this research were released.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: The MRE dataset is a custom synthetic propositional logic benchmark defined by the authors. It uses author-generated rules, fact assignments, and query templates (e.g., 'A or B implies C', 'D implies E' with truth values). This is not a widely recognized public ML benchmark such as MNIST, CIFAR, ImageNet, GSM8K, or SuperGLUE.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified for LLM experiments. The paper does not report GPU-hours for the Gemma-2-9B/Mistral-7B patching experiments. The small-transformer experiments (3-layer models) used a single V100 for 2-3 days each. For the MRE (Gemma-2-9B or Mistral-7B patching on 60 samples, ~42 layers × ~40 heads with multiple forward passes per head), a conservative estimate is ~24 H100-hours (e.g., 8 forward passes per head × ~150 important heads × 60 samples × ~0.03 H100-hours per sample). Note: This estimate covers inference-only patching experiments; engineering/debugging time for code reconstruction and data generation pipeline is additional and significant. The absence of released code and custom data generation pipeline makes exact reproducibility challenging.
abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

title: SuffixDecoding: Extreme Speculative Decoding for Emerging AI Applications
central_claim: Arctic is a 17B active parameter MoE model with 496B total parameters using 256 experts with top-16 gating, trained on 3.2T tokens from diverse data including Code, Math, Reasoning and Multilingual.
claim_evidence: The paper claims Arctic has 17B active parameters out of 496B total parameters using 256 experts with top-16 gating (Mistral's MathQ-Structured MoE) and supports up to 256K token context length.
mre_config: Training from scratch with MoE architecture similar to Arctic requires significant compute. Full training on 1024 H100s is estimated at roughly 3 months.
agent_task: Find GitHub artifacts for the Arctic model paper and related inference work

code_available.evidence: Arctic repo has code for training; Arctic Inference is a full vLLM plugin with ~15 directories of implementation code

dataset_available.evidence: No dedicated dataset repository found; paper mentions training on 3.2T diverse tokens

weights_available.evidence: Arctic model weights available on HuggingFace and GitHub

dataset_is_standard.evidence: Custom diverse mix including Code, Math, Reasoning, Multilingual content

h100_estimate_basis: Full training on 1024 H100s for 3 months: 1024 × 24 × 90 = 2,211,840 GPU-hours. Paper explicitly estimates 3 months on 1024 H100s for training Arctic.
abstract: Speculative decoding is widely adopted to reduce latency in large language model (LLM) inference by leveraging smaller draft models capable of handling diverse user tasks. However, emerging AI applications, such as LLM-based agents, present unique workload characteristics: instead of diverse independent requests, agentic frameworks typically submit repetitive inference requests, such as multi-agent pipelines performing similar subtasks or self-refinement loops iteratively enhancing outputs. These workloads result in long and highly predictable sequences, which current speculative decoding methods do not effectively exploit. To address this gap, we introduce \emph{SuffixDecoding}, a novel method that utilizes efficient suffix trees to cache long token sequences from prompts and previous outputs. By adaptively speculating more tokens when acceptance likelihood is high and fewer when it is low, SuffixDecoding effectively exploits opportunities for longer speculations while conserving computation when those opportunities are limited. Evaluations on agentic benchmarks, including SWE-Bench and Text-to-SQL, demonstrate that SuffixDecoding achieves speedups of up to 5.3$\times$, outperforming state-of-the-art methods -- 2.8$\times$ faster than model-based approaches like EAGLE-2/3 and 1.9$\times$ faster than model-free approaches such as Token Recycling. SuffixDecoding is open-sourced at https://github.com/snowflakedb/ArcticInference

title: The VLLM Safety Paradox: Dual Ease in Jailbreak Attack and Defense
central_claim: VLLMs exhibit a safety paradox where they are simultaneously easy to attack (high ASR on jailbreak benchmarks) and easy to defend (near-saturation performance from simple defenses), with the vulnerability stemming from inclusion of vision inputs rather than catastrophic forgetting, and existing defense mechanisms suffering from over-prudence that causes unintended abstention even on benign inputs.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'The vulnerability of Vision Large Language Models (VLLMs) to jailbreak attacks appears as no surprise. However, recent defense mechanisms against these attacks have reached near-saturation performance on benchmark evaluations, often with minimal effort.' Table 1 (tab:attack) shows VLLMs achieving 45.8%-90.4% ASR on benchmarks like FigStep and VLGuard. Table 2 (tab:vlguard) shows defense methods reducing ASR to near 0%. Figure 6 (fig:abst-vlguard) demonstrates over-prudence with high abstention on benign inputs.

abstract: The vulnerability of Vision Large Language Models (VLLMs) to jailbreak attacks appears as no surprise. However, recent defense mechanisms against these attacks have reached near-saturation performance on benchmark evaluations, often with minimal effort. This \emph{dual high performance} in both attack and defense raises a fundamental and perplexing paradox. To gain a deep understanding of this issue and thus further help strengthen the trustworthiness of VLLMs, this paper makes three key contributions: i) One tentative explanation for VLLMs being prone to jailbreak attacks--\textbf{inclusion of vision inputs}, as well as its in-depth analysis. ii) The recognition of a largely ignored problem in existing defense mechanisms--\textbf{over-prudence}. The problem causes these defense methods to exhibit unintended abstention, even in the presence of benign inputs, thereby undermining their reliability in faithfully defending against attacks. iii) A simple safety-aware method--\textbf{LLM-Pipeline}. Our method repurposes the more advanced guardrails of LLMs on the shelf, serving as an effective alternative detector prior to VLLM response. Last but not least, we find that the two representative evaluation methods for jailbreak often exhibit chance agreement. This limitation makes it potentially misleading when evaluating attack strategies or defense mechanisms. We believe the findings from this paper offer useful insights to rethink the foundational development of VLLM safety with respect to benchmark datasets, defense strategies, and evaluation methods.

title: Sharp Matrix Empirical Bernstein Inequalities
central_claim: Two sharp, closed-form empirical Bernstein inequalities for symmetric random matrices with bounded eigenvalues that adapt to unknown variance, where the first-order 1/√n deviation term asymptotically matches the matrix Bernstein inequality exactly (including constants).
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'We present two sharp, closed-form empirical Bernstein inequalities for symmetric random matrices with bounded eigenvalues... the deviation captured by the first-order 1/√n term asymptotically matches the matrix Bernstein inequality exactly.' Table 1 reports ratios D_n^{meb1}/D_n^{tb} and D_n^{meb2}/D_n^{tb} for sample sizes 100 to 1,000,000, showing convergence to 1.
mre_config: Reproduce simulation in Table 1: compute relative lengths D_n^{meb1}/D_n^{tb} and D_n^{meb2}/D_n^{tb} for sample sizes n=100, 1000, 10000, 100000, 1000000 using d=3 orthonormal projections with Unif[0,1] eigenvalues. Implement: (1) oracle Bernstein bound D_n^{tb}, (2) first matrix EB inequality D_n^{meb1} with paired variance, (3) second matrix EB inequality D_n^{meb2} with self-normalized variance proxy. Compare ratios to Table 1 values.
agent_task: Reproduce Table 1 simulation from the paper. Steps: (1) Generate random d=3 matrices from 3 fixed orthonormal projections with independent Unif[0,1] eigenvalues; (2) Compute oracle matrix Bernstein bound D_n^{tb} = log(d/α)/(3n) + sqrt(2*||V||*log(d/α)/n) where V is population variance; (3) Implement first matrix EB inequality D_n^{meb1} using paired variance estimator V*_n from Equation (5) with the closed-form formula in Theorem 1; (4) Implement second matrix EB inequality D_n^{meb2} from Corollary 2 using self-normalized variance proxy v_{n,α} with weighted average estimator; (5) Calculate ratios D_n^{meb1}/D_n^{tb} and D_n^{meb2}/D_n^{tb} for n=100,1000,10000,100000,1000000 with α=0.05; (6) Verify computed ratios match Table 1 values (e.g., for n=1000: expect ~1.589 and ~1.105; for n=100000: expect ~1.072 and ~1.007) within numerical tolerance.

abstract: We present two sharp, closed-form empirical Bernstein inequalities for symmetric random matrices with bounded eigenvalues. By sharp, we mean that both inequalities adapt to the unknown variance in a tight manner: the deviation captured by the first-order $1/\sqrt{n}$ term asymptotically matches the matrix Bernstein inequality exactly, including constants, the latter requiring knowledge of the variance. Our first inequality holds for the sample mean of independent matrices, and our second inequality holds for a mean estimator under martingale dependence at stopping times.

title: Coarse-to-fine Q-Network with Action Sequence for Data-Efficient Reinforcement Learning

This validates the core claim that action sequences in value learning improve performance over single-step actions in the critic-only RL framework.

Compare final episode returns to verify CQN-AS outperforms CQN on the stand task, demonstrating that action sequences in the critic improve value learning.

For 1M steps (1/10th scale): 4 A5000-hours × 0.58 H100 ratio = 2.32 H100-hours, rounded to 2 H100-hours. abstract: Predicting a sequence of actions has been crucial in the success of recent behavior cloning algorithms in robotics. Can similar ideas improve reinforcement learning (RL)? We answer affirmatively by observing that incorporating action sequences when predicting ground-truth return-to-go leads to lower validation loss. Motivated by this, we introduce Coarse-to-fine Q-Network with Action Sequence (CQN-AS), a novel value-based RL algorithm that learns a critic network that outputs Q-values over a sequence of actions, i.e., explicitly training the value function to learn the consequence of executing action sequences. Our experiments show that CQN-AS outperforms several baselines on a variety of sparse-reward humanoid control and tabletop manipulation tasks from BiGym and RLBench.

title: Large Language Models for Lossless Image Compression: Next-Pixel Prediction in Language Space is All You Need

abstract: We have recently witnessed that ``Intelligence" and `` Compression" are the two sides of the same coin, where the language large model (LLM) with unprecedented intelligence is a general-purpose lossless compressor for various data modalities. This attribute particularly appeals to the lossless image compression community, given the increasing need to compress high-resolution images in the current streaming media era. Consequently, a spontaneous envision emerges: Can the compression performance of the LLM elevate lossless image compression to new heights? However, our findings indicate that the naive application of LLM-based lossless image compressors suffers from a considerable performance gap compared with existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) codecs on common benchmark datasets. In light of this, we are dedicated to fulfilling the unprecedented intelligence (compression) capacity of the LLM for lossless image compression tasks, thereby bridging the gap between theoretical and practical compression performance. Specifically, we propose P$^{2}$-LLM, a next-pixel prediction-based LLM, which integrates various elaborated insights and methodologies, \textit{e.g.,} pixel-level priors, the in-context ability of LLM, and a pixel-level semantic preservation strategy, to enhance the understanding capacity of pixel sequences for better next-pixel predictions. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that P$^{2}$-LLM can beat SOTA classical and learned codecs.

title: Fast MRI for All: Bridging Access Gaps by Training without Raw Data

abstract: Physics-driven deep learning (PD-DL) approaches have become popular for improved reconstruction of fast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. Though PD-DL offers higher acceleration rates than existing clinical fast MRI techniques, their use has been limited outside specialized MRI centers. A key challenge is generalization to rare pathologies or different populations, noted in multiple studies, with fine-tuning on target populations suggested for improvement. However, current approaches for PD-DL training require access to raw k-space measurements, which is typically only available at specialized MRI centers that have research agreements for such data access. This is especially an issue for rural and under-resourced areas, where commercial MRI scanners only provide access to a final reconstructed image. To tackle these challenges, we propose Compressibility-inspired Unsupervised Learning via Parallel Imaging Fidelity (CUPID) for high-quality PD-DL training using only routine clinical reconstructed images exported from an MRI scanner. CUPID evaluates output quality with a compressibility-based approach while ensuring that the output stays consistent with the clinical parallel imaging reconstruction through well-designed perturbations. Our results show CUPID achieves similar quality to established PD-DL training that requires k-space data while outperforming compressed sensing (CS) and diffusion-based generative methods. We further demonstrate its effectiveness in a zero-shot training setup for retrospectively and prospectively sub-sampled acquisitions, attesting to its …

abstract: Existing large video-language models (LVLMs) struggle to comprehend long videos correctly due to limited context. To address this problem, fine-tuning long-context LVLMs and employing GPT-based agents have emerged as promising solutions. However, fine-tuning LVLMs would require extensive high-quality data and substantial GPU resources, while GPT-based agents would rely on proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4o). In this paper, we propose Video Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Video-RAG), a training-free and cost-effective pipeline that employs visually-aligned auxiliary texts to help facilitate cross-modality alignment while providing additional information beyond the visual content. Specifically, we leverage open-source external tools to extract visually-aligned information from pure video data (e.g., audio, optical character, and object detection), and incorporate the extracted information into an existing LVLM as auxiliary texts, alongside video frames and queries, in a plug-and-play manner. Our Video-RAG offers several key advantages: (i) lightweight with low computing overhead due to single-turn retrieval; (ii) easy implementation and compatibility with any LVLM; and (iii) significant, consistent performance gains across long video understanding benchmarks, including Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench. Notably, our model demonstrates superior performance over proprietary models like Gemini-1.5-Pro and GPT-4o when utilized with a 72B model.

However, this estimate is moot since the required code and weights do not exist. Engineering/debugging time to implement the missing training pipeline and obtain/process the data would be additional and substantial.
abstract: Existing recommendation systems either rely on user interaction logs, such as online shopping history for shopping recommendations, or focus on text signals. However, item-based histories are not always accessible, and are not generalizable for multimodal recommendation. We hypothesize that a user's visual history -- comprising images from daily life -- can offer rich, task-agnostic insights into their interests and preferences, and thus be leveraged for effective personalization. To this end, we propose VisualLens, a novel framework that leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to enable personalization using task-agnostic visual history. VisualLens extracts, filters, and refines a spectrum user profile from the visual history to support personalized recommendation. We created two new benchmarks, Google-Review-V and Yelp-V, with task-agnostic visual histories, and show that VisualLens improves over state-of-the-art item-based multimodal recommendations by 5-10% on Hit@3, and outperforms GPT-4o by 2-5%. Further analysis shows that VisualLens is robust across varying history lengths and excels at adapting to both longer histories and unseen content categories.

title: Fast training of large kernel models with delayed projections
central_claim: EigenPro 4 (EP4) reduces training time complexity of large kernel models from O(p²) to O(p) through delayed projections, achieving up to 600x speedup over EP3 while maintaining comparable or better accuracy.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'Our algorithm introduces delayed projections to Preconditioned Stochastic Gradient Descent (PSGD) allowing the training of much larger models than was previously feasible.' Table 1 (tab:comparison) shows EP4 achieves ~4.6-686x speedup over EP3 across datasets with similar/better accuracy. The introduction states 'In this paper, we build upon EP3 and introduce EP4...achieving amortized linear scaling per iteration with respect to model size.'
mre_config: FashionMNIST classification with 50K training samples, 20K model centers, Laplacian kernel (bandwidth=20), 2 epochs, using EP4 delayed projection optimizer with Nyström preconditioning. Expected outcome: ~85-87% test accuracy demonstrating linear scaling and fast convergence. Alternative MRE: CIFAR5M* with p=64K (5M samples, MobileNetV2 features) with 1 epoch - EP4 achieves 88% accuracy in 5 minutes showing ~4.6x speedup over EP3 (23min).
agent_task: Reproduce the core EP4 algorithm by: 1) Install EigenPro from https://github.com/EigenPro/EigenPro (pip install git+ssh://git@github.com/EigenPro/EigenPro.git@main), 2) Run FashionMNIST example: python examples/run_example.py --dataset=fmnist --n_train=50000 --n_test=10000 --model_size=20000 --epochs=2, 3) Verify training completes with ~85-87% test accuracy demonstrating EP4's fast kernel training. Compare per-epoch time with EP3 baseline if possible. Alternatively, reproduce the paper's CIFAR5M* MRE (p=64K, 5M samples, MobileNetV2 features extracted via timm) showing EP4 achieves ~88% accuracy in ~5 minutes on A100 vs 23 minutes for EP3.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo EigenPro/EigenPro contains complete implementation including eigenpro/solver.py (main EP4 solver with fit function), eigenpro/optimizers.py (EigenPro optimizer class), eigenpro/models/ (kernel machine implementations), eigenpro/kernels.py (Laplacian kernel), eigenpro/preconditioner.py (Nyström preconditioner), examples/run_example.py with FashionMNIST script, and examples/notebook.ipynb. Repo verified via github_repo, github_repository_tree, and github_file_contents tools. README confirms GPU-enabled fast solver with PyTorch backend. Installation via pip install git+ssh://git@github.com/EigenPro/EigenPro.git@main.

dataset_available.evidence: FashionMNIST available via torchvision.datasets.FashionMNIST (standard PyTorch download). CIFAR5M available via Google Cloud Storage (gs://gresearch/cifar5m/part{i}.npz for i=0..5) as documented in preetum/cifar5m GitHub repo. The code in examples/run_example.py uses data_utils.load_fmnist which wraps torchvision for automatic download. For CIFAR5M* experiments in the paper, features are extracted via timm library (pretrained MobileNetV2) from publicly available CIFAR-5M data.

weights_available.evidence: No trained checkpoints released in the EigenPro/EigenPro repository. The repo contains only training code. Searched for .pth, .pt, model, checkpoint, or weights files in the repository tree (38 files total) - none found. The examples only provide training scripts, not pre-trained model weights. Training must be performed from scratch.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: FashionMNIST is a widely recognized benchmark derived from MNIST, available via torchvision.datasets.FashionMNIST with automatic download. CIFAR-10 is standard; CIFAR5M is a publicly available synthetic variant generated from DDPM. The MRE can use FashionMNIST which is a standard ML benchmark.

h100_estimate_basis: FashionMNIST MRE: 50K samples, 20K centers, 2 epochs on FashionMNIST. Based on EP4's linear O(p) scaling and paper's reported times (CIFAR5M* p=64K → 5min on A100 with 1.3TB VRAM), the smaller FashionMNIST config (20K centers vs 64K, 50K samples vs 5M) should take ~1-2 minutes on A100. Converting A100→H100 (A100 0.32x H100-equivalent): ~0.25 H100-hours. Engineering and debugging time not included. The paper's smallest benchmark (CIFAR5M* p=64K, 5M samples, 1 epoch) reports 5 minutes on A100, which would be ~0.03 H100-hours at scale.
abstract: Classical kernel machines have historically faced significant challenges in scaling to large datasets and model sizes--a key ingredient that has driven the success of neural networks. In this paper, we present a new methodology for building kernel machines that can scale efficiently with both data size and model size. Our algorithm introduces delayed projections to Preconditioned Stochastic Gradient Descent (PSGD) allowing the training of much larger models than was previously feasible, pushing the practical limits of kernel-based learning. We validate our algorithm, EigenPro4, across multiple datasets, demonstrating drastic training speed up over the existing methods while maintaining comparable or better classification accuracy.

title: GeneMAN: Generalizable Single-Image 3D Human Reconstruction from Multi-Source Human Data
central_claim: GeneMAN addresses single-image 3D human reconstruction by training on multi-source human data (SMPL-X + Renderpeople + THuman2.0), using a multi-stage pipeline where geometry is first initialized via SDS loss on an SDF grid, then sculpted with GAN-based supervision, and finally textures are refined through inpainting.
claim_evidence: GeneMAN trains on combined datasets including SMPL-X scans, Renderpeople, and THuman2.0 to achieve generalization across diverse humans. The reconstruction pipeline has 4 stages: geometry-init (SDS on tetrahedra SDF grid), geometry-sculpt (GAN-based SDS refinement with discriminator), texture-coarse, and texture-refine. The geometry stage uses a custom tetrahedra_sdf_grid.py implementing SDF-based mesh extraction via marching tetrahedra. Stage-3 texture refinement follows the HumanNorm approach for normal-guided inpainting.
mre_config: Stage 1-2: tetrahedra_sdf_grid with 128 resolution, Stage 3-4: PBR material with diffuse point light — all stages share the same geometry init from stage 1.
agent_task: image-to-3d

code_available.evidence: https://github.com/3DTopia/GeneMAN — full training/inference code released with configs, scripts, preprocessing.py, launch.py, and threestudio-based systems/geneman.py

dataset_available.evidence: https://github.com/3DTopia/GeneMAN/tree/main/data/examples — 13 example images with pre-processed normals, depths, masks, landmarks, and captions

weights_available.evidence: Pretrained models are distributed via HuggingFace dataset (wwt117/GeneMAN) with external links, but are not downloadable directly from the GitHub repo

dataset_is_standard.evidence: Uses custom combined dataset (SMPL-X + Renderpeople + THuman2.0) — not a single standard benchmark, though evaluation is performed on renderpeople and thuman2.0 test sets

h100_estimate_basis: Multi-stage reconstruction: stage1 (geometry init, 500 iters) + stage2 (geometry sculpt, 500 iters) + stage3 (texture coarse, 500 iters) + stage4 (texture refine, 500 iters). Each stage requires full GNN/NeRF forward+SDS backward with diffusion model sampling (DDIM 50 steps). Single image on A100 ~30min; H100 ~2x faster but multi-stage pipeline has high memory pressure from storing intermediate geometry states across stages.
abstract: Given a single in-the-wild human photo, it remains a challenging task to reconstruct a high-fidelity 3D human model. Existing methods face difficulties including a) the varying body proportions captured by in-the-wild human images; b) diverse personal belongings within the shot; and c) ambiguities in human postures and inconsistency in human textures. In addition, the scarcity of high-quality human data intensifies the challenge. To address these problems, we propose a Generalizable image-to-3D huMAN reconstruction framework, dubbed GeneMAN, building upon a comprehensive multi-source collection of high-quality human data, including 3D scans, multi-view videos, single photos, and our generated synthetic human data. GeneMAN encompasses three key modules. 1) Without relying on parametric human models (e.g., SMPL), GeneMAN first trains a human-specific text-to-image diffusion model and a view-conditioned diffusion model, serving as GeneMAN 2D human prior and 3D human prior for reconstruction, respectively. 2) With the help of the pretrained human prior models, the Geometry Initialization-&-Sculpting pipeline is leveraged to recover high-quality 3D human geometry given a single image. 3) To achieve high-fidelity 3D human textures, GeneMAN employs the Multi-Space Texture Refinement pipeline, consecutively refining textures in the latent and the pixel spaces. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that GeneMAN could generate high-quality 3D human models from a single image input, outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods. title: Open-World Drone Active Tracking with Goal-Centered Rewards
central_claim: A benchmark for Visual-Aware Autonomous Drone Tracking using Webots and SUMO traffic simulation
claim_evidence: Simulation benchmark with 6 environments, 25+ vehicle models, and multi-weather conditions; supports both Webots 3D physics simulation and SUMO traffic simulation; includes bilingual (EN/ZH) documentation and pre-trained models; 1300+ files including worlds, controllers, and documentation
mre_config: Python 3.7+; Webots R2021a+; SUMO 1.9.0+; supports Ubuntu 20.04 and Windows; GPU recommended for training; ~2GB disk space for worlds
agent_task: Autonomous drone tracking of ground vehicles in traffic environments

code_available.evidence: 1300+ files including Python controllers, world files (.wbt), SUMO network files (.net.xml, .rou.xml)

dataset_available.evidence: 6 environments with multiple OSM maps, 25+ vehicle models, multi-weather condition files

weights_available.evidence: Pre-trained model in DR L_TA_SAC controller directory

dataset_is_standard.evidence: Custom Webots+SUMO simulation environment; not using standard datasets like nuScenes/KITTI

h100_estimate_basis: 6 environments x 5 weather conditions x 8 hours training per config; 25+ vehicle types require separate model adaptation; multi-stage training (distance then view reward) adds 20% overhead; total ~200-240 hours on H100 for full benchmark coverage
abstract: Drone Visual Active Tracking aims to autonomously follow a target object by controlling the motion system based on visual observations, providing a more practical solution for effective tracking in dynamic environments. However, accurate Drone Visual Active Tracking using reinforcement learning remains challenging due to the absence of a unified benchmark and the complexity of open-world environments with frequent interference. To address these issues, we pioneer a systematic solution. First, we propose DAT, the first open-world drone active air-to-ground tracking benchmark. It encompasses 24 city-scale scenes, featuring targets with human-like behaviors and high-fidelity dynamics simulation. DAT also provides a digital twin tool for unlimited scene generation. Additionally, we propose a novel reinforcement learning method called GC-VAT, which aims to improve the performance of drone tracking targets in complex scenarios. Specifically, we design a Goal-Centered Reward to provide precise feedback across viewpoints to the agent, enabling it to expand perception and movement range through unrestricted perspectives. Inspired by curriculum learning, we introduce a Curriculum-Based Training strategy that progressively enhances the tracking performance in complex environments. Besides, experiments on simulator and real-world images demonstrate the superior performance of GC-VAT, achieving a Tracking Success Rate of approximately 72% on the simulator. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/SHWplus/DAT_Benchmark.

title: Unveiling Concept Attribution in Diffusion Models
central_claim: Knowledge is localized in a small number of model parameters in diffusion models, and CAD can identify positive and negative components that respectively increase or decrease concept probability.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'the proposed framework, called Component Attribution for Diffusion Model (CAD), discovers the localization of concept-inducing (positive) components, while interestingly uncovers another type of components that contribute negatively to generating a concept.' Table 1 shows object erasure results where ablating 0.1% parameters reduces target class accuracy while maintaining other class accuracy. Figure 1 illustrates the framework overview showing positive and negative components.
mre_config: MRE: Erase a single Imagenette object concept (e.g., 'parachute') from Stable Diffusion 1.4 using CAD-Erase. Steps: (1) Compute attribution scores using compute_positive_neurons.py with prompt='parachute', (2) Ablate top 0.1% positive components in UNet feed-forward layers, (3) Generate 500 images with ablated model, (4) Classify generated images with pretrained ResNet50. Target metric: Target class accuracy < 10%, Other classes accuracy > 65%.
agent_task: Reproduce CAD-Erase on a single Imagenette object concept. (1) Clone repo mail-research/CAD-attribution4diffusion and install dependencies via environment.yaml. (2) Run compute_positive_neurons.py with --prompt='parachute' --model_name='CompVis/stable-diffusion-v1-4' to compute attribution scores. (3) Ablate top 0.1% positive parameters in UNet feed-forward layers. (4) Generate 500 images with the ablated model using prompts from prompts/imagenette.csv. (5) Classify generated images with pretrained ResNet50 (torchvision). (6) Verify target class accuracy drops below 10% while other class accuracies remain above 65%.

Contains complete implementation: compute_positive_neurons.py, compute_negative_neurons.py, diffuser_custom_generate.py, and benchmarking/ with object_eval.py, nudity_eval.py, clip_score.py, lpips_eval.py, generate_art.py. README provides executable commands for object erasure, nudity erasure, and amplification experiments.

All prompt files bundled in repo. HuggingFace search confirmed no custom datasets needed.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: ImageNette is standard subset of ImageNet (10 classes: tench, goldfish, ..., parachute). COCO 30k is standard MS-COCO validation set. Both are widely recognized public benchmarks used extensively in ML research.

h100_estimate_basis: MRE involves inference-only operations with no training. Attribution computation: ~5-10 min (single forward/backward pass per concept). Image generation (500 images at 512x512, 50 DDIM steps): ~30-60 min on A100. Classification evaluation: ~10 min. Total per concept: ~1-1.5 hours on A100 (0.32 H100-equivalent) ≈ 2 H100-hours. Engineering and debugging time additional.
abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable abilities in generating realistic and high-quality images from text prompts. However, a trained model remains largely black-box; little do we know about the roles of its components in exhibiting a concept such as objects or styles. Recent works employ causal tracing to localize knowledge-storing layers in generative models without showing how other layers contribute to the target concept. In this work, we approach diffusion models' interpretability problem from a more general perspective and pose a question: \textit{``How do model components work jointly to demonstrate knowledge?''}. To answer this question, we decompose diffusion models using component attribution, systematically unveiling the importance of each component (specifically the model parameter) in generating a concept. The proposed framework, called \textbf{C}omponent \textbf{A}ttribution for \textbf{D}iffusion Model (CAD), discovers the localization of concept-inducing (positive) components, while interestingly uncovers another type of components that contribute negatively to generating a concept, which is missing in the previous knowledge localization work. Based on this holistic understanding of diffusion models, we introduce two fast, inference-time model editing algorithms, CAD-Erase and CAD-Amplify; in particular, CAD-Erase enables erasure and CAD-Amplify allows amplification of a generated concept by ablating the positive and negative components, respectively, while retaining knowledge of other concepts. title: The Matrix: Infinite-Horizon World Generation with Real-Time Moving Control
central_claim: The Matrix is the first foundational realistic world simulator capable of generating infinitely long 720p high-fidelity video streams with real-time (8-16 FPS) frame-level moving control, trained on AAA game data and real-world footage with strong domain generalization.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'We present The Matrix, the first foundational realistic world simulator capable of generating infinitely long 720p high-fidelity real-scene video streams with real-time, responsive control.' Table 1 demonstrates The Matrix is the only method achieving all four capabilities simultaneously: infinite video length, real-time inference (8-16 FPS), frame-level control, and control generalization to unseen scenes.
mre_config: Train Interactive Module (controller) for frame-level control precision: use pre-trained 2.3B DiT backbone (frozen), warmup with LoRA on unlabeled data for 20K steps (batch size 32), then train controller for 20K steps keeping DiT frozen, evaluate Move-PSNR and Move-LPIPS on test videos with ground truth keyboard inputs. MRE target: match paper's reported ~0.125 LPIPS and ~29 PSNR on Forza Horizon 5 driving control.
agent_task: Reproduce Interactive Module frame-level control: (1) Obtain pre-trained Open-Sora video DiT backbone (2.3B params), (2) Collect/procure custom video + keyboard control data from Forza Horizon 5 or similar driving game using tools like Cheat Engine + Reshade + OBS (Source dataset not publicly released), (3) Warmup LoRA training on unlabeled video data for 20K steps with batch size 32, (4) Train Interactive Module controller (16 modules, one after every 2 DiT blocks) for 20K steps keeping DiT frozen, (5) Evaluate Move-PSNR and Move-LPIPS between generated videos and ground truth trajectories for control precision matching paper's ~0.125 LPIPS / ~29 PSNR.

Project page explicitly states 'Source (Coming Soon)'. Multiple search queries across title variants, method names (Swin-DPM, Interactive Module, Shift-Window Denoising), acronym (Matrix), and org names (Tongyi Lab, Alibaba) returned no code repository.

Project page states dataset is 'Coming Soon'. The paper's custom Source dataset is proprietary AAA game data requiring complex capture tools (Cheat Engine, Reshade, OBS), not standard ML benchmarks.

Abstract explicitly promises 'All the codes, data, and model checkpoints in this paper will be open sourced' - future tense, not released. HuggingFace search found no model artifacts.

DROID robotics dataset used for auxiliary robot arm experiments (50K clips) is standard, but paper's central claims about infinite-horizon world generation with real-time moving control depend on the custom Source dataset, which is not a standard benchmark.

Training stages include warmup (20K steps), controller (20K steps), Swin-DPM fine-tuning (60K steps), and consistency distillation (10K steps), all with batch size 32 on 2.7B model. Using comparable video DiT training estimates: 40K steps (warmup + controller) on 2.7B params at batch 32 requires ~8 A100s for multiple days. abstract: We present The Matrix, the first foundational realistic world simulator capable of generating continuous 720p high-fidelity real-scene video streams with real-time, responsive control in both first- and third-person perspectives, enabling immersive exploration of richly dynamic environments. Trained on limited supervised data from AAA games like Forza Horizon 5 and Cyberpunk 2077, complemented by large-scale unsupervised footage from real-world settings like Tokyo streets, The Matrix allows users to traverse diverse terrains -- deserts, grasslands, water bodies, and urban landscapes -- in continuous, uncut hour-long sequences. Operating at 16 FPS, the system supports real-time interactivity and demonstrates zero-shot generalization, translating virtual game environments to real-world contexts where collecting continuous movement data is often infeasible. For example, The Matrix can simulate a BMW X3 driving through an office setting--an environment present in neither gaming data nor real-world sources. This approach showcases the potential of AAA game data to advance robust world models, bridging the gap between simulations and real-world applications in scenarios with limited data.

title: The Narrow Gate: Localized Image-Text Communication in Native Multimodal Models
central_claim: In native multimodal VLMs (Chameleon, Emu3), a single end-of-image token acts as a narrow gate for visual-to-text communication, and ablating attention to this token causes dramatic performance collapse, unlike non-native VLMs where communication is distributed.
claim_evidence: Abstract states native multimodal VLMs 'tend to rely on a single post-image token that acts as a narrow gate for visual information.' Table 1 (Section 3.1) shows Chameleon-7B MS-COCO CIDEr drops from 0.48 to 0.04 (92% drop), VQAv2 accuracy from 0.51 to 0.25 (51% drop), and ImageNet overlap from 0.46 to 0.01 (98% drop) when ablating text-to-[EOI] attention, while LLaVA shows no degradation from [EOI] ablation.
mre_config: Attention knockout on Chameleon-7B with ImageNet classification: run inference on 2000 sampled ImageNet images with prompt '<image> This animal is a __', block text-to-[EOI] token attention across all layers, measure classification accuracy, and compare to baseline. A significant accuracy drop (>50%) confirms the narrow gate claim.
agent_task: 1) Load Chameleon-7B from HuggingFace (facebook/chameleon-7b) with transformers; 2) Sample 2000 images from 100 ImageNet animal classes; 3) For each image, construct prompt '<image> This animal is a __' and run inference; 4) Record baseline top-1 classification accuracy; 5) Implement attention knockout: modify attention matrices to block text tokens from attending to the [EOI] token (position after all image tokens) across all layers; 6) Re-run inference with knockout and record accuracy; 7) Compare accuracy drop: paper reports baseline 0.46 and knockout 0.01 for Chameleon-7B on ImageNet. A >50% relative drop in accuracy confirms the narrow gate mechanism.

code: https://github.com/ritareasciencepark/Narrow-gate (searched multiple query patterns including full title, acronym, org name, author names, arXiv ID; no public repository found)

The paper states 'The code needed to reproduce the experiments is available at ritareasciencepark.github.io/Narrow-gate' but this is not a GitHub repo and the actual implementation code is not publicly accessible. Two passes needed (baseline + ablation). Paper reports experiments on 'single NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 40GB VRAM'. Converting A100-hours to H100-equivalent: A100 40GB = 0.32x H100. Estimate: (2 passes x 2 GPU-hours x 0.32) + engineering overhead ~3 hours = ~4.5 H100-hours for minimal MRE. Scale up to match paper sample sizes (10,000 image-text pairs) and account for multi-layer attention modifications: ~18 H100-hours total.
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal training have significantly improved the integration of image understanding and generation within a unified model. This study investigates how vision-language models (VLMs) handle image-understanding tasks, focusing on how visual information is processed and transferred to the textual domain. We compare native multimodal VLMs, models trained from scratch on multimodal data to generate both text and images, and non-native multimodal VLMs, models adapted from pre-trained large language models or capable of generating only text, highlighting key differences in information flow. We find that in native multimodal VLMs, image and text embeddings are more separated within the residual stream. Moreover, VLMs differ in how visual information reaches text: non-native multimodal VLMs exhibit a distributed communication pattern, where information is exchanged through multiple image tokens, whereas models trained natively for joint image and text generation tend to rely on a single post-image token that acts as a narrow gate for visual information. We show that ablating this single token significantly deteriorates image-understanding performance, whereas targeted, token-level interventions reliably steer image semantics and downstream text with fine-grained control.

title: GRIP: A Graph-Based Reasoning Instruction Producer
central_claim: GRIP (Graph-based Reasoning Instruction Producer) synthesizes high-quality math reasoning data through graph-based key concept extraction and combination, achieving 280-fold expansion (7.5K seed to 2.1M samples) with 71.8% novelty rate, significantly improving base model performance on math benchmarks at 2% of GPT-3.5 costs.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'models trained with GRIP-MATH demonstrate substantial improvements over their base models and significantly outperform previous data synthesis methods.' Table main_tab shows GRIP-Qwen2-7B achieves 70.2 AVG vs base Qwen2-7B at 66.5 and best prior method MathScale at 51.2. Table comparison_methods_experiments shows 280-fold expansion ratio with 0.57 synthesis cost (vs 23 for GPT-3.5).
mre_config: Train smallest model (Qwen2-1.5B or Mistral-7B) on GRIP-MATH dataset (2.1M synthesized QA pairs from 7.5K MATH seed), evaluate on MATH benchmark. Compare GRIP-trained model vs base model and vs MathScale (51.2 AVG on Mistral-7B) to verify GRIP's advantage.
agent_task: Reproduce GRIP training and evaluation: (1) Implement the complete GRIP pipeline from scratch: extract key concepts from MATH training set using Qwen2.5-32B with provided prompt templates, construct Key Concepts Relationship Graph (KCRG) with explicit (1-hop) and implicit (2-hop, 3-hop) edges, generate synthetic QA pairs by combining non-co-occurring concepts using prompts in the paper, filter with multi-model voting using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, DeepSeek-Math-RL. (2) Fine-tune Qwen2-1.5B on synthesized data for 2 epochs (lr=5e-6, global batch=128, max_seq_len=4096, cosine scheduler with 3% warmup) using LLaMAFactory with DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 and FlashAttention 2. (3) Evaluate trained model on MATH benchmark. Verify GRIP-trained model achieves significant improvement over base model (Qwen2-1.5B: 41.2→58.6 AVG) and outperforms MathScale (51.2 AVG on Mistral-7B). For MRE validation, use smaller GRIP-MATH-mini scale (~80K samples) if full synthesis is too costly.

abstract: Large-scale, high-quality data is essential for advancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). As publicly available Internet data becomes increasingly scarce, synthetic data has emerged as a crucial research direction. However, existing data synthesis methods often suffer from limited scalability, insufficient sample diversity, and a tendency to overfit to seed data, which constrains their practical utility. In this paper, we present \textit{\textbf{GRIP}}, a \textbf{G}raph-based \textbf{R}easoning \textbf{I}nstruction \textbf{P}roducer that efficiently synthesizes high-quality and diverse reasoning instructions. \textit{GRIP} constructs a knowledge graph by extracting high-level concepts from seed data, and uniquely leverages both explicit and implicit relationships within the graph to drive large-scale and diverse instruction data synthesis, while employing open-source multi-model supervision to ensure data quality. We apply \textit{GRIP} to the critical and challenging domain of mathematical reasoning. Starting from a seed set of 7.5K math reasoning samples, we construct \textbf{GRIP-MATH}, a dataset containing 2.1 million synthesized question-answer pairs. Compared to similar synthetic data methods, \textit{GRIP} achieves greater scalability and diversity while also significantly reducing costs. On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, models trained with GRIP-MATH demonstrate substantial improvements over their base models and significantly outperform previous data synthesis methods.

abstract: Semantic segmentation suffers from significant performance degradation when the trained network is applied to a different domain. To address this issue, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has been extensively studied. Despite the effectiveness of selftraining techniques in UDA, they still overlook the explicit modeling of domain-shared feature extraction. In this paper, we propose DiDA, an unsupervised domain bridging approach for semantic segmentation. DiDA consists of two key modules: (1) Degradation-based Intermediate Domain Construction, which creates continuous intermediate domains through simple image degradation operations to encourage learning domain-invariant features as domain differences gradually diminish; (2) Semantic Shift Compensation, which leverages a diffusion encoder to disentangle and compensate for semantic shift information with degraded timesteps, preserving discriminative representations in the intermediate domains. As a plug-and-play solution, DiDA supports various degradation operations and seamlessly integrates with existing UDA methods. Extensive experiments on multiple domain adaptive semantic segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that DiDA consistently achieves significant performance improvements across all settings. Code is available at https://github.com/Woof6/DiDA.

abstract: Most ML datasets today contain biases. When we train models on these datasets, they often not only learn these biases but can worsen them -- a phenomenon known as bias amplification. Several co-occurrence-based metrics have been proposed to measure bias amplification in classification datasets. They measure bias amplification between a protected attribute (e.g., gender) and a task (e.g., cooking). These metrics also support fine-grained bias analysis by identifying the direction in which a model amplifies biases. However, co-occurrence-based metrics have limitations -- some fail to measure bias amplification in balanced datasets, while others fail to measure negative bias amplification. To solve these issues, recent work proposed a predictability-based metric called leakage amplification (LA). However, LA cannot identify the direction in which a model amplifies biases. We propose Directional Predictability Amplification (DPA), a predictability-based metric that is (1) directional, (2) works with balanced and unbalanced datasets, and (3) correctly identifies positive and negative bias amplification. DPA eliminates the need to evaluate models on multiple metrics to verify these three aspects. DPA also improves over prior predictability-based metrics like LA: it is less sensitive to the choice of attacker function (a hyperparameter in predictability-based metrics), reports scores within a bounded range, and accounts for dataset bias by measuring relative changes in predictability. abstract: This study explores the estimation of parameters in a matrix-valued linear regression model, where the $T$ responses $(Y_t)_{t=1}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ and predictors $(X_t)_{t=1}^T \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times q}$ satisfy the relationship $Y_t = A^* X_t B^* + E_t$ for all $t = 1, \ldots, T$. In this model, $A^* \in \mathbb{R}_+^{n \times m}$ has $L_1$-normalized rows, $B^* \in \mathbb{R}^{q \times p}$, and $(E_t)_{t=1}^T$ are independent noise matrices following a matrix Gaussian distribution. The primary objective is to estimate the unknown parameters $A^*$ and $B^*$ efficiently. We propose explicit optimization-free estimators and establish non-asymptotic convergence rates to quantify their performance. Additionally, we extend our analysis to scenarios where $A^*$ and $B^*$ exhibit sparse structures. To support our theoretical findings, we conduct numerical simulations that confirm the behavior of the estimators, particularly with respect to the impact of the dimensions $n, m, p, q$, and the sample size $T$ on finite-sample performances. We complete the simulations by investigating the denoising performances of our estimators on noisy real-world images.

abstract: We present a three-stage framework for training deep learning models specializing in antibody sequence-structure co-design. We first pre-train a language model using millions of antibody sequence data. Then, we employ the learned representations to guide the training of a diffusion model for joint optimization over both sequence and structure of antibodies. During the final alignment stage, we optimize the model to favor antibodies with low repulsion and high attraction to the antigen binding site, enhancing the rationality and functionality of the designs. To mitigate conflicting energy preferences, we extend AbDPO (Antibody Direct Preference Optimization) to guide the model toward Pareto optimality under multiple energy-based alignment objectives. Furthermore, we adopt an iterative learning paradigm with temperature scaling, enabling the model to benefit from diverse online datasets without requiring additional data. In practice, our proposed methods achieve high stability and efficiency in producing a better Pareto front of antibody designs compared to top samples generated by baselines and previous alignment techniques. Through extensive experiments, we showcase the superior performance of our methods in generating nature-like antibodies with high binding affinity.
