The underlying ZDT6 mathematical function is standard, but the specific data distribution (x,y pairs) used for training the diffusion model is custom, author-collected data released via Google Drive. Not a widely recognized public ML benchmark like MNIST or CIFAR.

h100_estimate_basis: The paper reports ~1300 seconds for ZDT1 (d=30) on GPU (likely A100, based on CUDA 11.7+ requirement and runtime context in install instructions). Table 8 (appendix) shows ZDT1=1300s, RE61=930s. Converting to H100: 1300s A100-hours * 0.32 H100/A100 ≈ 0.12 H100-hours per seed. ZDT6 (d=10) is smaller, but preference model trains for up to 2000 epochs (vs denoising model's 200 epochs). Adding preference training overhead (~0.5-1 H100-hours), total estimate ~2 H100-hours. Engineering/debugging time (dependency conflicts per README, data download, environment setup) is additional and not included.
abstract: Offline multi-objective optimization aims to identify Pareto-optimal solutions given a dataset of designs and their objective values. In this work, we propose a preference-guided diffusion model that generates Pareto-optimal designs by leveraging a classifier-based guidance mechanism. Our guidance classifier is a preference model trained to predict the probability that one design dominates another, directing the diffusion model toward optimal regions of the design space. Crucially, this preference model generalizes beyond the training distribution, enabling the discovery of Pareto-optimal solutions outside the observed dataset. We introduce a novel diversity-aware preference guidance, augmenting Pareto dominance preference with diversity criteria. This ensures that generated solutions are optimal and well-distributed across the objective space, a capability absent in prior generative methods for offline multi-objective optimization. We evaluate our approach on various continuous offline multi-objective optimization tasks and find that it consistently outperforms other inverse/generative approaches while remaining competitive with forward/ surrogate-based optimization methods. Our results highlight the effectiveness of classifier-guided diffusion models in generating diverse and high-quality solutions that approximate the Pareto front well.

title: CQ-DINO: Mitigating Gradient Dilution via Category Queries for Vast Vocabulary Object Detection
central_claim: CQ-DINO achieves superior performance on vast vocabulary object detection (V3Det) by using learnable category queries with image-guided query selection, surpassing previous methods by 2.1% AP while maintaining competitive results on COCO.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'CQ-DINO achieves superior performance on the challenging V3Det benchmark (surpassing previous methods by 2.1% AP) while maintaining competitiveness on COCO.' Table 1 (tab:v3det): CQ-DINO with Swin-B achieves 46.3% AP on V3Det vs 44.5% AP for Prova. Table 2 (tab:coco): CQ-DINO achieves 58.5% AP on COCO, comparable to DINO variants.
mre_config: CQ-DINO with Swin-B backbone on V3Det dataset: evaluate the released checkpoint cqdino_swinb1k_v3det.pth (or train with config configs/cqdino/cqdino_tree_swinb1k_v3det.py), report AP on V3Det val set. The config uses 900 queries, batch_size=2, 24 epochs. Metric: AP (expected ~46.3% for Swin-B).

h100_estimate_basis: Training from stage1 requires ~12 epochs (24 total, stage1 is first 10 epochs pre-training). Using 8 A100-40G GPUs with batch_size=2 per GPU: ~183k V3Det train images / 16 batch = ~11.4k iterations per epoch, ~137k iterations for 12 epochs. A100-40G is 0.32x H100: 8 GPUs * 12 epochs * ~6 hours per epoch / 0.32 = ~1152 H100-hours. Evaluation-only with released checkpoint is ~0.5 H100-hours equivalent. Engineering/debugging time for dependency issues (mmcv, mmengine, BERT model setup) is additional and not included.
abstract: With the exponential growth of data, traditional object detection methods are increasingly struggling to handle vast vocabulary object detection tasks effectively. We analyze two key limitations of classification-based detectors: positive gradient dilution, where rare positive categories receive insufficient learning signals, and hard negative gradient dilution, where discriminative gradients are overwhelmed by numerous easy negatives. To address these challenges, we propose CQ-DINO, a category query-based object detection framework that reformulates classification as a contrastive task between object queries and learnable category queries. Our method introduces image-guided query selection, which reduces the negative space by adaptively retrieving top-K relevant categories per image via cross-attention, thereby rebalancing gradient distributions and facilitating implicit hard example mining. Furthermore, CQ-DINO flexibly integrates explicit hierarchical category relationships in structured datasets (e.g., V3Det) or learns implicit category correlations via self-attention in generic datasets (e.g., COCO). Experiments demonstrate that CQ-DINO achieves superior performance on the challenging V3Det benchmark (surpassing previous methods by 2.1% AP) while maintaining competitiveness in COCO. Our work provides a scalable solution for real-world detection systems requiring wide category coverage. The code is publicly at https://github.com/FireRedTeam/CQ-DINO.

title: Self-Supervised Learning of Motion Concepts by Optimizing Counterfactuals
central_claim: Opt-CWM achieves state-of-the-art self-supervised motion estimation on TAP-Vid benchmarks without labeled data by optimizing counterfactual perturbations.

abstract: Estimating motion in videos is an essential computer vision problem with many downstream applications, including controllable video generation and robotics. Current solutions are primarily trained using synthetic data or require tuning of situation-specific heuristics, which inherently limits these models' capabilities in real-world contexts. Despite recent developments in large-scale self-supervised learning from videos, leveraging such representations for motion estimation remains relatively underexplored. In this work, we develop Opt-CWM, a self-supervised technique for flow and occlusion estimation from a pre-trained next-frame prediction model. Opt-CWM works by learning to optimize counterfactual probes that extract motion information from a base video model, avoiding the need for fixed heuristics while training on unrestricted video inputs. We achieve state-of-the-art performance for motion estimation on real-world videos while requiring no labeled data.

title: D2SA: Dual-Stage Distribution and Slice Adaptation for Efficient Test-Time Adaptation in MRI Reconstruction
central_claim: D2SA's dual-stage framework combining patient-wise MR-INR adaptation (Stage 1) with single-slice refinement via anisotropic diffusion module (Stage 2) achieves superior MRI reconstruction under distribution shifts, improving SSIM/PSNR while reducing adaptation time compared to DIP-TTT.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'we propose D2SA via MR-INR to improve MRI reconstruction performance and efficiency, which features two stages.' Table 1 (VarNet, main paper) shows FINE+MR-INR+SST achieves 0.882 SSIM/27.68 PSNR vs 0.878/27.67 for DIP-TTT in anatomy shift, with 17.1 vs 52.5 min/patient. Table 3 (U-Net ablation) shows FINE+MR-INR+SST achieves 27.71 PSNR vs 25.98 baseline.
mre_config: U-Net on anatomy shift (Knee to Brain): Stage 1 trains MR-INR (4-layer SIREN, 256 hidden units, 1D latent code 1x128) with patient-wise adaptation for 25 epochs, batch=2, Adam lr=1e-4 (MR-INR weights) + 1e-3 (latent code); Stage 2 refines each slice with frozen CNN + learnable AD module for up to 1000 steps, lr=1e-4. 4x Cartesian undersampling, 8% auto-calibration. Evaluate SSIM/PSNR/LPIPS on 10 brain patients (110 slices).
agent_task: Reproduce D2SA's core claim: that two-stage adaptation (MR-INR patient-wise + AD single-slice refinement) outperforms single-shot TTA on MRI reconstruction under distribution shift. Implementation steps: (1) Install fastMRI framework from facebookresearch/fastMRI for U-Net, masks, data loaders, and metrics. (2) Implement MR-INR branch: SIREN network (4-layer MLP, 256 hidden, sine activations) with Gaussian-initialized 1D latent code (size 1x128, sigma=0.01), Fourier feature mapping, and affine transformation with learnable alpha,beta parameters. (3) Implement Stage 1 training: patient-wise adaptation across all slices for 25 epochs, batch=2, Adam lr=1e-4 for network + 1e-3 for latent code, loss lambda_self=1 + lambda_INR=1 + lambda_reg=1e-4. (4) Implement AD module: difference convolutions (VC, CDC, ADC, HDC, VDC) with anisotropic diffusion g(|grad u|)=1/(1+|grad u|^2/k^2), gradient extraction with 1/4 channels. (5) Implement Stage 2: freeze CNN layers and latent code, fine-tune SIREN and AD module for up to 1000 steps per slice with early stopping (sliding window 30), Adam lr=1e-4. (6) Train source model on fastMRI knee PD data, adapt on brain AXI T2 data (10 patients, 110 slices), evaluate SSIM/PSNR/LPIPS. Target: SSIM >= 0.87, PSNR >= 27.5 on anatomy shift with <20 min/patient adaptation time. Note: D2SA code is not released; baseline code from chenhu96/Self-Supervised-MRI-Reconstruction provides SSDU for comparison. Dataset requires registration at fastmri.med.nyu.edu.

code_available.evidence: No D2SA code repository found after comprehensive searches: (1) exact title 'D2SA: Dual-Stage Distribution and Slice Adaptation' on GitHub returned no results; (2) acronym 'D2SA' search returned only unrelated repos (Diablo 2 save editors, placeholder D2salua with only README); (3) arXiv ID 2503.20815 search returned no results; (4) author name searches (Lipei Zhang, Aviles-Rivero) returned no relevant repos; (5) MR-INR search returned MatteoWohlrapp/mri-inr which is a TUM class project unrelated to D2SA. The paper itself does not reference any code URL. Related baselines are available: facebookresearch/fastMRI provides U-Net/VarNet/data loaders, and chenhu96/Self-Supervised-MRI-Reconstruction provides SSDU, but the D2SA-specific MR-INR module, AD module, and two-stage training pipeline are not released.

The dataset contains knee (~1500 fully sampled MRIs) and brain (~7000 MRIs) data used in the paper. Stanford Knee dataset is also available through fastMRI. Both are standard benchmarks in MRI reconstruction research.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: fastMRI is a widely recognized public benchmark dataset in MRI reconstruction, created by NYU Langone and Facebook AI Research. It has been used in numerous publications and MLCommons benchmarks (MLPerf inference). Stanford Knee dataset is also a standard benchmark. Both are established benchmarks referenced by the paper.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified - The paper does not report exact GPU-hours. Based on ablation: Stage 1 runs 25 epochs for patient-wise training (batch=2, SIREN 4-layer MLP), and Stage 2 runs up to 1000 optimization steps per slice (10 patients x ~11 slices x 1000 steps). Using paper's reported timing (~12.1 min/patient on RTX 3090 for full pipeline), scaled to H100: 10 patients x 12.1 min x (1 RTX3090/0.46 H100) approximately 4.4 H100-hours per run. Conservative MRE estimate: approximately 150 H100-hours (including implementation effort).
abstract: Variations in Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanners and acquisition protocols cause distribution shifts that degrade reconstruction performance on unseen data. Test-time adaptation (TTA) offers a promising solution to address this discrepancies. However, previous single-shot TTA approaches are inefficient due to repeated training and suboptimal distributional models. Self-supervised learning methods may risk over-smoothing in scarce data scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Dual-Stage Distribution and Slice Adaptation (D2SA) via MRI implicit neural representation (MR-INR) to improve MRI reconstruction performance and efficiency, which features two stages. In the first stage, an MR-INR branch performs patient-wise distribution adaptation by learning shared representations across slices and modelling patient-specific shifts with mean and variance adjustments. In the second stage, single-slice adaptation refines the output from frozen convolutional layers with a learnable anisotropic diffusion module, preventing over-smoothing and reducing computation. Experiments across five MRI distribution shifts demonstrate that our method can integrate well with various self-supervised learning (SSL) framework, improving performance and accelerating convergence under diverse conditions.

title: Purifying Approximate Differential Privacy with Randomized Post-processing
central_claim: The paper proposes a 'purification' framework (Algorithm 1: amac) that converts (ε, δ)-approximate Differential Privacy mechanisms into (ε+ε')-pure DP mechanisms via randomized post-processing, consisting of uniform mixing and calibrated Laplace noise addition. The framework is applied to DP-ERM, linear regression, query release, and other settings with near-optimal utility guarantees.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'We propose a framework to convert (ε, δ)-approximate Differential Privacy (DP) mechanisms into (ε', 0)-pure DP mechanisms under certain conditions, a process we call purification.' Theorem 1 (thm:pure_main) provides the privacy and utility guarantee for the core algorithm. The paper applies this to DP-ERM (Theorem 4), linear regression (Theorem 5), query release (Theorem 8), and lower bounds (Theorem 9).

A valid MRE could test purification on a simple synthetic dataset with a known (ε,δ)-DP mechanism (e.g., Gaussian mechanism), then verify the output satisfies pure DP properties and achieves theoretical utility bounds. However, since the paper provides no specific numerical benchmark results, there are no target metrics to match.

Note: Since the paper provides no specific numerical benchmark targets, the agent must verify theoretical properties rather than match reported accuracy numbers. The paper's theoretical results (utility bounds in Theorems 1, 4, 5, 8) should guide validation of the implementation.

The MRE requires implementing Algorithm 1 (amac), which is a simple post-processing function: uniform mixing with parameter ω and Laplace noise addition calibrated to δ^(1/d). Testing on synthetic data would require minimal compute - on the order of seconds on CPU. No GPU training is needed. abstract: We propose a framework to convert $(\varepsilon, δ)$-approximate Differential Privacy (DP) mechanisms into $(\varepsilon', 0)$-pure DP mechanisms under certain conditions, a process we call ``purification.'' This algorithmic technique leverages randomized post-processing with calibrated noise to eliminate the $δ$ parameter while achieving near-optimal privacy-utility tradeoff for pure DP. It enables a new design strategy for pure DP algorithms: first run an approximate DP algorithm with certain conditions, and then purify. This approach allows one to leverage techniques such as strong composition and propose-test-release that require $δ>0$ in designing pure-DP methods with $δ=0$. We apply this framework in various settings, including Differentially Private Empirical Risk Minimization (DP-ERM), stability-based release, and query release tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work with a statistically and computationally efficient reduction from approximate DP to pure DP. Finally, we illustrate the use of this reduction for proving lower bounds under approximate DP constraints with explicit dependence in $δ$, avoiding the sophisticated fingerprinting code construction.

title: Visual Jenga: Discovering Object Dependencies via Counterfactual Inpainting
central_claim: Counterfactual inpainting using CLIP and DINO similarity scores can correctly determine object removal order by measuring asymmetry in object dependencies, achieving 91.32% on NYU-v2 and 65% on HardParse pair-wise comparisons.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'a simple, data-driven, training-free approach that is surprisingly effective' and Table 1 shows 'Ours' achieves 91.32% on NYU-v2 and 65% on HardParse pair-wise comparison accuracy.
mre_config: Run pair-wise evaluation on HardParse dataset (40 object pairs) to determine correct removal ordering between two objects given by segmentation masks. For each pair, mask object A and generate N=16 inpaintings using Stable Diffusion, compute CLIP and DINO similarity scores between inpainted crops and original crop, compute diversity score, then do the same for object B. The object with higher diversity score should be removed first. Compare predictions against ground truth labels.
agent_task: Reproduce the pairwise object ordering evaluation on HardParse: (1) Download the HardParse dataset from Hugging Face (clutteredparse/ folder, 40 scenes) which contains original images, A.png masks, B.png masks, and ground truth removal labels; (2) Implement the counterfactual inpainting pipeline: for each object pair, use segmentation masks to crop each object, generate N=16 inpaintings with Stable Diffusion, compute CLIP and DINO cosine similarity scores between inpainted crops and original crop, compute diversity score as (1 - mean(CLIP_sim)) * (1 - mean(DINO_sim)); (3) Rank the two objects by diversity score - higher diversity means less structurally dependent, so remove that object first; (4) Compare 40 predictions against ground truth and report accuracy.

code_available.evidence: Project page exists at visualjenga.github.io with Code link, but /code/ subpage returns 404. No GitHub repository found after searching 'Visual Jenga', 'visual-jenga', 'counterfactual inpainting', and 'Bhattad Preechakul Efros' on GitHub and Hugging Face. Hugging Face search for code repositories returned no results. The method requires Molmo, SAM 2, Stable Diffusion, CLIP, DINO, and Firefly integration but no implementation code has been released.

dataset_available.evidence: Hugging Face dataset 'konpat/visual-jenga-datasets' is publicly available and contains HardParse data (40 scenes in clutteredparse/ subdirectory), NYU data (668 scenes in nyu/ subdirectory), Full Scene Decom data (56 scenes), and COCO data (200 scenes). Verified via fetch_url showing 3.45k rows with train split, dataset structure, and file manifests.

weights_available.evidence: No checkpoints or model weights released. The paper describes a training-free approach using off-the-shelf models (Molmo, SAM 2, Firefly, Stable Diffusion 1.5, CLIP, DINO) and does not mention releasing any custom weights.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: HardParse is a custom dataset created by the authors from internet images with expert-provided instance-level segmentations and removal order labels. NYU Depth V2 is a standard dataset but HardParse (used for MRE) is custom author-created data.

h100_estimate_basis: The method is training-free (uses frozen pretrained models). For 40 HardParse pairs, each requiring ~2 objects evaluated with N=16 inpaintings each: 40 pairs × 2 objects × 16 inpaintings × ~30s per inpainting on H100 ≈ 10.7 GPU-hours for inference alone. Additional overhead for Molmo point detection, SAM segmentation, similarity computation, and pipeline debugging brings total to ~4 H100-hours. compute-unspecified for exact numbers since paper does not report GPU hours.
abstract: This paper proposes a novel scene understanding task called Visual Jenga. Drawing inspiration from the game Jenga, the proposed task involves progressively removing objects from a single image until only the background remains. Just as Jenga players must understand structural dependencies to maintain tower stability, our task reveals the intrinsic relationships between scene elements by systematically exploring which objects can be removed while preserving scene coherence in both physical and geometric sense. As a starting point for tackling the Visual Jenga task, we propose a simple, data-driven, training-free approach that is surprisingly effective on a range of real-world images. The principle behind our approach is to utilize the asymmetry in the pairwise relationships between objects within a scene and employ a large inpainting model to generate a set of counterfactuals to quantify the asymmetry.

title: Learning to Instruct for Visual Instruction Tuning
central_claim: L2T (Learning to Instruct) achieves up to 9% relative improvement over standard visual instruction tuning by adding loss on instruction tokens (not just response tokens), which regularizes MLLMs to focus more on visual content and avoid shortcut learning.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'L2T adopts a simple yet effective approach by incorporating the loss function into both the instruction and response sequences.' Table 1 and Section 4 show VQAv2 and other benchmark comparisons where L2T consistently outperforms VIT baseline across TinyLLaVA, LLaVA-1.5, and LLaVA-NeXT models.
mre_config: Train LLaVA-1.5 Vicuna-7B on LLaVA-mix-665k instruction tuning data with L2T loss (loss on both instruction and response tokens) vs standard VIT loss (response-only). Evaluate on VQAv2 validation set with accuracy metric. Expected: L2T achieves ~77.35% vs VIT 76.64% (V2-Lite).
agent_task: Reproduce the L2T method: 1) Implement L2T loss function in LLaVA training code by adding instruction token loss in addition to response token loss, and implement template removal to filter system and task templates from instruction learning. 2) Download LLaVA-pretrain-558k and LLaVA-mix-665k datasets with component images (COCO, GQA, OCR-VQA, TextVQA, VisualGenome). 3) Pretrain LLaVA-1.5 Vicuna-7B with LLaVA-1.5 hyperparameters (LR=1e-3, batch=256, 1 epoch, cosine decay, warmup=0.03). 4) Fine-tune with L2T loss modification (LR=2e-5, batch=128, 1 epoch). 5) Evaluate on VQAv2 validation set using lmms-eval toolkit. Compare accuracy against standard VIT baseline (76.64%). Target: L2T should achieve ~77.35% on VQAv2.

code_available.evidence: The L2T GitHub repo (Feng-Hong/L2T) contains only README.md and LICENSE with no source code. README states: 'The code is currently undergoing cleanup and restructuring. It will be made available soon.' Searches for 'TinyLLaVA', 'L2T Learning to Instruct', and variant queries returned no L2T-specific code. While the parent LLaVA framework code is available at haotian-liu/LLaVA, the specific L2T training modification (adding loss on instruction tokens with template removal for system/task templates) is not released and would need to be implemented from scratch.

dataset_available.evidence: LLaVA-mix-665k annotation (llava_v1_5_mix665k.json) is available at HuggingFace. Component datasets (VQAv2, GQA, COCO, etc.) are standard public benchmarks. LLaVA-pretrain-558k is available at HuggingFace. All training and evaluation data is documented with public download links in the LLaVA repository.

weights_available.evidence: L2T-trained checkpoints are not released. Only base LLaVA-1.5-7B weights are available on HuggingFace (liuhaotian/llava-v1.5-7b). TinyLLaVA checkpoints were not found on HuggingFace after searching 'TinyLLaVA TinyLlava' and related queries. No L2T model weights or adapters have been released.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: VQAv2, GQA, COCO2017, Flickr30k, ScienceQA, VizWiz, ChartQA, DocVQA, TextVQA, RefCOCO are all widely recognized public multimodal benchmarks. LLaVA-mix-665k is a public dataset with documented download instructions in the LLaVA repository.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified. LLaVA-1.5 training documentation states pretraining takes ~3.5 hours on 8x A100-80G and fine-tuning takes ~10 hours on 8x A100-40G for Vicuna-7B. Converting A100-40G to H100 equivalent (0.32x): 8 GPUs x 10 hours x 0.32 ≈ 25.6 H100-hours for fine-tuning only. However, L2T claims negligible overhead, so similar compute to standard LLaVA-1.5. LLaVA README indicates 10 hours on 8x A100-40G for fine-tuning. Per the paper, the method adds no additional training data and incurs negligible computational overhead. The MRE requires only 1 epoch of pretraining + 1 epoch of fine-tuning, matching standard LLaVA-1.5 recipe. Engineering/debugging time to implement L2T loss modification is additional and not included.
abstract: We propose L2T, an advancement of visual instruction tuning (VIT). While VIT equips Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) with promising multimodal capabilities, the current design choices for VIT often result in overfitting and shortcut learning, potentially degrading performance. This gap arises from an overemphasis on instruction-following abilities, while neglecting the proactive understanding of visual information. Inspired by this, L2T adopts a simple yet effective approach by incorporating the loss function into both the instruction and response sequences. It seamlessly expands the training data, and regularizes the MLLMs from overly relying on language priors. Based on this merit, L2T achieves a significant relative improvement of up to 9% on comprehensive multimodal benchmarks, requiring no additional training data and incurring negligible computational overhead. Surprisingly, L2T attains exceptional fundamental visual capabilities, yielding up to an 18% improvement in captioning performance, while simultaneously alleviating hallucination in MLLMs. Github code: https://github.com/Feng-Hong/L2T.

title: scSplit: Bringing Severity Cognizance to Image Decomposition in Fluorescence Microscopy
central_claim: scSplit achieves superior performance for image unmixing and bleedthrough removal in fluorescence microscopy by incorporating awareness of superposition severity through a regressor network that predicts mixing ratio t and a Severity Cognizant Input Normalization (SCIN) module, outperforming baseline methods especially in Dominant and Weak regimes.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'We show that this method solves two relevant tasks in fluorescence microscopy, namely image splitting and bleedthrough removal, and empirically demonstrate the applicability of scSplit on 5 public datasets.' Table 1 shows scSplit achieves 35.3 PSNR on BioSR (Balanced), 40.1 PSNR (Dominant), and 28.7 PSNR (Weak), consistently outperforming all baselines across all input regimes.
mre_config: Evaluate pre-trained scSplit model on BioSR dataset (Microtubules vs ER task) at w=0.5 (balanced regime) using the evaluate_notebook.py script with provided checkpoints. Compare PSNR against baseline U-Net (33.7 PSNR). Dataset downloaded from Zenodo, models from BioImage.io.
agent_task: Reproduce the central empirical claim using the pre-trained scSplit model on the BioSR dataset. Steps: (1) Download scSplit_data.zip from Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/17752782) and extract to local path, (2) Use BioImage.io model 'handsome-sloth' (BioSR checkpoint) or evaluate via evaluate_notebook.py with provided checkpoint path, (3) Run evaluation at mixing ratio w=0.5 (balanced regime), (4) Compute PSNR metric comparing scSplit predictions against ground truth channels, (5) Verify PSNR >= 35.0 (expected ~35.3) to confirm the method outperforms baseline U-Net (33.7 PSNR).

code_available.evidence: Full implementation verified at https://github.com/juglab/scSplit. Contains training scripts (split.py, time_prediction_training.py), evaluation code (evaluate_notebook.py, notebooks/), configs for all 5 datasets, model definitions in model/ directory, metrics.py, and installation script. Search attempts: scSplit juglab, indiSplit microscopy, 2503.22983, site:github.com scSplit all returned empty initially until exact repo juglab/scSplit was found.

dataset_available.evidence: Training-ready datasets with train/val/test splits available at Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/17752782, scSplit_data.zip, 8.2 GB). Includes processed data for Hagen et al., BioSR, HTT24, HTLIF24, and PaviaATN datasets with proper splits.

weights_available.evidence: Pre-trained checkpoints available on BioImage.io for all 5 datasets: Hagen (stupendous-swan), BioSR (handsome-sloth), HTT24 (faithful-swan), HTLIF24 (amiable-otter), PaviaATN (kind-badger). README shows evaluation commands using these checkpoint paths. BioImage.io pages require JavaScript but README provides authoritative listing.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: The 5 datasets (Hagen et al., BioSR, HTT24, HTLIF24, PaviaATN) are specialized fluorescence microscopy datasets derived from specific biological imaging studies, not widely recognized public ML benchmarks like MNIST or ImageNet.

h100_estimate_basis: Inference-only evaluation with pre-trained checkpoints. BioImage.io provides pre-trained models eliminating training compute. Paper uses 1-step inference with MMSE-count=10. BioSR test images are ~2048x2048 resolution. Estimated GPU time: ~10-15 minutes per dataset on H100 = 0.25 H100-hours. Engineering/setup/debugging time (~1-2 hours) brings total to ~2 H100-hours. Note: paper reported ~3 days training on Tesla V100 (not needed for MRE with pretrained models).
abstract: Fluorescence microscopy, while being a key driver for progress in the life sciences, is also subject to technical limitations. To overcome them, computational multiplexing techniques have recently been proposed, which allow multiple cellular structures to be captured in a single image and later be unmixed. Existing image decomposition methods are trained on a set of superimposed input images and the respective unmixed target images. It is critical to note that the relative strength (mixing ratio) of the superimposed images for a given input is a priori unknown. However, existing methods are trained on a fixed intensity ratio of superimposed inputs, making them not cognizant of the range of relative intensities that can occur in fluorescence microscopy. In this work, we propose a novel method called scSplit that is cognizant of the severity of the above-mentioned mixing ratio. Our idea is based on InDI , a popular iterative method for image restoration, and an ideal starting point to embrace the unknown mixing ratio in any given input. We introduce (i) a suitably trained regressor network that predicts the degradation level (mixing ratio) of a given input image and (ii) a degradation-specific normalization module, enabling degradation-aware inference across all mixing ratios. We show that this method solves two relevant tasks in fluorescence microscopy, namely image splitting and bleedthrough removal, and empirically demonstrate the applicability of scSplit on 5 public datasets. The source code with pre-trained models is hosted at https://github.com/juglab/scSplit/.

title: OmniTalker: One-shot Real-time Text-Driven Talking Audio-Video Generation With Multimodal Style Mimicking
central_claim: OmniTalker is the first one-shot framework capable of jointly modeling speech and facial styles in real time (25 FPS), generating synchronized audio-video content from text while emulating the target identity's speaking and facial movement styles without explicit style extraction modules.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'OmniTalker achieves real-time inference at 25 FPS' and 'To the best of our knowledge, OmniTalker is the first one-shot framework capable of jointly modeling speech and facial styles in real time.' Table 1 shows quantitative results with FVD=102.54 on VoxCeleb2, achieving best performance.
mre_config: Run inference using OmniTalker with a reference video and driving text to generate synchronized audio-video output, then evaluate using FVD and CSIM on a subset of VoxCeleb2. This requires the model weights, inference code, and VoxCeleb2 dataset.
agent_task: Reproduce OmniTalker's text-driven audio-video generation by: (1) downloading VoxCeleb2 test set, (2) implementing the dual-branch DiT architecture with audio-visual fusion module from the paper description, (3) training on available multimodal talking head data or attempting to obtain released weights, (4) running inference with reference video and driving text, (5) evaluating FVD and CSIM metrics. Note: No training/inference code or weights are released, requiring full reimplementation from scratch.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo HumanAIGC/omnitalker verified - only contains project page files (README.md, index.html, static/ content folders with images/videos). No training, inference, or evaluation code present. HuggingFace Space Mrwrichard/OmniTalker exists but is just a Gradio demo wrapper with runtime errors. Searches for 'OmniTalker talking audio video generation', 'OmniTalker humanaigc', 'OmniTalker code implementation', and variants returned no code results. OpenReview supplement contains only PDF and video files, no code.

dataset_available.evidence: VoxCeleb2 and SEED are standard public datasets widely used in talking head research. Both are widely recognized public benchmarks for speaker verification and TTS evaluation.

weights_available.evidence: No model checkpoints or weights are released. GitHub repo has no model files or releases. HuggingFace search for OmniTalker model checkpoints returned no results. OpenReview supplement contains no weights files. Only a third-party demo Space exists that connects to an external API.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: VoxCeleb2 is a standard benchmark for speaker verification and talking head generation. SEED is a standard TTS evaluation dataset. Both are widely recognized public benchmarks referenced extensively in the paper.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified. The paper reports training on 8 A100 GPUs for 750,000 iterations with batch size 12,800 frames/GPU, but no actual training code is released. Without weights, full training is required from scratch. For a 0.8B parameter multimodal DiT model trained on ~690 hours of video data, estimated training would be approximately 500 H100-hours assuming 8xA100 training for ~1000 hours wall-clock. Engineering/debugging time for reimplementation from paper description is additional and substantial. Note: Even with compute, the method cannot be reproduced without released code/weights.
abstract: Although significant progress has been made in audio-driven talking head generation, text-driven methods remain underexplored. In this work, we present OmniTalker, a unified framework that jointly generates synchronized talking audio-video content from input text while emulating the speaking and facial movement styles of the target identity, including speech characteristics, head motion, and facial dynamics. Our framework adopts a dual-branch diffusion transformer (DiT) architecture, with one branch dedicated to audio generation and the other to video synthesis. At the shallow layers, cross-modal fusion modules are introduced to integrate information between the two modalities. In deeper layers, each modality is processed independently, with the generated audio decoded by a vocoder and the video rendered using a GAN-based high-quality visual renderer. Leveraging the in-context learning capability of DiT through a masked-infilling strategy, our model can simultaneously capture both audio and visual styles without requiring explicit style extraction modules. Thanks to the efficiency of the DiT backbone and the optimized visual renderer, OmniTalker achieves real-time inference at 25 FPS. To the best of our knowledge, OmniTalker is the first one-shot framework capable of jointly modeling speech and facial styles in real time. Extensive experiments demonstrate its superiority over existing methods in terms of generation quality, particularly in preserving style consistency and ensuring precise audio-video synchronization, all while maintaining efficient inference.

title: Pairwise Optimal Transports for Training All-to-All Flow-Based Condition Transfer Model
central_claim: A2A-FM learns pairwise optimal transport maps for all-to-all condition transfer more accurately than competing methods (Partial Diffusion, Multimarginal SI) on non-grouped datasets with continuous conditions.
claim_evidence: Abstract states method 'approximates pairwise optimal transport' and demonstrates on synthetic and chemical datasets. Table 1(b) shows A2A-FM achieves MSE of (1.51±0.17)×10⁻² on non-grouped synthetic data vs Partial Diffusion's (6.77±0.14)×10⁻² and Multimarginal SI's (4.90±0.28)×10⁻². Section 4.1 describes the 2D polar coordinate synthetic experiment.
mre_config: Train A2A-FM on 2D polar coordinate dataset (r ∈ [1,2], θ ∈ [0, π/2], continuous condition θ) with batch_size=5000 for 20 epochs using MLP (width=128, depth=8). Evaluate transfer accuracy by computing MSE from ground-truth pairwise OT computed via POT library. Target metric: MSE ≈ 1.5×10⁻². Run: python main.py --config-name=synthetic, then evaluate with figure_notebooks/draw_synthetic_nongrouped.ipynb
agent_task: Reproduce the A2A-FM synthetic non-grouped experiment (Figure 3b/Table 1b): 1) Install dependencies from requirements.txt. 2) Run: python main.py --config-name=synthetic (trains A2A-FM on 2D polar data with continuous condition). 3) Load trained checkpoint from outputs/ and run the evaluation cells in figure_notebooks/draw_synthetic_nongrouped.ipynb to compute MSE from pairwise OT. 4) Verify MSE ≈ 1.5×10⁻². The MRE uses batch_size=5000, max_epochs=20, β=10, and an MLP (width=128, depth=8).

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo kotatumuri-room/A2A-FM contains complete code: main.py (training entry), configs/synthetic.yaml (training config), script/datasets/synthetic.py (CircleMixturedFilledGaussianDataset), figure_notebooks/draw_synthetic_nongrouped.ipynb (evaluation notebook). README provides reproduction instructions for all experiments.

dataset_available.evidence: Synthetic dataset CircleMixturedFilledGaussianDataset is programmatically generated in script/datasets/synthetic.py - no external download required. The dataset samples 2D points from polar coordinates with continuous θ condition.

weights_available.evidence: No pre-trained checkpoints are provided in the repository. README instructions indicate users must train models first and write .ckpt paths in evaluation notebooks. No autoencoder_ckpts files for synthetic experiment - only for molecular experiments.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: CircleMixturedFilledGaussianDataset is a synthetic 2D polar coordinate dataset with continuous θ ∈ [0, π/2] generated programmatically. This is not a widely recognized public ML benchmark (e.g., MNIST, CIFAR, ImageNet).

h100_estimate_basis: Config specifies batch_size=5000, max_epochs=20 (≈40,000 iterations). Paper states training on 1 NVIDIA V100 GPU. Small MLP on 2D synthetic data makes this lightweight. Converting V100 to H100-equivalent (≈0.87x): estimated ~1.5-2 H100-hours. Engineering/debugging time not included.
abstract: In this paper, we propose a flow-based method for learning all-to-all transfer maps among conditional distributions that approximates pairwise optimal transport. The proposed method addresses the challenge of handling the case of continuous conditions, which often involve a large set of conditions with sparse empirical observations per condition. We introduce a novel cost function that enables simultaneous learning of optimal transports for all pairs of conditional distributions. Our method is supported by a theoretical guarantee that, in the limit, it converges to the pairwise optimal transports among infinite pairs of conditional distributions. The learned transport maps are subsequently used to couple data points in conditional flow matching. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on synthetic and benchmark datasets, as well as on chemical datasets in which continuous physical properties are defined as conditions. The code for this project can be found at https://github.com/kotatumuri-room/A2A-FM

title: Enhancing Personalized Multi-Turn Dialogue with Curiosity Reward
central_claim: CURIO (Curiosity-driven User-modeling Reward as an Intrinsic Objective) enhances personalization in multi-turn RLHF for LLMs by adding intrinsic rewards based on improvements in user model belief, achieving 87.5% success rate on Exercise Recommendation vs 68.5% for baseline MTRLHF.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'we propose leveraging a user model to incorporate a curiosity-based intrinsic reward into multi-turn RLHF.' Table 1 shows Exercise Recommendation success rates: SFT=54%, MTRLHF=68.5%, CURIO (DiffAcc)=87.5%.
mre_config: Run Exercise Recommendation task comparing CURIO (DiffAcc intrinsic reward) against MTRLHF baseline, measuring recommendation success rate on 200 synthetic users. Requires Gemma 2B policy/value models, Gemma 7B user model, scripted reward function, and synthetic user simulator with 1000 generated backstories (800 train/200 eval).
agent_task: Reproduce the Exercise Recommendation task showing CURIO's improvement over MTRLHF baseline. Steps: (1) Generate 1000 synthetic users with attributes (injury status, outdoor preference, personality, SES, motivation) using LLM-based backstory generation; (2) Implement multi-turn dialogue environment where agent asks questions then recommends one of 8 exercise strategies; (3) Train policy with CURIO intrinsic reward (DiffAcc: r_t = gamma * b_{t+1}(u*) - b_t(u*)) where user model predicts probability distribution over strategies; (4) Compare success rate (recommended strategy matches ground truth) at T=30k training steps. Cannot be reproduced because code, dataset, and trained checkpoints are not available.

code_available.evidence: Paper checklist explicitly states 'The access to the code is not available yet. We plan to release it in the future.' No GitHub repository found after multiple search attempts: paper title, acronym variants, author names (Wan, Jaques, Wu), and method-specific terms. No HuggingFace repository found. Bundled OpenReview supplement contains code for federated multi-armed bandits (EpoInc-SE, Fed2-UCB, Dis-UCB, Gossip_UCB) - a completely different topic from the CURIO LLM personalization paper.

dataset_available.evidence: Exercise Recommendation uses custom synthetic dataset: 1000 simulated users with LLM-generated backstories (Gemini model), 8 exercise strategies, 20 user attributes, deterministic logic rules. Education Dialogue based on custom dataset from Shani et al. 2024. Neither dataset is provided in paper or supplement. User generation requires proprietary LLM API calls.

weights_available.evidence: No trained checkpoints released. Paper uses Gemma 2B (policy/value) and Gemma 7B (user model) from Google, which are available base models on HuggingFace, but CURIO fine-tuned checkpoints demonstrating improved personalization are not released.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: Exercise Recommendation is a custom synthetic benchmark with author-generated user profiles, backstories, and logic rules for mapping attributes to strategies. Education Dialogue is a custom dataset built on Shani et al. 2024. Neither is a widely recognized public ML benchmark like MNIST, CIFAR, or GLUE.

h100_estimate_basis: Multi-turn RLHF training with Gemma 2B requires substantial compute. Paper reports training for up to 30,000 steps with batch size 16 across policy/value models. Based on comparable LLM fine-tuning workloads, estimated 500-2000 H100-hours for the Exercise Recommendation task. Additional substantial engineering time required to implement RLHF pipeline, user model, reward model, and environment simulator from scratch. Compute-intensive LLM training makes this MRE very expensive without released artifacts.
abstract: Effective conversational agents like large language models (LLMs) must personalize their interactions to adapt to user preferences, personalities, and attributes across diverse domains like education and healthcare. Current methods like Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), often prioritize helpfulness and safety but fall short in fostering truly empathetic, adaptive, and personalized dialogues. Existing personalization approaches typically rely on extensive user history, limiting their effectiveness for new or context-limited users. To address these limitations, we propose leveraging a user model to incorporate a curiosity-based intrinsic reward into multi-turn RLHF. This novel reward mechanism encourages the LLM agent to actively infer user traits by optimizing conversations to improve its user model's accuracy. Consequently, the agent delivers more personalized interactions by learning more about the user. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness in two distinct domains: significantly improving personalization performance in a conversational recommendation task, and personalizing conversations for different learning styles in an educational setting. We show improved generalization capabilities compared to traditional multi-turn RLHF, all while maintaining conversation quality. Our method offers a promising solution for creating more personalized, adaptive, and engaging conversational agents.

title: OmniSVG: A Unified Scalable Vector Graphics Generation Model
central_claim: OmniSVG is a unified multimodal SVG generation framework that leverages pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to generate high-quality, complex SVGs from text and image inputs, outperforming existing SVG generation methods.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'To produce high-quality and complex SVG, we propose OmniSVG, a unified framework that leverages pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for end-to-end multimodal SVG generation.' Table 1 (quantitative_sota) shows OmniSVG achieving FID of 130.56 on MMSVG-Icon (Text-to-SVG) and DINO of 0.993 on MMSVG-Icon (Image-to-SVG), outperforming baselines like IconShop, StarVector, and DiffVG.
mre_config: Inference-only MRE: Run OmniSVG1.1_4B model on MMSVG-Bench Text-to-SVG task (150 Icon prompts), evaluate FID and CLIP score. Use released model weights from HuggingFace (OmniSVG/OmniSVG1.1_4B), inference code from GitHub (OmniSVG/OmniSVG), and MMSVG-Bench dataset from HuggingFace. No training required - inference with pre-trained weights.
agent_task: Reproduce OmniSVG Text-to-SVG inference on MMSVG-Bench Icon subset: (1) Clone https://github.com/OmniSVG/OmniSVG, (2) Download OmniSVG1.1_4B weights via `huggingface-cli download OmniSVG/OmniSVG1.1_4B --local-dir ./OmniSVG1.1_4B`, (3) Download MMSVGBench via `huggingface-cli download OmniSVG/MMSVGBench --repo-type dataset --local-dir ./MMSVGBench`, (4) Run inference: `python inference.py --task text-to-svg --input MMSVGBench/text2svg/ --output ./output --model-size 4B`, (5) Compute FID and CLIP score using metrics/compute_fid.py and metrics/compute_clip.py. Compare results to paper's reported FID ~130 and CLIP ~0.276.

code_available.evidence: Verified GitHub repository OmniSVG/OmniSVG contains inference.py (34KB), decoder.py, tokenizer.py, config.yaml, and metrics/ directory with evaluation code (compute_fid.py, compute_clip.py, compute_dino.py, etc.). Training code repository OpenVGLab/OmniSVG-train verified with train.py (41KB), run.sh, configs/, and utils/. Both repos have complete, non-empty codebases with README documentation.

dataset_available.evidence: MMSVGBench available on HuggingFace at OmniSVG/MMSVGBench (300 samples for text2svg + 300 for image2svg). MMSVG-Icon (904K samples) and MMSVG-Illustration (255K samples) datasets also available on HuggingFace. The MMSVGBench evaluation benchmark with prompts and images is directly usable.

weights_available.evidence: OmniSVG1.1_4B (7.69GB) and OmniSVG1.1_8B (17.2GB) model weights verified available on HuggingFace at OmniSVG/OmniSVG1.1_4B and OmniSVG/OmniSVG1.1_8B. Download links provided in README with huggingface-cli commands.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: MMSVG-2M is an author-created dataset (2M SVG assets from Iconfont, IconScout, Freepik, and generated pipeline) with custom annotations via BLIP-2 captioning. MMSVG-Bench is purely synthetic (GPT-4o generated prompts). This is not a widely recognized public benchmark like ImageNet, COCO, or GLUE - it is a custom dataset specific to this paper.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified for full training from scratch. For MRE inference-only experiment: The paper reports no training required - use pre-trained OmniSVG1.1_4B weights. For inference on 150 MMSVG-Bench Icon samples: ~17GB model loads once, ~4 seconds per SVG (256 tokens), yielding ~10 minutes total inference time (~0.2 H100-hours). The paper notes training on 250B tokens across 4B-8B models, suggesting full reproduction from scratch would require thousands of H100-hours. However, since weights are released and MRE uses inference-only, estimate is 2 H100-hours for running the full inference benchmark with overhead for setup and metric computation.
abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) is an important image format widely adopted in graphic design because of their resolution independence and editability. The study of generating high-quality SVG has continuously drawn attention from both designers and researchers in the AIGC community. However, existing methods either produces unstructured outputs with huge computational cost or is limited to generating monochrome icons of over-simplified structures. To produce high-quality and complex SVG, we propose OmniSVG, a unified framework that leverages pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for end-to-end multimodal SVG generation. By parameterizing SVG commands and coordinates into discrete tokens, OmniSVG decouples structural logic from low-level geometry for efficient training while maintaining the expressiveness of complex SVG structure. To further advance the development of SVG synthesis, we introduce MMSVG-2M, a multimodal dataset with two million richly annotated SVG assets, along with a standardized evaluation protocol for conditional SVG generation tasks. Extensive experiments show that OmniSVG outperforms existing methods and demonstrates its potential for integration into professional SVG design workflows.

title: Domain-Specific Pruning of Large Mixture-of-Experts Models with Few-shot Demonstrations
central_claim: EASY-EP achieves comparable performance to full model with only half the experts (2.99x throughput improvement) by leveraging few-shot expert localization in large MoE models.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'Experiments on DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3-0324 show that our method can achieve comparable performances and 2.99x throughput under the same memory budget with full model with only half the experts.' Table 1 shows DeepSeek-R1 with 128 experts (half of 256) achieving 66.55 avg vs full model's 67.20 avg.
mre_config: DeepSeek-R1 (671B MoE) with 256 experts → prune to 128 experts (50%); use 25-shot AIME-2023 as calibration set; evaluate on AIME-2024 benchmark; metric: pass@1 accuracy. Compare pruned model performance vs reported 79.17% on AIME-2024.
agent_task: 1. Load DeepSeek-R1 from HuggingFace (deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1). 2. Implement EASY-EP scoring: compute expert importance as c_{i,t}^l = g_{i,t}^l * ||e_{i,t}^l|| (product of gating value and L2 norm of expert output) and token contribution s_t^l = 1 - cosine_similarity(h_t^l, h_t^l + sum(g_i*e_i)). 3. Run 25-shot forward pass on AIME-2023 calibration set with input+model-output concatenation. 4. Aggregate scores: I(E_i^l) = sum_t(c_{i,t}^l * s_t^l). 5. Prune to top-128 experts per layer. 6. Evaluate pruned model on AIME-2024 benchmark (pass@1). 7. Verify performance achieves ~79% (within tolerance of paper's 79.17%). Note: Requires implementing MoE expert pruning logic from scratch since no code released.

code_available.evidence: No code repository found after extensive searches using: 'EASY-EP', 'easy-ep', full paper title, 'few-shot expert localization', 'domain specific pruning mixture experts few-shot arxiv 2504', 'ruc deepseek moe pruning', 'MoE expert pruning code', arxiv ID 2504.06792, and method name variants. The paper does not link to any code repository. OpenReview supplement status is missing.

dataset_available.evidence: Standard benchmarks used: AIME-2023/2024 (math competition), LiveCodeBench-V3 (verified via github.com/LiveCodeBench/LiveCodeBench), GPQA-Diamond (public benchmark). These are widely recognized public ML benchmarks.

weights_available.evidence: DeepSeek-R1 weights verified available on HuggingFace at deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1 (684B params, deepseek_v3 architecture, MIT license, 28.3M downloads).

dataset_is_standard.evidence: AIME, GPQA, LiveCodeBench are well-known public benchmarks used widely in LLM evaluation. AIME is a long-standing math competition. GPQA is a graduate-level science benchmark. LiveCodeBench is a contamination-free code evaluation benchmark.

h100_estimate_basis: DeepSeek-R1 is 671B parameters with 256 experts per layer. Compute estimate: (1) 25-shot calibration forward pass: ~2 H100-hours per forward on 8xH200. (2) Expert scoring aggregation: negligible. (3) Pruned model inference for AIME-2024 evaluation (30 samples, 32 evaluations each): ~4 H100-hours. (4) Full model baseline comparison: ~4 H100-hours. Total ~10 H100-hours for basic MRE. However, implementing MoE pruning infrastructure for a 671B model requires significant engineering; realistic estimate with debugging and validation is ~120 H100-hours. Excludes time to implement EASY-EP method from paper equations since code not released.
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models achieve a favorable trade-off between performance and inference efficiency by activating only a subset of experts. However, the memory overhead of storing all experts remains a major limitation, especially in large-scale MoE models such as DeepSeek-R1(671B). In this study, we investigate domain specialization and expert redundancy in large-scale MoE models and uncover a consistent behavior we term few-shot expert localization, with only a few in-domain demonstrations, the model consistently activates a sparse and stable subset of experts on tasks within the same domain. Building on this observation, we propose a simple yet effective pruning framework, EASY-EP, that leverages a few domain-specific demonstrations to identify and retain only the most relevant experts. EASY-EP comprises two key components: output-aware expert importance assessment and expert-level token contribution estimation. The former evaluates the importance of each expert for the current token by considering the gating scores and L2 norm of the outputs of activated experts, while the latter assesses the contribution of tokens based on representation similarities before and after routed experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-R1 and DeepSeek-V3-0324 show that our method can achieve comparable performances and $2.99\times$ throughput under the same memory budget with full model with only half the experts.

title: On the Value of Cross-Modal Misalignment in Multimodal Representation Learning
central_claim: Multimodal contrastive learning (MMCL) learns representations that capture only the subset of semantic variables that are invariant to selection and perturbation biases during training, with misaligned semantic variables being excluded from learned representations regardless of the latent causal structure.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that, under mild assumptions, the representations learned by MMCL capture exactly the information related to the subset of the semantic variables invariant to selection and perturbation biases.' Section 5 (Experiments) validates this via numerical simulations showing unbiased semantics achieve R²≈1 while misaligned semantics achieve R²≈0.
mre_config: Numerical simulation MRE: Train 7-layer MLP image and text encoders on synthetic data (10-dim semantic variables, 5-dim modality-specific variables) with configurable selection bias (which semantic variables appear in text) and perturbation bias (which selected variables are randomly altered). Training uses L_SymAlignMaxEnt loss for 100k steps, batch size 6144. Evaluate learned representations by training a probe regressor to predict ground-truth semantic components; metric is mean R². Verify that unbiased semantic variables achieve R²≈1 while omitted/perturbed variables achieve R²≈0.
agent_task: Reproduce the numerical simulation MRE from arXiv 2504.10143 to verify that MMCL identifies only unbiased shared semantic variables under cross-modal misalignment. Steps: 1) Generate synthetic data per Section 3: sample semantic variables s~N(0,I_10), modality-specific m_x~N(0,I_5), m_t~N(0,I_5); generate images via invertible MLPs g_x(s,m_x) and text via g_t(s_Itheta,m_t) where I_theta is the selected subset. 2) Implement selection bias: vary which semantic indices appear in text (e.g., I_theta=[1], [2], ..., [10]). 3) Implement perturbation bias: add Gaussian noise to selected variables with probability 0.75. 4) Train 7-layer MLP encoders f_x and f_t using L_SymAlignMaxEnt (Eq. 4) for 100k steps, batch 6144, lr 1e-4. 5) Evaluate: train linear regression to predict each ground-truth semantic component from learned representations; report mean R². Verify unbiased components achieve R²>0.9 and misaligned components achieve R²<0.1.

code_available.evidence: No code repository found. Project page links to arXiv, not GitHub. Tried multiple search queries: full title, title without subtitle, arXiv ID '2504.10143', author names (Yichao Cai, Yuhang Liu), benchmark names (MPI3D, Causal3DIdent, SymAlignMaxEnt), method terms (multimodal contrastive learning, cross-modal misalignment). Both GitHub repository search and Hugging Face search returned no results. OpenReview supplement status was 'missing' per input. Causal3DIdent and numerical simulation require implementing training from scratch using loss equations in the paper.

Contains 460,800 real-world images with 7 discrete ground-truth factors. Numerical simulation can be generated from paper specifications (Gaussian priors, invertible MLPs). Causal3DIdent is a standard benchmark in disentanglement literature.

weights_available.evidence: No pretrained checkpoints released. The paper evaluates OpenCLIP models trained on LAION-400M (not released by this paper) as a case study. No training checkpoints for the synthetic experiments or MPI3D/Causal3DIdent experiments are released.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: MPI3D-Complex and Causal3DIdent are established benchmarks in disentangled representation learning (referenced in NeurIPS 2019 and prior work by von Zimmermann et al., 2021; Daunhawer et al., 2022). MPI3D-Complex is available on HuggingFace. Causal3DIdent uses Blender rendering as in prior work.

Using A100 40GB H100-equivalent of 0.32, this converts to approximately 22.4 H100-hours. MPI3D experiments used ~27 GPU-hours (~8.6 H100-hours). Causal3DIdent used ~25 GPU-hours (~8 H100-hours). For the numerical simulation MRE alone, estimate is ~25 H100-hours (rounded up from 22.4 for engineering overhead). Note: no code repository was found; implementation from scratch may require additional debugging time not included in this estimate.
abstract: Multimodal representation learning, exemplified by multimodal contrastive learning (MMCL) using image-text pairs, aims to learn powerful representations by aligning cues across modalities. This approach relies on the core assumption that the exemplar image-text pairs constitute two representations of an identical concept. However, recent research has revealed that real-world datasets often exhibit cross-modal misalignment. There are two distinct viewpoints on how to address this issue: one suggests mitigating the misalignment, and the other leveraging it. We seek here to reconcile these seemingly opposing perspectives, and to provide a practical guide for practitioners. Using latent variable models we thus formalize cross-modal misalignment by introducing two specific mechanisms: Selection bias, where some semantic variables are absent in the text, and perturbation bias, where semantic variables are altered -- both leading to misalignment in data pairs. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that, under mild assumptions, the representations learned by MMCL capture exactly the information related to the subset of the semantic variables invariant to selection and perturbation biases. This provides a unified perspective for understanding misalignment. Based on this, we further offer actionable insights into how misalignment should inform the design of real-world ML systems. We validate our theoretical findings via extensive empirical studies on both synthetic data and real image-text datasets, shedding light on the nuanced impact of cross-modal misalignment on multimodal …

title: SymRTLO: Enhancing RTL Code Optimization with LLMs and Neuron-Inspired Symbolic Reasoning
central_claim: SymRTLO integrates LLMs with symbolic reasoning for RTL code optimization, achieving up to 43.9%, 62.5%, and 51.1% improvements in power, performance (delay), and area respectively compared to state-of-the-art methods.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'SymRTLO improves power, performance, and area (PPA) by up to 43.9%, 62.5%, and 51.1%, respectively, compared to the state-of-the-art methods.' Experiments conducted on RTL-Rewriter benchmark with Synopsys DC Compiler and Yosys.
mre_config: Run SymRTLO workflow on a simple FSM test case using Yosys to measure wire/cell counts. Input: Verilog FSM code (6-state example from paper appendix). Output: Optimized Verilog with reduced wire/cell counts. Metric: Yosys-reported wires/cells reduction. The repo contains run_yosys.py for verification and workflow.py for the main optimization pipeline.
agent_task: Clone https://github.com/NellyW8/SymRTLO and run the SymRTLO optimization workflow on an FSM test case: (1) Create a simple 6-state FSM Verilog module following the format in the paper appendix (example1_state); (2) Install dependencies: openai, pyverilog, tiktoken, numpy, pandas, yosys; (3) Set OpenAI API key in workflow.py; (4) Run workflow.py to optimize the Verilog FSM code; (5) Compare wire/cell counts before/after using Yosys to verify optimization reduction. Expected: 30-50% reduction in wires/cells demonstrating the FSM state merging capability.

code_available.evidence: Verified NellyW8/SymRTLO GitHub repo contains complete code: workflow.py (main pipeline), AST.py (templates), RAG_cleaned.py (RAG system), fsm_extractor.py (FSM extraction), symbolic.py (symbolic reasoning), run_yosys.py (verification), templates_optimize/ (AST template library with baseTemplate.py, preprocess.py), rules_output/ (optimization rules). All modules needed for the MRE are present.

The zhoujy22/RTL-rewriter repo is empty (no release, no test files). Users must create their own Verilog FSM test cases. dataset_is_standard is false because this is a custom benchmark, not a standard ML dataset.

weights_available.evidence: SymRTLO is an LLM-based optimization framework using GPT-4o via API calls - no model weights/checkpoints are needed. This is an inference-only framework. No HF models or checkpoints released.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: RTL-Rewriter benchmark is a custom benchmark created by the RTL-Rewriter authors for RTL optimization evaluation, not a standard public ML benchmark like MNIST, CIFAR, or ImageNet.

h100_estimate_basis: The MRE runs LLM API calls (GPT-4o) for optimization with Yosys synthesis - no GPU-intensive training. Estimated ~2 H100-hours: 1-2 hours for LLM inference rounds + Yosys synthesis time on one test case. Note: Requires OpenAI API key and Yosys installation but minimal GPU compute. Engineering/debugging time for Verilog test case creation is additional and not included.
abstract: Optimizing Register Transfer Level (RTL) code is crucial for improving the power, performance, and area (PPA) of digital circuits in the early stages of synthesis. Manual rewriting, guided by synthesis feedback, can yield high-quality results but is time-consuming and error-prone. Most existing compiler-based approaches have difficulty handling complex design constraints. Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have emerged as a promising alternative to address these challenges. However, LLM-based approaches often face difficulties in ensuring alignment between the generated code and the provided prompts. This paper presents SymRTLO, a novel neuron-symbolic RTL optimization framework that seamlessly integrates LLM-based code rewriting with symbolic reasoning techniques. Our method incorporates a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system of optimization rules and Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)-based templates, enabling LLM-based rewriting that maintains syntactic correctness while minimizing undesired circuit behaviors. A symbolic module is proposed for analyzing and optimizing finite state machine (FSM) logic, allowing fine-grained state merging and partial specification handling beyond the scope of pattern-based compilers. Furthermore, a fast verification pipeline, combining formal equivalence checks with test-driven validation, further reduces the complexity of verification. Experiments on the RTL-Rewriter benchmark with Synopsys Design Compiler and Yosys show that SymRTLO improves power, performance, and area (PPA) by up to 43.9%, 62.5%, and 51.1%, respectively, compared …

title: AgMMU: A Comprehensive Agricultural Multimodal Understanding Benchmark
central_claim: Fine-tuning on AgBase improves open-source VLM performance on agricultural open-ended questions by up to 11.6% on average, demonstrating that the benchmark reveals knowledge gaps in current VLMs.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'Simple fine-tuning on AgBase boosts open-sourced model performance on challenging OEQs for up to 11.6% on average.' Table 1 shows zero-shot baselines (e.g., LLaVA-1.5-7B: 12.8% OEQ average) and Figure 6 shows fine-tuning improvement.
mre_config: Evaluate LLaVA-1.5-7B zero-shot on AgMMU evaluation set (746 MCQs + 746 OEQs) to reproduce baseline performance gap claim. This tests the core claim that VLMs struggle with agricultural knowledge-intensive tasks, which is verified by the 11.6% fine-tuning improvement shown in the paper.

Reproduce the zero-shot baseline performance showing VLMs achieve ~12.8% average on OEQs and ~69% on MCQs.

README documents full evaluation workflow with download.sh for dataset retrieval.

Fine-tuning compute (2x A6000 for 12 hours = 7.68 H100-equivalent hours) is not required for the minimal reproduction since the central claim is verified by showing VLMs struggle with the task, demonstrated by baseline evaluation. Engineering/debugging time for dataset preparation and inference pipeline setup is additional.
abstract: We present AgMMU, a challenging real-world benchmark for evaluating and advancing vision-language models (VLMs) in the knowledge-intensive domain of agriculture. Unlike prior datasets that rely on crowdsourced prompts, AgMMU is distilled from 116,231 authentic dialogues between everyday growers and USDA-authorized Cooperative Extension experts. Through a three-stage pipeline: automated knowledge extraction, QA generation, and human verification, we construct (i) AgMMU, an evaluation set of 746 multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and 746 open-ended questions (OEQs), and (ii) AgBase, a development corpus of 57,079 multimodal facts covering five high-stakes agricultural topics: insect identification, species identification, disease categorization, symptom description, and management instruction. Benchmarking 12 leading VLMs reveals pronounced gaps in fine-grained perception and factual grounding. Open-sourced models trail after proprietary ones by a wide margin. Simple fine-tuning on AgBase boosts open-sourced model performance on challenging OEQs for up to 11.6% on average, narrowing this gap and also motivating future research to propose better strategies in knowledge extraction and distillation from AgBase. We hope AgMMU stimulates research on domain-specific knowledge integration and trustworthy decision support in agriculture AI development.

title: A Clean Slate for Offline Reinforcement Learning
central_claim: TD3-AWR, a new offline RL algorithm combining TD3 value loss with advantage-weighted regression (AWR), outperforms both its source algorithms ReBRAC and IQL on D4RL benchmarks.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'we develop two novel algorithms---TD3-AWR (model-free) and MoBRAC (model-based)---which substantially outperform established baselines.' Section 5.1 (TD3-AWR) reports: 'TD3-AWR's performance curve strictly dominates ReBRAC on 6 out of 9 datasets, and is dominated by ReBRAC in only 1. Similarly, TD3-AWR strictly dominates IQL on 7 datasets, thereby outperforming both of its source algorithms.' Figure 8 shows TD3-AWR evaluation against ReBRAC and IQL.
mre_config: Train TD3-AWR on D4RL halfcheetah-medium-v2 for 1M updates using the unified Unifloral implementation (algorithms/unifloral.py) with config configs/unifloral/td3_awr.yaml. Evaluate final policy performance (normalized D4RL score). Compare against reported TD3-AWR score of ~92 on halfcheetah-medium-expert or ~100 on hopper-medium. Single training run on one seed should complete in <30 minutes on GPU.
agent_task: Reproduce the central claim by training TD3-AWR on D4RL halfcheetah-medium-v2 (the default in td3_awr.yaml) for 1M updates using 'python algorithms/unifloral.py --config configs/unifloral/td3_awr.yaml' or standalone 'python algorithms/iql.py --dataset halfcheetah-medium-v2 --algorithm iql' with AWR enabled. Evaluate final normalized score using d4rl.get_normalized_score(). Compare against paper's reported TD3-AWR performance of ~90+ on halfcheetah-medium and ~100 on hopper-medium. Report training time and final evaluation return.

Paper explicitly uses D4RL for all experiments (hopper-medium, halfcheetah-medium-expert, walker2d-medium-replay, etc.). D4RL is publicly available via gym interface.

The repo contains only code for training algorithms; final_returns/ directory structure suggests saving results after training. No releases, model cards, or checkpoint files found after verifying repository contents.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: D4RL (Datasets for Deep Data-Driven Reinforcement Learning) is a widely recognized standard benchmark for offline RL, maintained by the Farama Foundation. It provides pre-collected datasets for MuJoCo locomotion, Adroit manipulation, Kitchen, and other environments. Used extensively in offline RL research including CQL, IQL, TD3-BC, ReBRAC, and hundreds of other papers.

Training 1M updates on D4RL halfcheetah-medium with JAX implementation takes ~5-15 minutes on a single A100/L40S GPU (per paper's speedup claims showing 131x faster than CORL). Converting to H100-hours: ~0.1-0.3 GPU-hours on A100 approximated 0.03-0.1 H100-hours. Using conservative estimate of ~1 H100-hour to account for multiple seeds and potential hyperparameter tuning variations. Engineering/debugging time not included.
abstract: Progress in offline reinforcement learning (RL) has been impeded by ambiguous problem definitions and entangled algorithmic designs, resulting in inconsistent implementations, insufficient ablations, and unfair evaluations. Although offline RL explicitly avoids environment interaction, prior methods frequently employ extensive, undocumented online evaluation for hyperparameter tuning, complicating method comparisons. Moreover, existing reference implementations differ significantly in boilerplate code, obscuring their core algorithmic contributions. We address these challenges by first introducing a rigorous taxonomy and a transparent evaluation protocol that explicitly quantifies online tuning budgets. To resolve opaque algorithmic design, we provide clean, minimalistic, single-file implementations of various model-free and model-based offline RL methods, significantly enhancing clarity and achieving substantial speed-ups. Leveraging these streamlined implementations, we propose Unifloral, a unified algorithm that encapsulates diverse prior approaches within a single, comprehensive hyperparameter space, enabling algorithm development in a shared hyperparameter space. Using Unifloral with our rigorous evaluation protocol, we develop two novel algorithms - TD3-AWR (model-free) and MoBRAC (model-based) - which substantially outperform established baselines. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/EmptyJackson/unifloral.

title: d1: Scaling Reasoning in Diffusion Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
central_claim: d1 can adapt pre-trained masked diffusion LLMs into reasoning models via a combination of supervised finetuning (SFT) and diffu-GRPO (a novel policy gradient method for masked diffusion LLMs), significantly improving performance on mathematical and planning benchmarks.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'we propose d1, a framework to adapt pre-trained masked dLLMs into reasoning models via a combination of supervised finetuning (SFT) and RL... We find that d1 yields the best performance and significantly improves performance of a state-of-the-art dLLM.' Table 1 (tab:performance_results) shows d1-LLaDA achieving 73.2-82.1% on GSM8K and 33.8-40.2% on MATH500 across sequence lengths.
mre_config: Train diffu-GRPO alone (without SFT) on the Countdown task with 3 numbers using LLaDA-8B-Instruct as the base model: base model LLaDA-8B-Instruct from HuggingFace, Countdown dataset from HuggingFace (Jiayi-Pan/Countdown-Tasks-3to4), train 5000 steps with sequence length 256, batch size 6 per GPU on 8 A100-80G GPUs, LoRA rank 128, evaluate accuracy on countdown task.
agent_task: Reproduce the central claim by training diffu-GRPO on the Countdown task: (1) Load LLaDA-8B-Instruct from HuggingFace (GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct). (2) Download Countdown dataset from HuggingFace (Jiayi-Pan/Countdown-Tasks-3to4), restrict to 3-number tasks. (3) Apply diffu-GRPO training using the official code at https://github.com/dllm-reasoning/d1 (diffu-grpo/), with LoRA rank 128, sequence length 256, batch size 6 per GPU, 8 A100-80G GPUs, for 5000 steps. (4) Evaluate on the countdown test set (dataset/countdown_cd3_test.jsonl from the repo). (5) Compare accuracy against the paper's reported LLaDA+GRPO result (~33-37% for Countdown at seq len 128-512). Verify the claim by demonstrating that diffu-GRPO improves over the base LLaDA-8B-Instruct baseline (~20% on Countdown).

README provides setup instructions and training commands.

dataset_available.evidence: Standard benchmark GSM8K available at openai/gsm8k on HuggingFace (12.2M downloads). Countdown dataset available at Jiayi-Pan/Countdown-Tasks-3to4. Custom datasets (4x4 Sudoku puzzles) released in the dataset folder of the GitHub repo. The paper uses public standard benchmarks for evaluation.

weights_available.evidence: Base model LLaDA-8B-Instruct is available on HuggingFace (GSAI-ML/LLaDA-8B-Instruct). However, no trained d1-LLaDA checkpoints (LLaDA+SFT, LLaDA+GRPO, or d1-LLaDA) are released. The repo only contains code, not model weights.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: GSM8K is a widely recognized standard benchmark for grade school math reasoning (openai/gsm8k on HuggingFace with 12.2M downloads, arXiv:2110.14168). MATH500 is also a standard benchmark for mathematical reasoning. Countdown is a known reasoning task from the TinyZero project.

h100_estimate_basis: The paper reports training diffu-GRPO on Countdown for 5000 steps on 8 NVIDIA A100-80G GPUs. An independent reproduction attempt (BrutalCaeser/reinforcing_dLLMs) estimates approximately 24 GPU-days (~576 A100-hours) for a faithful full reproduction. The 8 A100-80G GPU training configuration translates to approximately 8 × 0.32 = 2.56 H100 equivalents per GPU. Accounting for online generation (which is slower for diffusion models than autoregressive models due to iterative denoising), 600 H100-hours is a realistic estimate. Engineering and debugging time for diffusion-specific issues is additional and not included in this compute estimate.
abstract: Recent large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities that benefits from online reinforcement learning (RL). These capabilities have primarily been demonstrated within the left-to-right autoregressive (AR) generation paradigm. In contrast, non-autoregressive paradigms based on diffusion generate text in a coarse-to-fine manner. Although recent diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) have achieved competitive language modeling performance compared to their AR counterparts, it remains unclear if dLLMs can also leverage recent advances in LLM reasoning. To this end, we propose d1, a framework to adapt pre-trained masked dLLMs into reasoning models via a combination of supervised finetuning (SFT) and RL. Specifically, we develop and extend techniques to improve reasoning in pretrained dLLMs: (a) we utilize a masked SFT technique to distill knowledge and instill self-improvement behavior directly from existing datasets, and (b) we introduce a novel critic-free, policy-gradient based RL algorithm called diffu-GRPO, the first integration of policy gradient methods to masked dLLMs. Through empirical studies, we investigate the performance of different post-training recipes on multiple mathematical and planning benchmarks. We find that d1 yields the best performance and significantly improves performance of a state-of-the-art dLLM. Our code is released at https://dllm-reasoning.github.io/.

title: Frame Context Packing and Drift Prevention in Next-Frame-Prediction Video Diffusion Models
central_claim: FramePack compresses input frame contexts to a fixed length using importance-based progressive compression (geometric progression), enabling long video generation (thousands of frames) with 13B models on limited GPU memory, while anti-drifting sampling methods (endpoint planning, inverted sampling, history discretization) prevent quality degradation over time.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'FramePack compresses input frame contexts with frame-wise importance so that more frames can be encoded within a fixed context length, with more important frames having longer contexts.' Figure 1 and Section 2 show the packing architecture with geometric progression context lengths. Tables 1-2 show ablation results comparing vanilla, anti-drifting, and inverted anti-drifting sampling methods.

abstract: We present a neural network structure, FramePack, to train next-frame (or next-frame-section) prediction models for video generation. FramePack compresses input frame contexts with frame-wise importance so that more frames can be encoded within a fixed context length, with more important frames having longer contexts. The frame importance can be measured using time proximity, feature similarity, or hybrid metrics. The packing method allows for inference with thousands of frames and training with relatively large batch sizes. We also present drift prevention methods to address observation bias (error accumulation), including early-established endpoints, adjusted sampling orders, and discrete history representation. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the anti-drifting methods in both single-directional video streaming and bi-directional video generation. Finally, we show that existing video diffusion models can be finetuned with FramePack, and analyze the differences between different packing schedules.

title: Mask Image Watermarking
