abstract: We present MaskWM, a simple, efficient, and flexible framework for image watermarking. MaskWM has two variants: (1) MaskWM-D, which supports global watermark embedding, watermark localization, and local watermark extraction for applications such as tamper detection; (2) MaskWM-ED, which focuses on local watermark embedding and extraction, offering enhanced robustness in small regions to support fine-grined image protection. MaskWM-D builds on the classical encoder-distortion layer-decoder training paradigm. In MaskWM-D, we introduce a simple masking mechanism during the decoding stage that enables both global and local watermark extraction. During training, the decoder is guided by various types of masks applied to watermarked images before extraction, helping it learn to localize watermarks and extract them from the corresponding local areas. MaskWM-ED extends this design by incorporating the mask into the encoding stage as well, guiding the encoder to embed the watermark in designated local regions, which improves robustness under regional attacks. Extensive experiments show that MaskWM achieves state-of-the-art performance in global and local watermark extraction, watermark localization, and multi-watermark embedding. It outperforms all existing baselines, including the recent leading model WAM for local watermarking, while preserving high visual quality of the watermarked images. In addition, MaskWM is highly efficient and adaptable. It requires only 20 hours of training on a single A6000 GPU, achieving 15x computational efficiency compared to WAM. By simply adjusting …

title: Taccel: Scaling Up Vision-based Tactile Robotics via High-performance GPU Simulation
central_claim: Taccel: GPU-accelerated physics simulation framework combining Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) collision detection with NVIDIA Warp for differentiable cloth and multi-body simulation
claim_evidence: Taccel repository contains pre-compiled Python extensions (.so files for Python 3.10 on x86_64 Linux) for collision detection, integration, and simulation; PTX kernels for GPU architectures sm60-sm86; warp_ipc module for IPC collision handling; taccel module for main simulation framework; integration with thirdparty/nvidia-warp for differentiable physics
mre_config: Python 3.10+, NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support, pre-built Linux x86_64 binaries
agent_task: code_analysis

code_available.evidence: Full repository with Python modules, C++/CUDA kernels, and pre-compiled .so extensions

dataset_available.evidence: No dataset files found in repository

weights_available.evidence: Pre-compiled PTX kernels and .so binaries provided

dataset_is_standard.evidence: No standard benchmark datasets found in repository

h100_estimate_basis: Repository structure analysis and kernel examination for simulation framework
abstract: Tactile sensing is crucial for achieving human-level robotic capabilities in manipulation tasks. As a promising solution, Vision-Based Tactile Sensors (VBTSs) offer high spatial resolution and cost-effectiveness, but present unique challenges in robotics for their complex physical characteristics and visual signal processing requirements. The lack of efficient and accurate simulation tools for VBTSs has significantly limited the scale and scope of tactile robotics research. We present Taccel, a high-performance simulation platform that integrates IPC and ABD to model robots, tactile sensors, and objects with both accuracy and unprecedented speed, achieving an 18-fold acceleration over real-time across thousands of parallel environments. Unlike previous simulators that operate at sub-real-time speeds with limited parallelization, Taccel provides precise physics simulation and realistic tactile signals while supporting flexible robot-sensor configurations through user-friendly APIs. Through extensive validation in object recognition, robotic grasping, and articulated object manipulation, we demonstrate precise simulation and successful sim-to-real transfer. These capabilities position Taccel as a powerful tool for scaling up tactile robotics research and development, potentially transforming how robots interact with and understand their physical environment.

title: FreshStack: Building Realistic Benchmarks for Evaluating Retrieval on Technical Documents
central_claim: Existing retrieval models significantly underperform oracle approaches on all five FreshStack topics, demonstrating significant headroom for IR quality improvement on challenging technical document retrieval tasks.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'Existing retrieval models, when applied out-of-the-box, significantly underperform oracle approaches on all five topics, denoting plenty of headroom to improve IR quality.' Table 1 (main-results): BM25 achieves 0.230 alpha-nDCG@10 on LangChain vs Oracle 0.519, showing the performance gap.
mre_config: Evaluate BM25 retrieval on the LangChain topic using the FreshStack evaluation framework. Load the dataset via DataLoader(topic='langchain'), run BM25 retrieval on the corpus (49,514 documents), compute alpha-nDCG@10, Coverage@20, and Recall@50 metrics using the freshstack.retrieval.evaluation.EvaluateRetrieval class. Compare BM25 results (alpha-nDCG@10=0.230, Coverage@20=0.475, Recall@50=0.261 from paper Table 1) against the oracle baseline (alpha-nDCG@10=0.519). The minimal configuration uses one topic, one baseline model (BM25), and standard evaluation metrics.
agent_task: Reproduce the core claim that existing retrieval models underperform oracle approaches by: (1) Install freshstack: pip install freshstack; (2) Load LangChain dataset: DataLoader(queries_repo='freshstack/queries-oct-2024', corpus_repo='freshstack/corpus-oct-2024', topic='langchain'); (3) Run BM25 retrieval on corpus using Pyserini or BEIR; (4) Compute metrics: EvaluateRetrieval(k_values=[10, 20, 50]).evaluate(qrels_nuggets, query_to_nuggets, qrels_query, results); (5) Verify BM25 achieves alpha-nDCG@10 ~0.23 and Coverage@20 ~0.47 on LangChain, demonstrating the gap with oracle (~0.52 alpha-nDCG@10). The MRE validates that the evaluation framework works and reproduces the reported performance gap.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo verified: fresh-stack/freshstack contains full evaluation pipeline including freshstack/retrieval/evaluation.py (EvaluateRetrieval class), freshstack/retrieval/metrics.py (alpha_ndcg, coverage, recall metrics), freshstack/datasets/data_loader.py (DataLoader for queries/corpus/nuggets), and examples/evaluation/metric_evaluation.py (complete evaluation script). Package installable via 'pip install freshstack'. Code under Apache 2.0 license.

dataset_available.evidence: HuggingFace datasets verified: freshstack/queries-oct-2024 (queries, answers, nuggets, nugget-level judgments for 5 topics) and freshstack/corpus-oct-2024 (document corpus ~25K-117K documents per topic). Both loadable via DataLoader API or datasets.load_dataset(). CC-BY-SA 4.0 license.

weights_available.evidence: No FreshStack-specific model weights released. The MRE uses BM25 (Pyserini) which requires no weights. For dense retrieval baselines, standard pretrained models from HuggingFace are used (BAAI/bge-multilingual-gemma2, intfloat/e5-mistral-7b-instruct) - these are third-party checkpoints, not FreshStack artifacts.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: FreshStack is a custom benchmark constructed from Stack Overflow Q&A pairs and GitHub technical documents. It is NOT a standard ML benchmark (not MNIST, ImageNet, BEIR, or similar). The 5 topics (LangChain, Yolo, Laravel, Angular, Godot4) are author-curated with niche technical content, making this a non-standard domain-specific benchmark.

h100_estimate_basis: BM25 retrieval is a CPU-friendly algorithm (no GPU training required). The MRE involves scoring ~50K documents against 203 queries using sparse retrieval, which is computationally inexpensive. Assuming ~1 H100-hour equivalent for corpus indexing and retrieval inference on LangChain (49,514 documents, 203 queries). No model training needed; BM25 is a lexical baseline. Engineering/debugging time for API calls, data loading, and metric computation is additional.
abstract: We introduce FreshStack, a holistic framework for automatically building information retrieval (IR) evaluation benchmarks by incorporating challenging questions and answers. FreshStack conducts the following steps: (1) automatic corpus collection from code and technical documentation, (2) nugget generation from community-asked questions and answers, and (3) nugget-level support, retrieving documents using a fusion of retrieval techniques and hybrid architectures. We use FreshStack to build five datasets on fast-growing, recent, and niche topics to ensure the tasks are sufficiently challenging. On FreshStack, existing retrieval models, when applied out-of-the-box, significantly underperform oracle approaches on all five topics, denoting plenty of headroom to improve IR quality. In addition, we identify cases where rerankers do not improve first-stage retrieval accuracy (two out of five topics) and oracle context helps an LLM generator generate a high-quality RAG answer. We hope FreshStack will facilitate future work toward constructing realistic, scalable, and uncontaminated IR and RAG evaluation benchmarks.

title: TTRL: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
central_claim: TTRL (Test-Time Reinforcement Learning) enables LLMs to self-improve via RL on unlabeled test data using majority voting as the reward signal, achieving substantial gains (e.g., 123% improvement on MATH-500 pass@1 for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B) without ground-truth labels.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'TTRL enables self-evolution of LLMs by utilizing the priors in the pre-trained models.' Table 1 (tab:main): Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on MATH-500 improves from 32.7 to 73.0 pass@1 (+123.2%). The central empirical claim is that majority voting provides effective reward estimation for unsupervised RL at test time, enabling models to exceed their initial majority-voting performance ceiling.
mre_config: Apply TTRL (GRPO algorithm) to Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on the MATH-TTT dataset (from the bundled supplement, equivalent to MATH benchmark) for 10 episodes, 64 rollouts per prompt for majority voting reward, 32 samples for training, batch size 32, learning rate 5e-7, temperature 1.0 for rollout, max response length 3072 tokens, on 8x A100 80GB GPUs. Verify that pass@1 on the test set improves substantially (from ~33 to ~70+), demonstrating the core self-improvement mechanism.
agent_task: Reproduce the TTRL self-improvement experiment on MATH benchmark. Steps: (1) Clone https://github.com/PRIME-RL/TTRL and enter the verl submodule: git clone https://github.com/PRIME-RL/TTRL.git && cd TTRL/verl. (2) Create conda environment and install: conda create -n ttrl python==3.10 && conda activate ttrl && bash scripts/install_ttrl_deps.sh && pip install -e . (3) Download the base model Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B from HuggingFace at https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B. (4) Obtain the MATH dataset: use the bundled MATH-TTT dataset from the supplement at TTRL_code/data/MATH-TTT/train.json and test.json, or download MATH-500 from HuggingFace. Convert JSON to Parquet format using verl/data/preprocess.py. (5) Run TTRL with GRPO for 10 episodes using verl/examples/ttrl/Qwen2.5-Math/math.sh (update DATA_LOCAL_DIR and BACKBONE_PATH placeholders to point to the dataset and model directories). The key training config: +ttrl.enable=True, n_votes_per_prompt=64, n_samples_per_prompt=32, temperature=1.0, lr=5e-7, GRPO advantage estimator, 8 GPUs. (6) Evaluate pass@1 on the test set using greedy decoding (n=16, temperature=0.6). Verify the model substantially improves from ~33 to ~70+ pass@1, demonstrating that TTRL enables self-improvement on unlabeled data through majority voting rewards.

The verl submodule contains TTRL-specific code in verl/verl/trainer/ppo/ray_trainer.py with ttrl.enable config, ttrl_utils imports, and the ppo_trainer_ttrl.yaml config file. GitHub code search confirmed the TTRL reward function path ./verl/utils/reward_score/ttrl_math/__init__.py is referenced in the example scripts (repo:PRIME-RL/TTRL verl examples ttrl grpo). The core TTRL implementation (majority voting reward + GRPO training loop) is verified present.

(2021). The README documents a data preprocessing script (verl/data/preprocess.py) to convert JSON to Parquet. The supplement provides all other benchmark datasets (AIME-TTT, AMC-TTT, MATH-L1-5-TTT) with train/test splits. MATH-500 (500-problem subset) is also publicly available on HuggingFace.

The README mentions three independent runs achieving pass@1 (greedy) of 43.3 and 46.7 on AIME 2024, but these results are logged on Weights & Biases, not released as downloadable model weights. The base model Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B is publicly available on HuggingFace (5.9M downloads, 1.5B parameters, apache-2.0 license) at https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B. The MRE requires training from this base model, not a released fine-tuned checkpoint. No weights/checkpoints are released for the trained TTRL model.

MATH-500 is a standard 500-problem subset of MATH used extensively in RL reasoning literature (DeepSeek-R1, DAPO, etc.). AIME 2024 and AMC are public mathematics competition problem sets. All four benchmarks are standard evaluation suites in the LLM reasoning domain.

h100_estimate_basis: The paper reports all experiments on 8x NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. For the MRE (MATH-TTT, Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, 10 episodes, batch_size=32): the scripts use 8 GPUs (trainer.nnodes=1, n_gpus_per_node=8). Training involves vLLM inference with 64 rollouts per prompt for majority voting reward plus 32 samples per prompt for GRPO training, which substantially increases per-episode wallclock time compared to standard RL. Estimated ~2.4 A100-hours per episode for this workload, yielding ~24 A100-hours for 10 episodes. Converting A100 80GB to H100-equivalent: 24 * 0.32 = ~8 H100-hours for training. However, accounting for the overhead from extensive rollouts (64+32 samples per prompt) which roughly doubles compute relative to simpler RL setups, the total scales to ~16 H100-hours. Adding ~10% engineering/debugging overhead for RL training stability gives ~18 H100-hours. Engineering/debugging time (debugging RL training instability, hyperparameter tuning, environment setup) is additional and not included in the estimate.
abstract: This paper investigates Reinforcement Learning (RL) on data without explicit labels for reasoning tasks in Large Language Models (LLMs). The core challenge of the problem is reward estimation during inference while not having access to ground-truth information. While this setting appears elusive, we find that common practices in Test-Time Scaling (TTS), such as majority voting, yield surprisingly effective rewards suitable for driving RL training. In this work, we introduce Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL), a novel method for training LLMs using RL on unlabeled data. TTRL enables self-evolution of LLMs by utilizing the priors in the pre-trained models. Our experiments demonstrate that TTRL consistently improves performance across a variety of tasks and models. Notably, TTRL boosts the pass@1 performance of Qwen-2.5-Math-7B by approximately 211% on the AIME 2024 with only unlabeled test data. Furthermore, although TTRL is only supervised by the maj@n metric, TTRL has demonstrated performance to consistently surpass the upper limit of the initial model maj@n, and approach the performance of models trained directly on test data with ground-truth labels. Our experimental findings validate the general effectiveness of TTRL across various tasks and highlight TTRL's potential for broader tasks and domains. GitHub: https://github.com/PRIME-RL/TTRL

title: Can Large Language Models Help Multimodal Language Analysis? MMLA: A Comprehensive Benchmark
central_claim: MMLA establishes comprehensive benchmarks to evaluate how effectively large language models perform on multimodal language analysis tasks.
claim_evidence: MMLA is a multimodal language analysis benchmark with 61K+ samples from 9 datasets including MOSI, MELD, IEMOCAP, covering text/video/audio modalities. The benchmark evaluates foundation models on classification tasks (sentiment, emotion, dialogue act, intent recognition) and generation tasks (video captioning, QA). It includes both fine-tuning frameworks (Swift, VideoLLaMA2) and zero-shot inference pipelines using LLMs (GPT-4) and MLLMs (LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen2-VL, MiniCPM-V-2_6).

agent_task: Multimodal classification and generation using vision-language models on video and text data for sentiment, emotion, dialogue act, and intent analysis.

code_available.evidence: Repository contains 2546 files with complete implementation: Swift training framework with LoRA/QLoRA support, VideoLLaMA2 model code, zero-shot inference pipelines for GPT-4 and MLLMs (LLaVA-NeXT, Qwen2-VL, MiniCPM-V-2_6)

dataset_available.evidence: HuggingFace dataset THUIAR/MMLA-Datasets with 5.5K downloads, containing 9 labeled datasets for sentiment/emotion/intent classification

weights_available.evidence: Supports multiple open-source models: LLaMA, Qwen, ChatGLM, Yi, Mixtral, Mistral, Phi-3, with scripts for downloading and fine-tuning

Assumes 8x H100 GPUs for distributed training with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, taking ~4 hours. This accounts for video frame extraction, multimodal attention computation, and the 9-dataset evaluation pipeline. Zero-shot evaluation with GPT-4 API would cost ~$50-100 in API credits; MLLM inference alone would take ~8 H100 hours on 8 GPUs.
abstract: Multimodal language analysis is a rapidly evolving field that leverages multiple modalities to enhance the understanding of high-level semantics underlying human conversational utterances. Despite its significance, little research has investigated the capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to comprehend cognitive-level semantics. In this paper, we introduce MMLA, a comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to address this gap. MMLA comprises over 61K multimodal utterances drawn from both staged and real-world scenarios, covering six core dimensions of multimodal semantics: intent, emotion, dialogue act, sentiment, speaking style, and communication behavior. We evaluate eight mainstream branches of LLMs and MLLMs using three methods: zero-shot inference, supervised fine-tuning, and instruction tuning. Extensive experiments reveal that even fine-tuned models achieve only about 60%~70% accuracy, underscoring the limitations of current MLLMs in understanding complex human language. We believe that MMLA will serve as a solid foundation for exploring the potential of large language models in multimodal language analysis and provide valuable resources to advance this field. The datasets and code are open-sourced at https://github.com/thuiar/MMLA.

title: Hardware-aligned Hierarchical Sparse Attention for Efficient Long-term Memory Access
central_claim: HSA (Hierarchical Sparse Attention) enables RAMba to achieve perfect accuracy in passkey retrieval across 64M context while pre-trained on only 4K context, demonstrating strong length extrapolation and efficient long-range random access.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'RAMba achieves perfect accuracy in passkey retrieval across 64 million contexts despite pre-training on only 4K-length contexts'. Figure 1 shows RAMba maintaining 100% accuracy at 64M context while baselines drop near zero. Table 3 shows RAMba achieving 24% accuracy at 1M context on S-NIAH.

All components needed for MRE are present.

weights_available.evidence: GitHub releases page shows 'There aren't any releases here'. Searched HuggingFace for 'RAMba', 'HSA', 'long-context-modeling', 'ant-research RAMba' with no results. Training scripts reference local checkpoint paths (e.g., '/ossfs/workspace/antnlp/...') that are not publicly available. No model weights, checkpoints, or adapters are released.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: Pile is a widely recognized public dataset for LLM pre-training. RULER is a standard benchmark for evaluating length generalization in language models (from Hsieh et al., 2024). Passkey retrieval is a well-known task for testing random access capability.

h100_estimate_basis: Full training: 16 PPUs * 60 hours = 960 GPU-hours. Paper notes PPUs have approximately half A100 compute (A100-H100 equiv = 0.32, half = 0.16). 960 * 0.16 = 154 H100-hours. Pre-training on 60B tokens at 370M scale. Minimal MRE could use 1-2% of tokens as a sanity check (~2-3 H100-hours), but full paper claim requires matching the 60B token training to achieve length extrapolation.
abstract: A key advantage of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) over Transformers is their linear computational and space complexity enables faster training and inference for long sequences. However, RNNs are fundamentally unable to randomly access historical context, and simply integrating attention mechanisms may undermine their efficiency advantages. To overcome this limitation, we propose Hierarchical Sparse Attention (HSA), a novel attention mechanism that enhances RNNs with long-range random access flexibility while preserving their merits in efficiency and length generalization. HSA divides inputs into chunks, selects the top-$k$ chunks and hierarchically aggregates information. The core innovation lies in learning token-to-chunk relevance based on fine-grained token-level information inside each chunk. This approach enhances the precision of chunk selection across both in-domain and out-of-domain context lengths. To make HSA efficient, we further introduce a hardware-aligned kernel design. By combining HSA with Mamba, we introduce RAMba, which achieves perfect accuracy in passkey retrieval across 64 million contexts despite pre-training on only 4K-length contexts, and significant improvements on various downstream tasks, with nearly constant memory footprint. These results show RAMba's huge potential in long-context modeling.

title: PolyMath: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning in Multilingual Contexts

claim_evidence: Abstract: 'we find that even Qwen-3-235B-A22B-Thinking and Gemini-2.5-pro, achieve only 54.6 and 52.2 benchmark scores, with about 40% accuracy under the highest level.' Section 4 (Experiments) and Table 2 (main-results) show detailed per-level accuracy for 16 LLMs across 18 languages.
mre_config: Evaluate any open-source model (e.g., Qwen-QwQ-32B) on a single language (e.g., English) at a single difficulty level (e.g., low or medium with 125 problems each) using the PolyMath benchmark. Download data from HuggingFace, run inference with prompts from instruction.py, format outputs to JSONL with 'thinking_pred' and 'answer_pred' fields, and compute accuracy using eval/run_eval.py. The minimum viable MRE is 125 problem evaluations yielding an accuracy percentage.
agent_task: Reproduce the paper's main empirical claim by evaluating Qwen-QwQ-32B on the PolyMath benchmark. Steps: (1) Install dependencies: pip install -r requirements.txt; (2) Download English low-level data from HuggingFace (Qwen/PolyMath, language='en', level='low'); (3) Run inference on 125 problems using prompts from instruction.py; (4) Save outputs to output/qwq-32b/low/en.jsonl with required fields (idx, question, answer, thinking_pred, answer_pred); (5) Run evaluation: cd eval && python run_eval.py --model qwq-32b --language en --level low; (6) Verify accuracy matches expected range (non-reasoning models ~90%, reasoning models ~90% at low level). The MRE tests whether the benchmark setup and evaluation code correctly reproduce reported accuracy numbers.

Full evaluation pipeline with output format specification and run_eval.sh provided.

Dataset has 62.9K downloads and is publicly accessible.

While it incorporates data from MGSM and HLE, the custom 18-language parallel dataset with 4 difficulty levels is specific to this work.

The MRE involves only evaluating 125 problems (one level, one language) on an existing model via API or local inference. No training is performed. The paper reports no GPU-hours since all experiments use pre-existing model weights and API access. Compute cost is negligible (<0.01 H100-hours equivalent for inference). Engineering/debugging time for output formatting (~2-4 hours) is not included.
abstract: In this paper, we introduce PolyMath, a multilingual mathematical reasoning benchmark covering 18 languages and 4 easy-to-hard difficulty levels. Our benchmark ensures difficulty comprehensiveness, language diversity, and high-quality translation, making it a highly discriminative multilingual mathematical benchmark in the era of reasoning LLMs. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation for advanced LLMs and find that even Qwen-3-235B-A22B-Thinking and Gemini-2.5-pro, achieve only 54.6 and 52.2 benchmark scores, with about 40% accuracy under the highest level From a language perspective, our benchmark reveals several key challenges of LLMs in multilingual reasoning: (1) Reasoning performance varies widely across languages for current LLMs; (2) Input-output language consistency is low in reasoning LLMs and may be correlated with performance; (3) The thinking length differs significantly by language for current LLMs. Additionally, we demonstrate that controlling the output language in the instructions has the potential to affect reasoning performance, especially for some low-resource languages, suggesting a promising direction for improving multilingual capabilities in LLMs.

title: AutoJudge: Judge Decoding Without Manual Annotation

Use pre-computed hidden states from HuggingFace (mightyneighbor/AutoJudge) to skip expensive mining/calculation steps. Train logistic regression classifier on downloaded hidden states. Evaluate accuracy vs. accepted tokens using eval/run_gsm8k.py. Compare against vanilla speculative decoding baseline.

abstract: We introduce AutoJudge, a method that accelerates large language model (LLM) inference with task-specific lossy speculative decoding. Instead of matching the original model output distribution token-by-token, we identify which of the generated tokens affect the downstream quality of the response, relaxing the distribution match guarantee so that the "unimportant" tokens can be generated faster. Our approach relies on a semi-greedy search algorithm to test which of the mismatches between target and draft models should be corrected to preserve quality and which ones may be skipped. We then train a lightweight classifier based on existing LLM embeddings to predict, at inference time, which mismatching tokens can be safely accepted without compromising the final answer quality. We evaluate the effectiveness of AutoJudge with multiple draft/target model pairs on mathematical reasoning and programming benchmarks, achieving significant speedups at the cost of a minor accuracy reduction. Notably, on GSM8k with the Llama 3.1 70B target model, our approach achieves up to $\approx2\times$ speedup over speculative decoding at the cost of $\le 1\%$ drop in accuracy. When applied to the LiveCodeBench benchmark, AutoJudge automatically detects programming-specific important tokens, accepting $\ge 25$ tokens per speculation cycle at $2\%$ drop in Pass@1. Our approach requires no human annotation and is easy to integrate with modern LLM inference frameworks.

title: Don't be lazy: CompleteP enables compute-efficient deep transformers
central_claim: CompleteP (α=1) achieves depth-wise hyperparameter transfer and enables compute-efficient deep transformers, delivering 12-34% FLOP savings over μP.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'CompleteP enables 12-34% compute efficiency improvements over the prior state-of-the-art.' Paper also states: 'We provide a minimal implementation of Table 1 which reproduces Figure 2 (nonlinear-coordinate-check) at: https://github.com/EleutherAI/nanoGPT-mup/tree/completep'
mre_config: Depth Coordinate Check (Figure 7 / nonlinear-coordinate-check from paper): Train Pre-LN transformers with width=256, depths ∈ {2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}, 10 steps, batch_size=2, block_size=1024, on Tiny Shakespeare character dataset. Compare activation norm stability across SP, μP, α=0.5, and CompleteP (α=1). CompleteP should show bounded activation norms across all depths, demonstrating training stability.
agent_task: Clone the EleutherAI/nanoGPT-mup repo (branch: completep). Download the Tiny Shakespeare dataset: python data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py. Reproduce the depth coordinate check experiment: bash completep_examples/coord_check_shakespeare_char/depth_alpha_1_aka_completep/run.sh (for CompleteP) and run.sh scripts for sp_and_mup and depth_alpha_05 subfolders. Then run completep_examples/coord_check_shakespeare_char/plot.ipynb to generate the stability plot. Verify that CompleteP (α=1) shows bounded activation norms across depths 2-64 while SP/μP diverges.

Contains CompleteP implementation in model.py (residual_scaling, depth_alpha_exp, AdamW epsilon scaling) and completep_examples/ folder with run.sh scripts for depth coordinate check (Figure 7) reproduction and relative_distance_from_linearization.ipynb for Figure 6. README at completep_examples/README.md provides explicit instructions: download shakespeare via data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py then run bash completep_examples/coord_check_shakespeare_char/depth_alpha_1_aka_completep/run.sh

It is a standard dataset included in nanoGPT's data/ directory and widely used in the ML community for small-scale language modeling experiments.

h100_estimate_basis: Each coordinate check run trains for only 10 steps with width=256, batch_size=2, block_size=1024. 6 depths × 3 seeds = 18 runs per parameterization (SP/μP, α=0.5, α=1). ~54 total runs across all parameterizations. Each run processes ~20K tokens (10 steps × batch_size 2 × block_size 1024). Total compute is ~1M tokens across all configs. Using small GPT models (~1-2M parameters for width=256, depth up to 64), this is negligible compute — estimated at ~0.25 H100-hours total. The paper reports the coordinate check uses batch_size=4, N=256, 10 steps.
abstract: We study compute efficiency of LLM training when using different parameterizations, i.e., rules for adjusting model and optimizer hyperparameters (HPs) as model size changes. Some parameterizations fail to transfer optimal base HPs (such as learning rate) across changes in model depth, requiring practitioners to either re-tune these HPs as they scale up (expensive), or accept sub-optimal training when re-tuning is prohibitive. Even when they achieve HP transfer, we develop theory to show parameterizations may still exist in the lazy learning regime where layers learn only features close to their linearization, preventing effective use of depth and nonlinearity. Finally, we identify and adopt the parameterization we call CompleteP that achieves both depth-wise HP transfer and non-lazy learning in all layers. CompleteP enables a wider range of model width/depth ratios to remain compute-efficient, unlocking shapes better suited for different hardware settings and operational contexts. Moreover, CompleteP enables 12-34% compute efficiency improvements over the prior state-of-the-art. All experiments were run on Cerebras CS-3 systems. A minimal implementation is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/nanoGPT-mup/tree/completep.

title: LISAT: Language-Instructed Segmentation Assistant for Satellite Imagery
central_claim: LISAt outperforms state-of-the-art open-domain models on remote-sensing reasoning segmentation by 143.36% (gIoU), achieving gIoU of 0.275 on the GRES test set compared to LISA-7B's gIoU of 0.113.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'LISAT outperforms existing geospatial foundation models such as RS-GPT4V by over 10.04% (BLEU-4) on remote-sensing visual description tasks and outperforms state-of-the-art open-domain models on remote-sensing reasoning segmentation tasks by 143.36% (gIoU).' Table 1 (lisa_models_performance): LISAt achieves gIoU=0.275 vs LISA-7B gIoU=0.113 on GRES test set.
mre_config: Evaluate the released LISAt-7B checkpoint (huggingface.co/jquenum/LISAt-7b) on the GRES test set (1500 images) using eval_lisat.sh to compute gIoU metric. The model should achieve gIoU ~0.275.

weights_available.evidence: LISAt-7B checkpoint verified at huggingface.co/jquenum/LISAt-7b with pytorch_model.bin files (~16GB total). Also LISAt_PRE-7B at jquenum/LISAt_PRE-7b. Both model cards are complete with config.json and tokenizer.

h100_estimate_basis: MRE is evaluation-only with pretrained checkpoint on 1500 GRES test images. Paper reports 8x A100 80GB for 12 hours training (96 A100-hours ≈ 30.7 H100-hours). For evaluation with SAM inference, 7B VLM inference, and batch processing: ~18 H100-hours estimate. Engineering/debugging time for environment setup (FlashAttention, pybind11, SAM dependencies) is additional.
abstract: Segmentation models can recognize a pre-defined set of objects in images. However, models that can reason over complex user queries that implicitly refer to multiple objects of interest are still in their infancy. Recent advances in reasoning segmentation--generating segmentation masks from complex, implicit query text--demonstrate that vision-language models can operate across an open domain and produce reasonable outputs. However, our experiments show that such models struggle with complex remote-sensing imagery. In this work, we introduce LISAt, a vision-language model designed to describe complex remote-sensing scenes, answer questions about them, and segment objects of interest. We trained LISAt on a new curated geospatial reasoning-segmentation dataset, GRES, with 27,615 annotations over 9,205 images, and a multimodal pretraining dataset, PreGRES, containing over 1 million question-answer pairs. LISAt outperforms existing geospatial foundation models such as RS-GPT4V by over 10.04 % (BLEU-4) on remote-sensing description tasks, and surpasses state-of-the-art open-domain models on reasoning segmentation tasks by 143.36 % (gIoU). Our model, datasets, and code are available at https://lisat-bair.github.io/LISAt/

title: Put CASH on Bandits: A Max K-Armed Problem for Automated Machine Learning
central_claim: MaxUCB (Algorithm 1), a max k-armed bandit method with distribution-adapted exploration bonus `(α*log(t)/n)²`, outperforms prior approaches on the CASH problem in AutoML.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'MaxUCB is specifically designed for the light-tailed and bounded reward distributions arising in this setting and, thus, provides an efficient alternative compared to classic max k-armed bandit methods...' 'We theoretically and empirically evaluate our method on four standard AutoML benchmarks demonstrating superior performance over prior approaches.' Table 1 and Figure 2 show MaxUCB achieves the best average ranking on TabRepo, TabRepoRaw, YaHPOGym, and HEBO benchmarks.
mre_config: Run MaxUCB on YaHPOGym benchmark (6 classifiers, 103 datasets, 32 repetitions, 200 iterations) vs UCB baseline, comparing cumulative regret or average ranking. The Bandits/main_reproducing_results.py script tests this by running bandit algorithms on pre-computed HPO trajectories.
agent_task: Clone https://github.com/amirbalef/CASH_with_Bandits, install dependencies (smac3, yahpo-gym, tabrepo as per HPO_Runs/requirements.txt). Due to gitignored trajectory data, agent must: (1) Run `python HPO_Runs/main_run_hpo.py` to generate HPO trajectories using SMAC (expensive, requires Bayesian optimization with 200 iterations per dataset-classifier pair); (2) Run `python HPO_Runs/extract_HPO_runs.py` to create Bandits/datasets/*.csv; (3) Run `python Bandits/main_reproducing_results.py` with dataset_name='YaHPOGym' to test MaxUCB vs UCB. Verify MaxUCB achieves lower cumulative regret than UCB baseline. Note: Steps 1-2 are computationally expensive and represent the main barrier to reproduction.

code_available.evidence: Complete GitHub repository at amirbalef/CASH_with_Bandits contains: (1) Bandits/policies/MaxUCB.py with Algorithm 1 implementation using `policy[i] = max_X + (α*log(t)/n)²`; (2) Bandits/main_reproducing_results.py with full bandit experiment framework; (3) 17+ baseline bandit algorithms (UCB, QuantileUCB, Max_Median, etc.); (4) Bandits/plotting_scripts/ for visualization and HPO_Runs/ for trajectory generation with SMAC.

dataset_available.evidence: GitHub repo .gitignore explicitly excludes Bandits/datasets/* (the pre-computed trajectory CSV files that main_reproducing_results.py requires). While YaHPOGym and TabRepo are standard public benchmarks, the specific trajectory data format expected by the bandit evaluation script is not released. Users must first run the expensive HPO_Runs pipeline (SMAC with 200 iterations per dataset-classifier pair across 200 TabRepo datasets with 32 repetitions) to generate Bandits/datasets/YaHPOGym.csv before bandit selection can be evaluated.

weights_available.evidence: No model weights or checkpoints needed. MaxUCB is a bandit policy algorithm implemented in Bandits/policies/MaxUCB.py, not a trained model. The policy parameters are derived during runtime from observed rewards. No pre-computed results or checkpoints are included in the repository.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: YaHPOGym (https://github.com/slds-lmu/yahpo_gym) and TabRepo (https://github.com/autogluon/tabrepo) are established public AutoML benchmarks. YaHPOGym contains 103 datasets with 6 classifiers; TabRepo contains 200 datasets with 7 classifiers; HEBO is also a standard AutoML benchmark.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified: The paper does not report exact GPU-hours for experiments. However, the main barrier is that Bandits/datasets/ trajectory files are gitignored, requiring users to run the expensive HPO_Runs pipeline first. Generating full HPO trajectories requires SMAC Bayesian optimization with 200 iterations per (dataset, classifier) pair across 200 TabRepo datasets with 32 repetitions, or 103 YaHPOGym datasets with 6 classifiers. Based on comparable AutoML benchmarks (TabRepo), this requires approximately 50 H100-hours. The bandit selection experiments themselves are CPU-only and negligible compute once trajectories exist.
abstract: The Combined Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameter optimization (CASH) is a challenging resource allocation problem in the field of AutoML. We propose MaxUCB, a max k-armed bandit method to trade off exploring different model classes and conducting hyperparameter optimization. MaxUCB is specifically designed for the light-tailed and bounded reward distributions arising in this setting and, thus, provides an efficient alternative compared to classic max k-armed bandit methods assuming heavy-tailed reward distributions. We theoretically and empirically evaluate our method on four standard AutoML benchmarks, demonstrating superior performance over prior approaches. We make our code and data available at https://github.com/amirbalef/CASH_with_Bandits

title: Beyond $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ Constraint Violation for Online Convex Optimization with Adversarial Constraints
central_claim: The paper proposes an online policy for the Constrained Expert problem that achieves O(sqrt(T ln N) + T^beta) regret and O~(T^(1-beta) ln N) CCV, breaking the O~(sqrt(T)) CCV barrier by trading off regret.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'we propose a computationally efficient policy for the Constrained Expert problem, that attains O(sqrt(T ln N)+T^beta) regret and O~(T^(1-beta) ln N) CCV for N number of experts.' Experiments (Section 5, Appendix): 'We consider the Constrained Expert problem on a synthetic dataset with N=20 experts over a horizon of T=5000. Two experts are designated as special: the best feasible expert E* and the best unconstrained expert UE*.'
mre_config: Constrained Expert problem on synthetic data: N=20 experts, T=5000, beta=0.75. The adaptive_hedge() function from the released Jupyter notebook generates adversarial cost/constraint vectors and runs the proposed algorithm, comparing against gradient-based baseline. Metric: final regret and CCV values plus cumulative curves.
agent_task: Run the Adaptive Hedge algorithm on the Constrained Expert problem with N=20 experts, T=5000 rounds, and beta=0.75, using the synthetic data generation function from the released notebook. Verify that the algorithm achieves sublinear regret vs the best feasible expert and sublinear CCV growth. Plot cumulative regret and CCV over time. Compare with the gradient-based baseline. Check that the final CCV is significantly lower than T^0.5 (the prior best bound) while regret remains sublinear.

Both notebooks are complete, runnable Python implementations of the paper's proposed method.

No external dataset download is required. The notebook also optionally downloads standard UCI datasets (Diabetes-130, Pima Indians Diabetes) for additional experiments.

This is author-generated adversarial data, not a standard public benchmark. The notebook optionally uses UCI Diabetes-130 dataset for supplemental experiments, but the core MRE relies on synthetic data.

On a modern CPU this runs in under 1 minute. GPU not required. Estimate: ~0.5 H100-hours equivalent for single run (negligible). Engineering/debugging overhead is minimal given the self-contained notebook.
abstract: We study Online Convex Optimization with adversarial constraints (COCO). At each round a learner selects an action from a convex decision set and then an adversary reveals a convex cost and a convex constraint function. The goal of the learner is to select a sequence of actions to minimize both regret and the cumulative constraint violation (CCV) over a horizon of length $T$. The best-known policy for this problem achieves $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret and $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ CCV. In this paper, we improve this by trading off regret to achieve substantially smaller CCV. This trade-off is especially important in safety-critical applications, where satisfying the safety constraints is non-negotiable. Specifically, for any bounded convex cost and constraint functions, we propose an online policy that achieves $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{dT}+ T^β)$ regret and $\tilde{O}(dT^{1-β})$ CCV, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision set and $β\in [0,1]$ is a tunable parameter. We begin with a special case, called the $\textsf{Constrained Expert}$ problem, where the decision set is a probability simplex and the cost and constraint functions are linear. Leveraging a new adaptive small-loss regret bound, we propose a computationally efficient policy for the $\textsf{Constrained Expert}$ problem, that attains $O(\sqrt{T\ln N}+T^β)$ regret and $\tilde{O}(T^{1-β} \ln N)$ CCV for $N$ number of experts. The original problem is then reduced to the $\textsf{Constrained Expert}$ problem via a covering argument. Finally, with an additional $M$-smoothness assumption, we propose a computationally efficient …

title: MLE-Dojo: Interactive Environments for Empowering LLM Agents in Machine Learning Engineering
central_claim: MLE-Bench is a benchmark that evaluates LLMs and ML agents on Kaggle competitions by measuring their performance against gold medal thresholds

mre_config: Evaluations run in sandboxed Docker containers with Kaggle API credentials, supporting both API and offline evaluation modes
agent_task: Evaluate ML agent performance on Kaggle competitions by submitting predictions and comparing against leaderboard thresholds

code_available.evidence: GitHub repository exists at MLE-Dojo/MLE-Dojo with competition definitions and evaluation infrastructure

dataset_available.evidence: HuggingFace dataset contains 201 competition configurations with leaderboard data

weights_available.evidence: HuggingFace weights and biases available for MLE-Bench

dataset_is_standard.evidence: Dataset standardized with public/private leaderboard CSVs and consistent metric definitions across competitions

h100_estimate_basis: Based on 201 competitions, each requiring estimated 1-4 hours of GPU time for training and inference, with 3x safety margin for infrastructure overhead and retry handling
abstract: We introduce MLE-Dojo, a Gym-style framework for systematically reinforcement learning, evaluating, and improving autonomous large language model (LLM) agents in iterative machine learning engineering (MLE) workflows. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily rely on static datasets or single-attempt evaluations, MLE-Dojo provides an interactive environment enabling agents to iteratively experiment, debug, and refine solutions through structured feedback loops. Built upon 200+ real-world Kaggle challenges, MLE-Dojo covers diverse, open-ended MLE tasks carefully curated to reflect realistic engineering scenarios such as data processing, architecture search, hyperparameter tuning, and code debugging. Its fully executable environment supports comprehensive agent training via both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, facilitating iterative experimentation, realistic data sampling, and real-time outcome verification. Extensive evaluations of eight frontier LLMs reveal that while current models achieve meaningful iterative improvements, they still exhibit significant limitations in autonomously generating long-horizon solutions and efficiently resolving complex errors. Furthermore, MLE-Dojo's flexible and extensible architecture seamlessly integrates diverse data sources, tools, and evaluation protocols, uniquely enabling model-based agent tuning and promoting interoperability, scalability, and reproducibility. We open-source our framework and benchmarks to foster community-driven innovation towards next-generation MLE agents.

title: Generating Full-field Evolution of Physical Dynamics from Irregular Sparse Observations
central_claim: SDIFT (Sequential DIffusion in Functional Tucker space) generates full-field evolution of physical dynamics from irregular sparse observations, achieving state-of-the-art VRMSE reconstruction accuracy and faster sampling speed than prior methods like CoNFiLD.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'we present SDIFT...a novel framework that generates full-field evolution of physical dynamics from irregular sparse observations' with significant improvements in 'both reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency compared to state-of-the-art approaches.' abstract: Modeling and reconstructing multidimensional physical dynamics from sparse and off-grid observations presents a fundamental challenge in scientific research. Recently, diffusion-based generative modeling shows promising potential for physical simulation. However, current approaches typically operate on on-grid data with preset spatiotemporal resolution, but struggle with the sparsely observed and continuous nature of real-world physical dynamics. To fill the gaps, we present SDIFT, Sequential DIffusion in Functional Tucker space, a novel framework that generates full-field evolution of physical dynamics from irregular sparse observations. SDIFT leverages the functional Tucker model as the latent space representer with proven universal approximation property, and represents observations as latent functions and Tucker core sequences. We then construct a sequential diffusion model with temporally augmented UNet in the functional Tucker space, denoising noise drawn from a Gaussian process to generate the sequence of core tensors. At the posterior sampling stage, we propose a Message-Passing Posterior Sampling mechanism, enabling conditional generation of the entire sequence guided by observations at limited time steps. We validate SDIFT on three physical systems spanning astronomical (supernova explosions, light-year scale), environmental (ocean sound speed fields, kilometer scale), and molecular (organic liquid, millimeter scale) domains, demonstrating significant improvements in both reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

title: Path Gradients after Flow Matching

abstract: Boltzmann Generators have emerged as a promising machine learning tool for generating samples from equilibrium distributions of molecular systems using Normalizing Flows and importance weighting. Recently, Flow Matching has helped speed up Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs), scale them to more complex molecular systems, and minimize the length of the flow integration trajectories. We investigate the benefits of using path gradients to fine-tune CNFs initially trained by Flow Matching, in the setting where a target energy is known. Our experiments show that this hybrid approach yields up to a threefold increase in sampling efficiency for molecular systems, all while using the same model, a similar computational budget and without the need for additional sampling. Furthermore, by measuring the length of the flow trajectories during fine-tuning, we show that path gradients largely preserve the learned structure of the flow.

title: Plasticity as the Mirror of Empowerment
central_claim: Plasticity and empowerment are in fundamental tension: an agent cannot simultaneously maximize both quantities over the same interval, and the sum of plasticity and empowerment is upper-bounded by a quantity dependent on interface cardinality and interval length.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'Our main result establishes a tension between the plasticity and empowerment of an agent, suggesting that agent design needs to be mindful of both characteristics.' Theorem 4.8 (Section 4.3): 'For all intervals and any pair (agent, env), let m = min{(b-a+1) log|O|, (d-c+1) log|A|}. Then, emp(agent, env) + plast(agent, env) <= m is a tight upper bound on empowerment and plasticity.' Figure 3 demonstrates this tension empirically with tabular Q-learning on a two-armed Bernoulli bandit.
mre_config: Figure 3a: Epsilon-greedy tabular Q-learning on two-armed Bernoulli bandit (arm probabilities 0.9, 0.1), horizon=5, 10,000 trajectories per epsilon value, sweep epsilon from 0 to 1 in 30 steps. Measure plasticity (reverse GDI from observations [0:3] to actions [1:5]). Expected result: plasticity decreases monotonically from ~0.39 at epsilon=0 to ~0.01 at epsilon=1, demonstrating that exploration reduces plasticity.
agent_task: Clone the repository https://github.com/RafaStutz/Plasticity-as-the-Mirror-of-Empowerment, install dependencies with 'uv sync', and run Figure 3a experiment with 'uv run python -m plast_emp.experiments.figure3a'. This will generate plasticity estimates as a function of epsilon from 0 to 1. Verify that plasticity decreases monotonically from approximately 0.39 at epsilon=0 to approximately 0.01 at epsilon=1, confirming that exploration reduces plasticity. Compare generated artifacts/artifacts/figures/figure3a.png with the paper's Figure 3a.

abstract: Agents are minimally entities that are influenced by their past observations and act to influence future observations. This latter capacity is captured by empowerment, which has served as a vital framing concept across artificial intelligence and cognitive science. This former capacity, however, is equally foundational: In what ways, and to what extent, can an agent be influenced by what it observes? In this paper, we ground this concept in a universal agent-centric measure that we refer to as plasticity, and reveal a fundamental connection to empowerment. Following a set of desiderata on a suitable definition, we define plasticity using a new information-theoretic quantity we call the generalized directed information. We show that this new quantity strictly generalizes the directed information introduced by Massey (1990) while preserving all of its desirable properties. Under this definition, we find that plasticity is well thought of as the mirror of empowerment: The two concepts are defined using the same measure, with only the direction of influence reversed. Our main result establishes a tension between the plasticity and empowerment of an agent, suggesting that agent design needs to be mindful of both characteristics. We explore the implications of these findings, and suggest that plasticity, empowerment, and their relationship are essential to understanding agency

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at complex tasks thanks to advances in their reasoning abilities. However, existing methods overlook the trade-off between reasoning effectiveness and efficiency, often encouraging unnecessarily long reasoning chains and wasting tokens. To address this, we propose Learning to Think (L2T), an information-theoretic reinforcement fine-tuning framework for LLMs to make the models achieve optimal reasoning with fewer tokens. Specifically, L2T treats each query-response interaction as a hierarchical session of multiple episodes and proposes a universal dense process reward, i.e., quantifies the episode-wise information gain in parameters, requiring no extra annotations or task-specific evaluators. We propose a method to quickly estimate this reward based on PAC-Bayes bounds and the Fisher information matrix. Theoretical analyses show that it significantly reduces computational complexity with high estimation accuracy. By immediately rewarding each episode's contribution and penalizing excessive updates, L2T optimizes the model via reinforcement learning to maximize the use of each episode and achieve effective updates. Empirical results on various reasoning benchmarks and base models demonstrate the advantage of L2T across different tasks, boosting both reasoning effectiveness and efficiency.

title: Superposition Yields Robust Neural Scaling
central_claim: Representation superposition (where LLMs represent more features than they have dimensions) causes loss to scale robustly as 1/m (inverse model dimension) in the strong superposition regime due to geometric constraints on representation overlaps.

Figure 5d shows the strong superposition results with model exponent α_m ≈ 1 for different feature frequency distributions.

abstract: The success of today's large language models (LLMs) depends on the observation that larger models perform better. However, the origin of this neural scaling law, that loss decreases as a power law with model size, remains unclear. We propose that representation superposition, meaning that LLMs represent more features than they have dimensions, can be a key contributor to loss and cause neural scaling. Based on Anthropic's toy model, we use weight decay to control the degree of superposition, allowing us to systematically study how loss scales with model size. When superposition is weak, the loss follows a power law only if data feature frequencies are power-law distributed. In contrast, under strong superposition, the loss generically scales inversely with model dimension across a broad class of frequency distributions, due to geometric overlaps between representation vectors. We confirmed that open-sourced LLMs operate in the strong superposition regime and have loss scaling inversely with model dimension, and that the Chinchilla scaling laws are also consistent with this behavior. Our results identify representation superposition as a central driver of neural scaling laws, providing insights into questions like when neural scaling laws can be improved and when they will break down.

abstract: In this work, we propose a computationally efficient algorithm for visual policy learning that leverages differentiable simulation and first-order analytical policy gradients. Our approach decouple the rendering process from the computation graph, enabling seamless integration with existing differentiable simulation ecosystems without the need for specialized differentiable rendering software. This decoupling not only reduces computational and memory overhead but also effectively attenuates the policy gradient norm, leading to more stable and smoother optimization. We evaluate our method on standard visual control benchmarks using modern GPU-accelerated simulation. Experiments show that our approach significantly reduces wall-clock training time and consistently outperforms all baseline methods in terms of final returns. Notably, on complex tasks such as humanoid locomotion, our method achieves a $4\times$ improvement in final return, and successfully learns a humanoid running policy within 4 hours on a single GPU.

abstract: This paper introduces \textsc{InfantAgent-Next}, a generalist agent capable of interacting with computers in a multimodal manner, encompassing text, images, audio, and video. Unlike existing approaches that either build intricate workflows around a single large model or only provide workflow modularity, our agent integrates tool-based and pure vision agents within a highly modular architecture, enabling different models to collaboratively solve decoupled tasks in a step-by-step manner. Our generality is demonstrated by our ability to evaluate not only pure vision-based real-world benchmarks (i.e., OSWorld), but also more general or tool-intensive benchmarks (e.g., GAIA and SWE-Bench). Specifically, we achieve $\mathbf{7.27\%}$ accuracy on OSWorld, higher than Claude-Computer-Use. Codes and evaluation scripts are open-sourced at https://github.com/bin123apple/InfantAgent.

title: Certifying Stability of Reinforcement Learning Policies using Generalized Lyapunov Functions

abstract: Establishing stability certificates for closed-loop systems under reinforcement learning (RL) policies is essential to move beyond empirical performance and offer guarantees of system behavior. Classical Lyapunov methods require a strict stepwise decrease in the Lyapunov function but such certificates are difficult to construct for learned policies. The RL value function is a natural candidate but it is not well understood how it can be adapted for this purpose. To gain intuition, we first study the linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem and make two key observations. First, a Lyapunov function can be obtained from the value function of an LQR policy by augmenting it with a residual term related to the system dynamics and stage cost. Second, the classical Lyapunov decrease requirement can be relaxed to a generalized Lyapunov condition requiring only decrease on average over multiple time steps. Using this intuition, we consider the nonlinear setting and formulate an approach to learn generalized Lyapunov functions by augmenting RL value functions with neural network residual terms. Our approach successfully certifies the stability of RL policies trained on Gymnasium and DeepMind Control benchmarks. We also extend our method to jointly train neural controllers and stability certificates using a multi-step Lyapunov loss, resulting in larger certified inner approximations of the region of attraction compared to the classical Lyapunov approach. Overall, our formulation enables stability certification for a broad class of systems with learned policies by making certificates …

title: Exploiting the Asymmetric Uncertainty Structure of Pre-trained VLMs on the Unit Hypersphere
central_claim: AsymVLM, a post-hoc probabilistic adaptation framework for pretrained VLMs, outperforms existing methods in both cross-modal retrieval Recall@1 and uncertainty quantification by modeling text embeddings as probabilistic distributions (von Mises-Fisher or Power Spherical) on the unit hypersphere while keeping image embeddings deterministic.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'AsymVLM to build probabilistic embeddings from pre-trained VLMs on the unit hypersphere, enabling uncertainty quantification.' Table 1 (tab:unc_ret): AsymVLM_vMF achieves Recall@1 of 0.561 (t2i) and 0.392 (i2t) on MS-COCO, outperforming all baselines. Figure 1 (fig:unc_ret) and ablation study confirm monotonic Recall@1 decrease with uncertainty.
mre_config: Train AsymVLM-PSD or AsymVLM-VMF adapter on MS-COCO using CLIP ViT-B/32 (frozen). Small 4-layer MLP text adapter (512→1024→1024→1024→512) predicts mean direction μ and concentration κ for vMF/PS distribution. Train with SGD (lr=0.01, momentum=0.9), batch size 2048, cosine annealing, 200 epochs. Evaluate Recall@1 on t2i and i2t retrieval, measuring Spearman correlation between uncertainty levels and recall error.
agent_task: Reproduce the core AsymVLM cross-modal retrieval result: (1) Install dependencies: pip install -r requirements.txt (includes pycocotools, torch, torchvision, clip from openai). (2) Download MS-COCO 2017 train/val images and caption annotations from official cocodataset.org. (3) Update cache_embeddings.py with correct paths to MS-COCO data. (4) Cache CLIP embeddings: python cache_embeddings.py --dataset coco. (5) Train AsymVLM-psd adapter: python train.py --dataset coco --method asymvlm-psd --seed 0 (SGD lr=0.01, batch=2048, 200 epochs, ~0.5h on A100). (6) Evaluate Recall@1: python eval.py --dataset coco --method asymvlm-psd --seed 0 --uncer_levels 10. (7) Verify Recall@1 > 0.55 for t2i and > 0.38 for i2t on MS-COCO val set, and that Recall@1 decreases monotonically as uncertainty increases.

README provides explicit usage commands for each step.

Dataset loading uses torchvision.datasets.coco.CocoDetection. Data must be downloaded from official Microsoft COCO site (cocodataset.org); the repo provides the loading code.

Training saves checkpoints to checkpoints/{dataset}/{seed}/{method}.pt but these files are not included in the repository. Base CLIP ViT-B/32 weights are loaded via openai/CLIP pip package. Adapter must be trained from scratch.

h100_estimate_basis: Paper appendix reports 'under one GPU-hour' for 200 epochs on NVIDIA A100 for MS-COCO adaptation. A100 BF16 ≈ 0.32x H100 SXM ratio. So 1 A100 GPU-hour × 0.32 = ~0.32 H100-hours, rounded to ~1 H100-hour as conservative estimate. The adaptation trains only a lightweight 4-layer MLP on cached CLIP embeddings (no gradient through CLIP), making it very cheap. Engineering and debugging time not included.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) as foundation models have significantly enhanced performance across a wide range of visual and textual tasks, without requiring large-scale training from scratch for downstream tasks. However, these deterministic VLMs fail to capture the inherent ambiguity and uncertainty in natural language and visual data. Recent probabilistic post-hoc adaptation methods address this by mapping deterministic embeddings onto probability distributions; however, existing approaches do not account for the asymmetric uncertainty structure of the modalities, and the constraint that meaningful deterministic embeddings reside on a unit hypersphere, potentially leading to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we address the asymmetric uncertainty structure inherent in textual and visual data, and propose AsymVLM to build probabilistic embeddings from pre-trained VLMs on the unit hypersphere, enabling uncertainty quantification. We validate the effectiveness of the probabilistic embeddings on established benchmarks, and present comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating the inherent nature of asymmetry in the uncertainty structure of textual and visual data.

title: BLEUBERI: BLEU is a surprisingly effective reward for instruction following
central_claim: BLEU can serve as an effective reward signal for LLM alignment, achieving competitive performance with reward model-guided RL (GRPO-RM) on instruction-following benchmarks without requiring expensive reward model training.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'BLEU, a basic string-matching metric, surprisingly matches strong reward models in agreement with human preferences on general instruction-following datasets.' Table 1 shows BLEUBERI-trained models achieving comparable scores to GRPO-RM across MT-Bench, ArenaHard v1/v2, and WildBench.
mre_config: Train Qwen2.5-3B base model with GRPO using BLEU reward on 1K hardest examples from the Tulu3 50K pool (selected by lowest BLEU scores against references), evaluate on MT-Bench (80 questions) with LLM-as-judge to verify BLEU-based RL alignment achieves competitive instruction-following performance (~64.6 MT-Bench score).
agent_task:
1. Install dependencies: conda env create -f environment.yml && conda activate bleuberi
2. Download Tulu3 50K data pool from Figshare (per README) or use HuggingFace dataset
3. Run inference with Qwen2.5-3B base on 50K prompts: python3 make_data/run_inference.py --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B --data_path ../data/tulu3_50k --out_dir ../data/inference_outputs
4. Compute BLEU scores against references and select 1K hardest examples: python create_training_data.py grpo --data_path ../data/tulu3_50k --ref_models gold --sort --model Qwen2.5-3B --metric bleu --num_examples 1000
5. Run GRPO training with BLEU reward: bash training/grpo.sh (modify for Qwen2.5-3B, group size 8, lr 1e-6, 1 epoch)
6. Evaluate on MT-Bench using gpt-4.1-mini as judge
7. Verify MT-Bench score achieves ~64.6 (matching paper's Qwen2.5-3B BLEUBERI result)

OpenReview supplement contains complete training code: training/grpo.py, training/sft.py, training/grpo.sh, training/config.py, training/data_loader.py, training/dataset.py. Data creation scripts: make_data/create_training_data.py, make_data/run_inference.py, make_data/chat_templates.py, make_data/utils.py. Base models (Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-14B, Llama-3.1-8B) available separately on HuggingFace but these are base checkpoints, not trained BLEUBERI models.

Estimated ~15-20 H100-hours for single small-model run with group size 8, max tokens 512, 1 epoch training. Engineering/debugging time additional and not included.
abstract: Reward models are central to aligning LLMs with human preferences, but they are costly to train, requiring large-scale human-labeled preference data and powerful pretrained LLM backbones. Meanwhile, the increasing availability of high-quality synthetic instruction-following datasets raises the question: can simpler, reference-based metrics serve as viable alternatives to reward models during RL-based alignment? In this paper, we show first that BLEU, a basic string-matching metric, surprisingly matches strong reward models in agreement with human preferences on general instruction-following datasets. Based on this insight, we develop BLEUBERI, a method that first identifies challenging instructions and then applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using BLEU directly as the reward function. We demonstrate that BLEUBERI-trained models are competitive with models trained via reward model-guided RL across four challenging instruction-following benchmarks and three different base language models. A human evaluation further supports that the quality of BLEUBERI model outputs is on par with those from reward model-aligned models. Moreover, BLEUBERI models generate outputs that are more factually grounded than competing methods. Overall, we show that given access to high-quality reference outputs (easily obtained via existing instruction-following datasets or synthetic data generation), string matching-based metrics are cheap yet effective proxies for reward models during alignment. We release our code and data at https://github.com/lilakk/BLEUBERI.

title: Fairness-aware Anomaly Detection via Fair Projection
central_claim: FairAD (Im-FairAD and Ex-FairAD) achieves improved trade-off between detection accuracy (AUC) and group fairness (ADPD) in unsupervised anomaly detection by mapping data from different demographic groups to a common target distribution using Sinkhorn distance optimization.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'Experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves an improved trade-off between detection accuracy and fairness under both balanced and skewed data across different groups.' Table 2 shows Im-FairAD achieving 63.89% AUC with 4.76% ADPD on COMPAS, outperforming Deep SVDD (57.58% AUC, 21.07% ADPD).
mre_config: Im-FairAD on COMPAS dataset (balanced split) with default config: epochs=50, batch_size=1000, lr=0.0001, MLP network, latent_dim=4. Compare AUC and ADPD against baseline LOF or Deep SVDD. Run command: python main.py --dataset_name compas --load_arguments compas.json --fairway implicit --balanced True

abstract: Unsupervised anomaly detection is a critical task in many high-social-impact applications such as finance, healthcare, social media, and cybersecurity, where demographics involving age, gender, race, disease, etc, are used frequently. In these scenarios, possible bias from anomaly detection systems can lead to unfair treatment for different groups and even exacerbate social bias. In this work, first, we thoroughly analyze the feasibility and necessary assumptions for ensuring group fairness in unsupervised anomaly detection. Second, we propose a novel fairness-aware anomaly detection method FairAD. From the normal training data, FairAD learns a projection to map data of different demographic groups to a common target distribution that is simple and compact, and hence provides a reliable base to estimate the density of the data. The density can be directly used to identify anomalies while the common target distribution ensures fairness between different groups. Furthermore, we propose a threshold-free fairness metric that provides a global view for model's fairness, eliminating dependence on manual threshold selection. Experiments on real-world benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves an improved trade-off between detection accuracy and fairness under both balanced and skewed data across different groups.

title: Search and Refine During Think: Facilitating Knowledge Refinement for Improved Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning

abstract: Large language models have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities but are inherently limited by their knowledge reservoir. Retrieval-augmented reasoning mitigates this limitation by allowing LLMs to query external resources, but existing methods often retrieve irrelevant or noisy information, hindering accurate reasoning. In this paper, we propose AutoRefine, a reinforcement learning post-training framework that adopts a new "search-and-refine-during-think" paradigm. AutoRefine introduces explicit knowledge refinement steps between successive search calls, enabling the model to iteratively filter, distill, and organize evidence before generating an answer. Furthermore, we incorporate tailored retrieval-specific rewards alongside answer correctness rewards using group relative policy optimization. Experiments on single-hop and multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that AutoRefine significantly outperforms existing approaches, particularly in complex, multi-hop reasoning scenarios. Detailed analysis shows that AutoRefine issues frequent, higher-quality searches and synthesizes evidence effectively.

title: Controlling the Flow: Stability and Convergence for Stochastic Gradient Descent with Decaying Regularization
central_claim: Regularized Stochastic Gradient Descent (reg-SGD) with decaying Tikhonov regularization converges to the minimum-norm solution of convex optimization problems, while vanilla SGD may converge to any minimum but not necessarily the minimum-norm solution.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'We prove strong convergence of reg-SGD to the minimum-norm solution of the original problem without additional boundedness assumptions.' Figure 1 (trajectories) shows SGD converging to arbitrary minima (red dots) while reg-SGD converges to minimum-norm solution x*=(0.5,0.5). Section A.2 (Toy_example) provides the numerical validation with main_L2rates.m and main_asrates.m generating Figures 6 and 7.
mre_config: Toy_example from OpenReview supplement: 2D quadratic function f(x1,x2)=0.5*(x1+x2-1)^2 where minimum-norm solution is x*=(0.5,0.5). Compare vanilla SGD (α_k = 0.1k^{-1/2}) vs reg-SGD (α_k = 0.1k^{-q}, λ_k = k^{-p} with p=(6ξ+3)^{-1}, q=2/3) with Gaussian gradient noise. Metric: distance to minimum-norm solution ||X_k - x*|| and optimality gap f(X_k)-f(x*).
agent_task: Reproduce the toy example to verify reg-SGD converges to minimum-norm solution. Use main_asrates.m from OpenReview supplement Code_Submission/Toy_example/. Run 10 Monte Carlo simulations of reg-SGD vs SGD on f(x1,x2)=0.5*(x1+x2-1)^2 with Gaussian gradient noise. Verify reg-SGD iterates converge to (0.5,0.5) while SGD does not. Plot pathwise optimality gap and squared error to minimum-norm solution across iterations. Expected: SGD achieves lower optimality gap but fails to converge to x*, while reg-SGD converges to x*=(0.5,0.5) at rate matching theoretical bounds.

code_available.evidence: OpenReview supplement provides MATLAB code bundles: Toy_example/ with main_L2rates.m (generates Figure 6 L2 rates), main_asrates.m (generates Figure 7 a.s. rates), main_comparison.m (generates Figure 8 comparison); Radon/ with main_radon.m, radon_forward.m; ODE_example/ with main_ODE.m, A_ellipticPDE.m. No external GitHub or HuggingFace repository found after searching: full title, arXiv ID '2505.11434', author names (Kassing, Weissmann, Döring), method names (reg-SGD, Tikhonov regularization, minimum-norm), and 'minimum-norm stochastic gradient regularization inverse'.

dataset_available.evidence: MRE uses synthetic 2D quadratic function f(x1,x2) defined analytically (no external data needed). All data is generated programmatically: Radon uses discretized 128x128 phantom, ODE uses random trigonometric series. No external dataset download required.

weights_available.evidence: No pretrained weights needed. This is an optimization algorithm theory paper; all experiments run from random/specified initializations without model checkpoints. Theoretical results validated through numerical simulation, not model training.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: MRE uses synthetic analytical functions: 2D quadratic for Toy_example, discretized Radon transform for tomography, ODE-based inverse problem. No standard ML benchmark (MNIST, CIFAR, ImageNet, etc.) is used. The paper validates theoretical convergence properties with controlled synthetic experiments.

h100_estimate_basis: Toy_example MRE: 10 MC runs × 10^6 iterations × 2D SGD update. Per iteration: ~10 FLOPs (2D gradient, 2 parameters). Total ~10^8 FLOPs ≈ 0.001 H100-hours. However, Monte Carlo variance estimation and plotting overhead adds ~100x. Total estimate: ~1 H100-hour. Note: Paper's larger experiments (Radon 5e6 iterations 16K-dim, ODE 1e7 iterations 256-dim) would require more compute but are not needed for MRE verification of central claim.
abstract: The present article studies the minimization of convex, L-smooth functions defined on a separable real Hilbert space. We analyze regularized stochastic gradient descent (reg-SGD), a variant of stochastic gradient descent that uses a Tikhonov regularization with time-dependent, vanishing regularization parameter. We prove strong convergence of reg-SGD to the minimum-norm solution of the original problem without additional boundedness assumptions. Moreover, we quantify the rate of convergence and optimize the interplay between step-sizes and regularization decay. Our analysis reveals how vanishing Tikhonov regularization controls the flow of SGD and yields stable learning dynamics, offering new insights into the design of iterative algorithms for convex problems, including those that arise in ill-posed inverse problems. We validate our theoretical findings through numerical experiments on image reconstruction and ODE-based inverse problems.

The paper reports costs in dollars (e.g., o4-mini on STARK-S costs ~$23) rather than GPU-hours. Actual inference compute runs on cloud providers' infrastructure and is not directly measurable. abstract: Spatiotemporal reasoning plays a key role in Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS). Despite advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), their capacity to reason about complex spatiotemporal signals remains underexplored. This paper proposes a hierarchical SpatioTemporal reAsoning benchmaRK, STARK, to systematically evaluate LLMs across three levels of reasoning complexity: state estimation (e.g., predicting field variables, localizing and tracking events in space and time), spatiotemporal reasoning over states (e.g., inferring spatial-temporal relationships), and world-knowledge-aware reasoning that integrates contextual and domain knowledge (e.g., intent prediction, landmark-aware navigation). We curate 26 distinct spatiotemporal tasks with diverse sensor modalities, comprising 14,552 challenges where models answer directly or by Python Code Interpreter. Evaluating 3 LRMs and 8 LLMs, we find LLMs achieve limited success in tasks requiring geometric reasoning (e.g., multilateration or triangulation), particularly as complexity increases. Surprisingly, LRMs show robust performance across tasks with various levels of difficulty, often competing or surpassing traditional first-principle-based methods. Our results show that in reasoning tasks requiring world knowledge, the performance gap between LLMs and LRMs narrows, with some LLMs even surpassing LRMs. However, the LRM o3 model continues to achieve leading performance across all evaluated tasks, a result attributed primarily to the larger size of the reasoning models. STARK motivates future …

abstract: Visual grounding is essential for precise perception and reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), especially in medical imaging domains. While existing medical visual grounding benchmarks primarily focus on single-image scenarios, real-world clinical applications often involve sequential images, where accurate lesion localization across different modalities and temporal tracking of disease progression (e.g., pre- vs. post-treatment comparison) require fine-grained cross-image semantic alignment and context-aware reasoning. To remedy the underrepresentation of image sequences in existing medical visual grounding benchmarks, we propose MedSG-Bench, the first benchmark tailored for Medical Image Sequences Grounding. It comprises eight VQA-style tasks, formulated into two paradigms of the grounding tasks, including 1) Image Difference Grounding, which focuses on detecting change regions across images, and 2) Image Consistency Grounding, which emphasizes detection of consistent or shared semantics across sequential images. MedSG-Bench covers 76 public datasets, 10 medical imaging modalities, and a wide spectrum of anatomical structures and diseases, totaling 9,630 question-answer pairs. We benchmark both general-purpose MLLMs (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL) and medical-domain specialized MLLMs (e.g., HuatuoGPT-vision), observing that even the advanced models exhibit substantial limitations in medical sequential grounding tasks. To advance this field, we construct MedSG-188K, a large-scale instruction-tuning dataset tailored for sequential visual grounding, and further develop …
