abstract: Current text-to-image diffusion generation typically employs complete-text conditioning. Due to the intricate syntax, diffusion transformers (DiTs) inherently suffer from a comprehension defect of complete-text captions. One-fly complete-text input either overlooks critical semantic details or causes semantic confusion by simultaneously modeling diverse semantic primitive types. To mitigate this defect of DiTs, we propose a novel split-text conditioning framework named DiT-ST. This framework converts a complete-text caption into a split-text caption, a collection of simplified sentences, to explicitly express various semantic primitives and their interconnections. The split-text caption is then injected into different denoising stages of DiT-ST in a hierarchical and incremental manner. Specifically, DiT-ST leverages Large Language Models to parse captions, extracting diverse primitives and hierarchically sorting out and constructing these primitives into a split-text input. Moreover, we partition the diffusion denoising process according to its differential sensitivities to diverse semantic primitive types and determine the appropriate timesteps to incrementally inject tokens of diverse semantic primitive types into input tokens via cross-attention. In this way, DiT-ST enhances the representation learning of specific semantic primitive types across different stages. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our proposed DiT-ST in mitigating the complete-text comprehension defect.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performance across diverse reasoning and generation tasks, and are increasingly deployed as agents in dynamic environments such as code generation and recommendation systems. However, many real-world applications, such as high-frequency trading and real-time competitive gaming, require decisions under strict latency constraints, where faster responses directly translate into higher rewards. Despite the importance of this latency quality trade off, it remains underexplored in the context of LLM based agents. In this work, we present the first systematic study of this trade off in real time decision making tasks. To support our investigation, we introduce two new benchmarks: HFTBench, a high frequency trading simulation, and StreetFighter, a competitive gaming platform. Our analysis reveals that optimal latency quality balance varies by task, and that sacrificing quality for lower latency can significantly enhance downstream performance. To address this, we propose FPX, an adaptive framework that dynamically selects model size and quantization level based on real time demands. Our method achieves the best performance on both benchmarks, improving win rate by up to 80% in Street Fighter and boosting daily yield by up to 26.52% in trading, underscoring the need for latency aware evaluation and deployment strategies for LLM based agents. These results demonstrate the critical importance of latency aware evaluation and deployment strategies for real world LLM based agents. Our benchmarks are available at Latency Sensitive …

title: Point-RFT: Improving Multimodal Reasoning with Visually Grounded Reinforcement Finetuning
abstract: Recent advances in large language models have significantly improved textual reasoning through the effective use of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and reinforcement learning. However, extending these successes to vision-language tasks remains challenging due to inherent limitations in text-only CoT, such as visual hallucinations and insufficient multimodal integration. In this paper, we introduce Point-RFT, a multimodal reasoning framework explicitly designed to leverage visually grounded CoT reasoning for visual document understanding. Our approach consists of two stages: First, we conduct format finetuning using a curated dataset of 71K diverse visual reasoning problems, each annotated with detailed, step-by-step rationales explicitly grounded to corresponding visual elements. Second, we employ reinforcement finetuning targeting visual document understanding. On ChartQA, our approach improves accuracy from 70.88% (format-finetuned baseline) to 90.04%, surpassing the 83.92% accuracy achieved by reinforcement finetuning relying solely on text-based CoT. The result shows that our grounded CoT is more effective for multimodal reasoning compared with the text-only CoT. Moreover, Point-RFT exhibits superior generalization capability across several out-of-domain visual document reasoning benchmarks, including CharXiv, PlotQA, IconQA, TabMWP, etc., and highlights its potential in complex real-world scenarios.

title: Data-Dependent Regret Bounds for Constrained MABs
central_claim: The paper introduces the first data-dependent regret bounds for constrained multi-armed bandit (MAB) settings, showing that in soft-constraints the regret is O(sqrt(sum of losses under optimal constrained policy)), and in hard-constraints it decomposes into two data-dependent terms capturing constraint satisfaction difficulty and bandit complexity separately. A matching lower bound shows both terms are fundamental.

We answer this question affirmatively.' Algorithms COLB (Alg. 1) and SOLB (Alg. 2) with Theorem 1, 2, 4, 5 regret bounds.

Verify observed regret follows O(sqrt(sum ell_t^top x*)) (soft) or the two-term bound (hard).

abstract: This paper initiates the study of data-dependent regret bounds in constrained MAB settings. These bounds depend on the sequence of losses that characterize the problem instance. Thus, they can be much smaller than classical $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bounds, while being equivalent to them in the worst case. Despite this, data-dependent regret bounds have been completely overlooked in constrained MAB settings. The goal of this paper is to answer the following question: Can data-dependent regret bounds be derived in the presence of constraints? We answer this question affirmatively in constrained MABs with adversarial losses and stochastic constraints. Specifically, our main focus is on the most challenging and natural settings with hard constraints, where the learner must ensure that the constraints are always satisfied with high probability. We design an algorithm with a regret bound consisting of two data-dependent terms. The first term captures the difficulty of satisfying the constraints, while the second one encodes the complexity of learning independently of the presence of constraints. We also prove a lower bound showing that these two terms are not artifacts of our specific approach and analysis, but rather the fundamental components that inherently characterize the complexities of the problem. Finally, in designing our algorithm, we also derive some novel results in the related (and easier) soft constraints settings, which may be of independent interest.

abstract: Long-horizon video-audio reasoning and fine-grained pixel understanding impose conflicting requirements on omnimodal models: dense temporal coverage demands many low-resolution frames, whereas precise grounding calls for high-resolution inputs. We tackle this trade-off with a two-system architecture: a Global Reasoning System selects informative keyframes and rewrites the task at low spatial cost, while a Detail Understanding System performs pixel-level grounding on the selected high-resolution snippets. Because ``optimal'' keyframe selection and reformulation are ambiguous and hard to supervise, we formulate them as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem and present Omni-R1, an end-to-end RL framework built on Group Relative Policy Optimization. Omni-R1 trains the Global Reasoning System through hierarchical rewards obtained via online collaboration with the Detail Understanding System, requiring only one epoch of RL on small task splits. Experiments on two challenging benchmarks, namely Referring Audio-Visual Segmentation (RefAVS) and Reasoning Video Object Segmentation (REVOS), show that Omni-R1 not only surpasses strong supervised baselines but also outperforms specialized state-of-the-art models, while substantially improving out-of-domain generalization and mitigating multimodal hallucination. Our results demonstrate the first successful application of RL to large-scale omnimodal reasoning and highlight a scalable path toward universally foundation models.

title: Time Series Generation Under Data Scarcity: A Unified Generative Modeling Approach
central_claim: The unified diffusion-based generative framework achieves state-of-the-art few-shot time series generation, outperforming domain-specific baselines across subset sizes with 55.72% and 54.25% performance gains on Discriminative Score and contextFID respectively.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'achieves state-of-the-art performance in few-shot settings—outperforming domain-specific baselines across a wide range of subset sizes' and reports 'over 55.72% and 54.25% performance gains on Discriminative Score and contextFID'. Table 1 (Tab:fewshot-results) shows results across 5%, 10%, 15%, #10, #25, #50 subset sizes demonstrating consistent improvement.
mre_config: Fine-tune pre-trained ImagenFew model on ETTm1 dataset using 10 samples (#10 subset), evaluate Discriminative Score and contextFID against paper's reported baseline of 0.357 and 5.393 respectively. Success criteria: Discriminative Score ≤ 0.30, contextFID ≤ 4.0
agent_task: Reproduce few-shot generation claim: (1) Install dependencies from requirements.txt; (2) Download pre-trained checkpoint from Google Drive link (if auth available) or prepare to train from scratch; (3) Run fine-tuning on ETTm1 with 10 samples: python run.py --subset_n 10 --model_ckpt ./models_ckpt/ImagenFew/dyConv_Basic_24.ckpt --config configs/finetune/ETTm1.yaml; (4) Evaluate using Discriminative Score and contextFID metrics from metrics/discriminative_torch.py and metrics/context_fid.py; (5) Verify Discriminative Score ≤ 0.30 and contextFID ≤ 4.0 to match paper's 26.61% improvement. If checkpoint unavailable, train from scratch on ETTm1 alone with 10 samples for 1000 epochs (requires ~5 H100-hours more compute).

For MRE: fine-tuning on 10 samples with 1000 epochs on 1 GPU estimated ~0.5-2 H100-hours. abstract: Generative modeling of time series is a central challenge in time series analysis, particularly under data-scarce conditions. Despite recent advances in generative modeling, a comprehensive understanding of how state-of-the-art generative models perform under limited supervision remains lacking. In this work, we conduct the first large-scale study evaluating leading generative models in data-scarce settings, revealing a substantial performance gap between full-data and data-scarce regimes. To close this gap, we propose a unified diffusion-based generative framework that can synthesize high-fidelity time series across diverse domains using just a few examples. Our model is pre-trained on a large, heterogeneous collection of time series datasets, enabling it to learn generalizable temporal representations. It further incorporates architectural innovations such as dynamic convolutional layers for flexible channel adaptation and dataset token conditioning for domain-aware generation. Without requiring abundant supervision, our unified model achieves state-of-the-art performance in few-shot settings-outperforming domain-specific baselines across a wide range of subset sizes. Remarkably, it also surpasses all baselines even when tested on full datasets benchmarks, highlighting the strength of pre-training and cross-domain generalization. We hope this work encourages the community to revisit few-shot generative modeling as a key problem in time series research and pursue unified solutions that scale efficiently across domains. title: AstroVisBench: A Code Benchmark for Scientific Computing and Visualization in Astronomy
central_claim: LLMs struggle with astronomy-specific scientific computing and visualization tasks, with even state-of-the-art models showing high crash rates (30-65%) and low variable inspection scores (0.47-0.69), demonstrating a significant gap in their ability to assist in astronomy research workflows.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'significant gap in their ability to engage in astronomy research as useful assistants.' Table 1 shows Gemini 2.5 Pro (best performer) has 30.8% crash rate on processing tasks and only 15.7% no-error rate on visualization tasks. Even the highest VIscore (o3-mini: 0.694) shows models produce only ~70% of required processing products.
mre_config: Evaluate a single LLM (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Pro or o3-mini) on a random sample of 20-50 benchmark tasks to measure crash rate and VIscore for processing tasks. This verifies the central claim that LLMs struggle with astronomy-specific scientific workflows. The evaluation requires downloading the benchmark JSON from HuggingFace, setting up the conda environment, downloading the bench environment tarball, and running exec_bench.py on the sample.
agent_task: Reproduce a subset of AstroVisBench evaluation: (1) Download benchmark JSON from HuggingFace (sebajoe/AstroVisBench) or Box link, (2) Set up conda environment with 'conda create -n astrovis python=3.10' and run reqs_resolve/install_packages.sh, (3) Download bench environment tarball (bench_env.tar.gz) to working directory, (4) Use an LLM API to generate code for a random sample of 20-50 benchmark tasks by filling in processing_gen_code and visualization_gen_code fields, (5) Run exec_bench.py to execute and evaluate the generated code against ground truth, (6) Measure crash rate and VIscore to verify that LLMs struggle with astronomy-specific code generation (expected: crash rate >30%, VIscore <0.70).

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo NSF-Simons-CosmicAI-Institute/AstroVisBench contains exec_bench.py (29KB execution engine), vis_evaluation/vis_evaluation.py (visualization evaluation), generate_code/generate_code.py (code generation), requirements.txt, and full README with setup instructions. All benchmark evaluation pipelines are implemented.

dataset_available.evidence: HuggingFace dataset sebajoe/AstroVisBench contains astrovisbench_queries.json (141MB). Benchmark environment and ground truth cache available via Box link as documented in README. Custom astronomy benchmark derived from NOIRLab and STScI Jupyter notebooks.

weights_available.evidence: No pretrained model weights or checkpoints are required or released for this benchmark evaluation task. The benchmark evaluates externally-hosted LLMs (Gemini, Claude, GPT, Qwen, Llama) via API calls.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: AstroVisBench is a custom benchmark with 864 tasks (432 processing + 432 visualization) sourced from 110 astronomy Jupyter notebooks. Not a standard ML benchmark like MNIST or ImageNet; it's a domain-specific benchmark for evaluating LLM code generation on astronomy research workflows.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified for API-based LLM evaluation. MRE involves sampling 20-50 tasks and making API calls to an LLM provider. The paper reports evaluation on 2x56-Core Intel Xeon MAX 9480 CPUs with 128GB RAM, requiring ~100GB storage. No GPU compute is required for API-based evaluation since the benchmark only evaluates LLM-generated code execution, not model training.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are being explored for applications in scientific research, including their capabilities to synthesize literature, answer research questions, generate research ideas, and even conduct computational experiments. Ultimately, our goal is for these to help scientists derive novel scientific insights. In many areas of science, such insights often arise from processing and visualizing data to understand its patterns. However, evaluating whether an LLM-mediated scientific workflow produces outputs conveying the correct scientific insights is challenging to evaluate and has not been addressed in past work. We introduce AstroVisBench, the first benchmark for both scientific computing and visualization in the astronomy domain. AstroVisBench judges a language model's ability to both (1) create astronomy-specific workflows to process and analyze data and (2) visualize the results of these workflows through complex plots. Our evaluation of visualizations uses a novel LLM-as-a-judge workflow, which is validated against annotation by five professional astronomers. Using AstroVisBench we present an evaluation of state-of-the-art language models, showing a significant gap in their ability to engage in astronomy research as useful assistants. This evaluation provides a strong end-to-end evaluation for AI scientists that offers a path forward for the development of visualization-based workflows, which are central to a broad range of domains from physics to biology.

title: Balancing Performance and Costs in Best Arm Identification
central_claim: The paper proposes a new Best Arm Identification framework that balances performance penalty (probability of misidentification or simple regret) with sampling costs through a risk functional. Their DBCARE algorithm achieves near-optimal risk matching theoretical lower bounds up to polylog factors on nearly all problem instances.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'We derive theoretical lower bounds for the risk of each of two choices for the performance penalty, the probability of misidentification and the simple regret, and propose an algorithm called DBCARE to match these lower bounds up to polylog factors on nearly all problem instances.' Figure 1 (fig:exp-two-arm) and Table 1 demonstrate DBCARE's uniformly good performance across all Δ values compared to fixed budget and fixed confidence baselines.
mre_config: 2-arm Gaussian bandit simulation comparing DBCARE against Sequential Halving (fixed budget T=10, T=500) and elimination procedures (fixed confidence δ=0.1, δ=0.01). Settings: σ²=1, means ±Δ/2 for Δ∈[0.05,2], cost c=10⁻⁴, 10⁵ runs per setting. Measure risk₁ (probability of misidentification + c×samples) and risk₂ (simple regret + c×samples) across Δ range.
agent_task: Implement the DBCARE (Dynamically Budgeted Cost-Adapted Risk-minimizing Elimination) algorithm for 2-arm best arm identification as specified in Algorithm 1. Run a simulation study with Gaussian arms (σ²=1, means ±Δ/2 for Δ∈[0.05,2], cost c=10⁻⁴) comparing against: (1) Sequential Halving with budgets T=10 and T=500, (2) elimination procedure with confidence bounds √(4σ²n⁻¹log(Knδ⁻¹)) with δ=0.1 and δ=0.01. Report risk₁ (P(misidentification) + c×samples) and risk₂ (simple_regret + c×samples) averaged over 10⁵ runs per Δ value. Plot results showing DBCARE's uniform performance across all Δ values.

code_available.evidence: No code repository found after exhaustive searches: full title 'Balancing Performance and Costs Best Arm Identification', algorithm name 'DBCARE', acronym variants, author names 'Harding Kandasamy', arXiv ID '2505.20583'. Author GitHub accounts have 0 public repositories (kandasamy). OpenReview supplement contains only the paper PDF (balancing-performance-and-costs-in-bai-FULL.pdf), no code files.

dataset_available.evidence: MRE uses synthetic Gaussian/Bernoulli bandit data that is trivially reproducible from paper specifications: Gaussian arms with σ²=1, means ±Δ/2 for Δ∈[0.05,2]; Bernoulli arms with means 0.5±Δ/2 for Δ∈[0.01,0.95]. Standard random sampling (numpy.random.normal, numpy.random.binomial) suffices to generate the data.

weights_available.evidence: Bandit algorithms do not require model weights or checkpoints. DBCARE operates on streaming samples and maintains only running statistics and confidence intervals; no pre-trained model files are involved.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: MRE uses synthetic Gaussian/Bernoulli distributions generated on-the-fly with parameters specified in the paper, not a widely recognized public ML benchmark such as MNIST, CIFAR, ImageNet, or GLUE.

h100_estimate_basis: Paper reports 7.5 hours total runtime on AMD Ryzen 9 5900X for all K-arm experiments. MRE (2-arm simulations) requires 10⁵ runs × ~40 Δ values × 2 reward types × 4 comparison methods = ~3.2M total bandit episodes. Extrapolating: estimated ~2-4 hours on a modern CPU equivalent to ~15 H100-hours for GPU-based simulation. Engineering/debugging time for implementing DBCARE, Sequential Halving, and elimination baselines from paper algorithm descriptions is additional.
abstract: We consider the problem of identifying the best arm in a multi-armed bandit model. Despite a wealth of literature in the traditional fixed budget and fixed confidence regimes of the best arm identification problem, it still remains a mystery to most practitioners as to how to choose an approach and corresponding budget or confidence parameter. We propose a new formalism to avoid this dilemma altogether by minimizing a risk functional which explicitly balances the performance of the recommended arm and the cost incurred by learning this arm. In this framework, a cost is incurred for each observation during the sampling phase, and upon recommending an arm, a performance penalty is incurred for identifying a suboptimal arm. The learner's goal is to minimize the sum of the penalty and cost. This new regime mirrors the priorities of many practitioners, e.g. maximizing profit in an A/B testing framework, better than classical fixed budget or confidence settings. We derive theoretical lower bounds for the risk of each of two choices for the performance penalty, the probability of misidentification and the simple regret, and propose an algorithm called DBCARE to match these lower bounds up to polylog factors on nearly all problem instances. We then demonstrate the performance of DBCARE on a number of simulated models, comparing to fixed budget and confidence algorithms to show the shortfalls of existing BAI paradigms on this problem.

title: Uni-Instruct: One-step Diffusion Model through Unified Diffusion Divergence Instruction
central_claim: Uni-Instruct unifies one-step diffusion distillation methods through an f-divergence framework and achieves new SoTA FID scores: 1.46 (CIFAR10 unconditional), 1.38 (CIFAR10 conditional), and 1.02 (ImageNet64 conditional).
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'On the CIFAR10 generation benchmark, Uni-Instruct achieves record-breaking Frechet Inception Distance (FID) values of 1.46 for unconditional generation and 1.38 for conditional generation.' Table 1 shows CIFAR10 unconditional FID 1.46 (JKL from scratch) and Table 2 shows ImageNet64 FID 1.02 (FKL longer training).
mre_config: CIFAR10 32x32 unconditional one-step generation: Train Uni-Instruct with Forward-KL or Jeffrey-KL divergence from pretrained EDM teacher (edm-cifar10-32x32-uncond-vp.pkl), batch size 256, learning rate 1e-5, duration 300 kimg, evaluate FID. Target: FID ≤ 1.52 within reasonable tolerance.
agent_task: Reproduce CIFAR10 unconditional generation with Uni-Instruct: 1) Create conda environment from environment.yaml and activate it. 2) Download CIFAR10 32x32 dataset (cifar10-32x32.zip). 3) Download pretrained EDM teacher from https://nvlabs-fi-cdn.nvidia.com/edm/pretrained/edm-cifar10-32x32-uncond-vp.pkl and FID detector from https://nvlabs-fi-cdn.nvidia.com/stylegan2-ada-pytorch/pretrained/metrics/inception-2015-12-05.pt. 4) Execute training: torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=2 fsim_train.py --data './datasets/cifar10-32x32.zip' --outdir './experiments/cifar10-uncond' --divergence 'Forward-KL' --arch ddpmpp --edm_model 'https://nvlabs-fi-cdn.nvidia.com/edm/pretrained/edm-cifar10-32x32-uncond-vp.pkl' --detector_url 'https://nvlabs-fi-cdn.nvidia.com/stylegan2-ada-pytorch/pretrained/metrics/inception-2015-12-05.pt' --batch 256 --batch-gpu 128 --lr 1e-5 --glr 1e-5 --duration 300 --use_gan 1 --metrics fid50k_full. 5) Evaluate FID score; target ≤ 1.52 to verify the method works.

Since H200 SXM has 1.00x H100-equivalent, this is approximately 20 H100-hours. Engineering and debugging time additional and not included.
abstract: In this paper, we unify more than 10 existing one-step diffusion distillation approaches, such as Diff-Instruct, DMD, SIM, SiD, $f$-distill, etc, inside a theory-driven framework which we name the \textbf{\emph{Uni-Instruct}}. Uni-Instruct is motivated by our proposed diffusion expansion theory of the $f$-divergence family. Then we introduce key theories that overcome the intractability issue of the original expanded $f$-divergence, resulting in an equivalent yet tractable loss that effectively trains one-step diffusion models by minimizing the expanded $f$-divergence family. The novel unification introduced by Uni-Instruct not only offers new theoretical contributions that help understand existing approaches from a high-level perspective but also leads to state-of-the-art one-step diffusion generation performances. On the CIFAR10 generation benchmark, Uni-Instruct achieves record-breaking Frechet Inception Distance (FID) values of \textbf{\emph{1.46}} for unconditional generation and \textbf{\emph{1.38}} for conditional generation. On the ImageNet-$64\times 64$ generation benchmark, Uni-Instruct achieves a new SoTA one-step generation FID of \textbf{\emph{1.02}}, which outperforms its 79-step teacher diffusion with a significant improvement margin of 1.33 (1.02 vs 2.35). We also apply Uni-Instruct on broader tasks like text-to-3D generation. For text-to-3D generation, Uni-Instruct gives decent results, which slightly outperforms previous methods, such as SDS and VSD, in terms of both generation quality and diversity. Both the solid theoretical and empirical contributions …

title: Rendering-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Vector Graphics Generation
central_claim: RLRF (Reinforcement Learning from Rendering Feedback) significantly outperforms supervised fine-tuning for SVG generation in autoregressive VLMs by leveraging feedback from rendered SVG outputs through a composite reward function combining image reconstruction, semantic similarity, and code efficiency signals.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'RLRF significantly outperforms supervised fine-tuning, addressing common failure modes and enabling precise, high-quality SVG generation with strong structural understanding and generalization.' Table 1 shows Qwen2.5VL-3B improves from 9.48 MSE (SVG-SFT) to 4.79 MSE (RLRF), and Table 3 shows ablation confirming SVG-SFT is essential before RLRF.
mre_config: RLRF training on Qwen2.5VL-3B for 500 steps with 32 images/batch and 64 rollouts/image on a curated 16k high-entropy SVG-Stack subset (>500 tokens), followed by evaluation on SVG-Stack-Hard (500 samples). Key metric: MSE improvement over SVG-SFT baseline. This tests the core claim that rendering-based RL improves SVG generation.
agent_task: Reproduce the RLRF MRE by: (1) Loading Qwen2.5VL-3B base model and performing SVG-SFT using LLaMA-Factory on SVG-Stack filtered subset; (2) Running GRPO-based RL training with custom rendering rewards (L2, DreamSim, length penalty) using the paper's hyperparameters (lr=1e-5, batch=32, rollouts=64, temp=1.1, epsilon=0.4, no KL penalty); (3) Evaluating on SVG-Stack-Hard comparing MSE against the SFT baseline. Key challenge: implementing the composite rendering reward from scratch since RLRF code is not released.

code_available.evidence: No dedicated RLRF code repository found after extensive searches. Searches tried: RLRF, 'Reinforcement Learning from Rendering Feedback', 'Rendering-Aware Reinforcement Learning', arXiv ID 2505.20793, ServiceNow Research, joanrod RLRF, starvector RLRF. StarVector repo (joanrod/star-vector) contains base SVG generation code but not RLRF-specific implementation. Paper mentions using EasyR1 and VERL frameworks for RL training, but these are general RL libraries without RLRF-specific reward functions or rendering pipeline. The bundled OpenReview supplement contains only a PDF, not runnable code.

dataset_available.evidence: SVG-Stack dataset verified available on HuggingFace (starvector/svg-stack) with 2.1M image-SVG pairs. The paper's RLRF training uses a filtered 16k high-entropy subset (>500 tokens) from this dataset. SVG-Stack-Hard test set (500 samples) is described in the paper appendix but appears to be derived from SVG-Stack with specific curation criteria; public release status unclear but construction process is documented.

weights_available.evidence: StarVector-1B base model weights are available on HuggingFace. However, RLRF-trained checkpoints (StarVector-1B+RLRF, Qwen2.5VL-3B+RLRF, Qwen2.5VL-7B+RLRF) are NOT released. Searches for RLRF-specific checkpoints on HuggingFace returned no results. The paper claims RLRF improvements but trained weights are not distributed.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: SVG-Stack is a custom dataset scraped from GitHub SVGs (rodriguez2025starvector), not a widely recognized public benchmark like MNIST, CIFAR, or ImageNet. While available on HuggingFace, it is author-created and domain-specific to SVG vectorization tasks.

h100_estimate_basis: Paper reports SFT training: 4×8 H100 GPUs for ~3 days for 3B model = 2304 GPU-hours. RLRF training: 4 nodes × 8×H100 for ~3 days = 2304 GPU-hours. Total: 4608 GPU-hours at H100-equivalent. Engineering/debugging time not included. Note: This is minimum for smallest model; larger models (7B) require double the resources.
abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) offer a powerful format for representing visual designs as interpretable code. Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled high-quality SVG generation by framing the problem as a code generation task and leveraging large-scale pretraining. VLMs are particularly suitable for this task as they capture both global semantics and fine-grained visual patterns, while transferring knowledge across vision, natural language, and code domains. However, existing VLM approaches often struggle to produce faithful and efficient SVGs because they never observe the rendered images during training. Although differentiable rendering for autoregressive SVG code generation remains unavailable, rendered outputs can still be compared to original inputs, enabling evaluative feedback suitable for reinforcement learning (RL). We introduce RLRF (Reinforcement Learning from Rendering Feedback), an RL method that enhances SVG generation in autoregressive VLMs by leveraging feedback from rendered SVG outputs. Given an input image, the model generates SVG roll-outs that are rendered and compared to the original image to compute a reward. This visual fidelity feedback guides the model toward producing more accurate, efficient, and semantically coherent SVGs. RLRF significantly outperforms supervised fine-tuning, addressing common failure modes and enabling precise, high-quality SVG generation with strong structural understanding and generalization.

title: Fully Spiking Neural Networks for Unified Frame-Event Object Tracking
central_claim: SpikeFET, the first fully spiking neural network for unified frame-event object tracking, achieves state-of-the-art tracking accuracy while maintaining significantly lower power consumption than existing methods (e.g., SpikeFET-Tiny achieves 68.5% AUC on FE108 with only 18.36mJ power consumption).
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'we propose the first fully Spiking Frame-Event Tracking framework called SpikeFET... achieves superior tracking accuracy over existing methods while significantly reducing power consumption.' Table 1: SpikeFET-Tiny achieves AUC 68.5% on FE108 with 18.36mJ power; SpikeFET-Base achieves AUC 68.7% on FE108 with 102.61mJ power.
mre_config: Evaluate pre-trained SpikeFET-Tiny on FE108 benchmark. Use config spikefet_fe108_tiny.yaml (SpikeFormer_tiny backbone, 29.33M params, 4 timesteps). Download pre-trained V3_19.0M_1x4.pth from Google Drive. Run inference with python tracking/test.py spikefet spikefet_fe108_tiny --dataset fe108 --threads 4 --num_gpus 1 --ckpt <checkpoint_path>. Analyze results with python tracking/analysis_results.py --dataset fe108 --parameter_name spikefet_fe108_tiny. Metric: AUC score, expected ~68.5%.

Verify AUC >= 68.0%.

COESOT available at github.com/Event-AHU/COESOT. Dataset loaders implemented in lib/test/evaluation/fe108dataset.py, viseventdataset.py, coesotdataset.py.

All trained checkpoints available at drive.google.com/drive/folders/1JlVOSm1dZM0_RjcwQ6bqdLa4JBBwPtGz.

h100_estimate_basis: Inference-only MRE using pre-trained weights: The paper reports 106 FPS inference speed for SpikeFET-Tiny on VisEvent. FE108 has 32 test sequences with ~500-2000 frames each (estimated ~30K total frames). Inference time on 1 GPU: ~30K/106 ≈ 283 seconds ≈ 0.08 GPU-hours. Adding data loading and result processing overhead: estimated 0.1-1.0 H100-hours. Note: Training from scratch would require ~100+ H100-hours (50 epochs, 60K samples/epoch, 2x RTX 4090).
abstract: The integration of image and event streams offers a promising approach for achieving robust visual object tracking in complex environments. However, current fusion methods achieve high performance at the cost of significant computational overhead and struggle to efficiently extract the sparse, asynchronous information from event streams, failing to leverage the energy-efficient advantages of event-driven spiking paradigms. To address this challenge, we propose the first fully Spiking Frame-Event Tracking framework called SpikeFET. This network achieves synergistic integration of convolutional local feature extraction and Transformer-based global modeling within the spiking paradigm, effectively fusing frame and event data. To overcome the degradation of translation invariance caused by convolutional padding, we introduce a Random Patchwork Module (RPM) that eliminates positional bias through randomized spatial reorganization and learnable type encoding while preserving residual structures. Furthermore, we propose a Spatial-Temporal Regularization (STR) strategy that overcomes similarity metric degradation from asymmetric features by enforcing spatio-temporal consistency among temporal template features in latent space. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior tracking accuracy over existing methods while significantly reducing power consumption, attaining an optimal balance between performance and efficiency.

title: Improved Bounds for Swap Multicalibration and Swap Omniprediction
central_claim: The paper proves that an efficient algorithm can achieve O(T^(1/3)) L2-swap multicalibration error against bounded linear functions, improving upon the O(T^(3/4)) bound of Garg et al. (2024) and O(T^(7/8)) bounds for swap omniprediction.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'We propose an efficient algorithm that achieves O(T^(1/3)) L2-swap multicalibration error (both in high probability and expectation).' Section 4 (Theorem 1, Theorem 4) formally establishes these improved bounds. Table 1 compares new rates with previous best-known bounds.
mre_config: No empirical MRE exists - this is a purely theoretical paper with no experiments. The 'reproduction' would require verifying mathematical proofs, not running code. No datasets, training protocols, or evaluation metrics are defined for empirical validation.
agent_task: This paper presents purely theoretical results (theorems, lemmas, and corollaries proving improved regret/sample complexity bounds). There is no code, data, or experiments to reproduce. The central claim can only be verified by reading and understanding the mathematical proofs in Sections 4-7 (reduction frameworks, Online Newton Step analysis, Freedman martingale inequalities). No automatic agent can reproduce these results through code execution - they require manual mathematical verification.

abstract: In this paper, we consider the related problems of multicalibration -- a multigroup fairness notion and omniprediction -- a simultaneous loss minimization paradigm, both in the distributional and online settings. The recent work of Garg et al. (2024) raised the open problem of whether it is possible to efficiently achieve $O(\sqrt{T})$ $\ell_{2}$-multicalibration error against bounded linear functions. In this paper, we answer this question in a strongly affirmative sense. We propose an efficient algorithm that achieves $O(T^{\frac{1}{3}})$ $\ell_{2}$-swap multicalibration error (both in high probability and expectation). On propagating this bound onward, we obtain significantly improved rates for $\ell_{1}$-swap multicalibration and swap omniprediction for a loss class of convex Lipschitz functions. In particular, we show that our algorithm achieves $O(T^{\frac{2}{3}})$ $\ell_{1}$-swap multicalibration and swap omniprediction errors, thereby improving upon the previous best-known bound of $O(T^{\frac{7}{8}})$. As a consequence of our improved online results, we further obtain several improved sample complexity rates in the distributional setting. In particular, we establish a $O(\varepsilon ^ {-3})$ sample complexity of efficiently learning an $\varepsilon$-swap omnipredictor for the class of convex and Lipschitz functions, $O(\varepsilon ^{-2.5})$ sample complexity of efficiently learning an $\varepsilon$-swap agnostic learner for the squared loss, and $O(\varepsilon ^ {-5}), O(\varepsilon ^ {-2.5})$ sample complexities of learning $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}$-swap …

abstract: World models have recently attracted growing interest in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) due to their ability to improve sample efficiency for policy learning. However, accurately modeling environments in MARL is challenging due to the exponentially large joint action space and highly uncertain dynamics inherent in multi-agent systems. To address this, we reduce modeling complexity by shifting from jointly modeling the entire state-action transition dynamics to focusing on the state space alone at each timestep through sequential agent modeling. Specifically, our approach enables the model to progressively resolve uncertainty while capturing the structured dependencies among agents, providing a more accurate representation of how agents influence the state. Interestingly, this sequential revelation of agents' actions in a multi-agent system aligns with the reverse process in diffusion models--a class of powerful generative models known for their expressiveness and training stability compared to autoregressive or latent variable models. Leveraging this insight, we develop a flexible and robust world model for MARL using diffusion models. Our method, Diffusion-Inspired Multi-Agent world model (DIMA), achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple multi-agent control benchmarks, significantly outperforming prior world models in terms of final return and sample efficiency, including MAMuJoCo and Bi-DexHands. DIMA establishes a new paradigm for constructing multi-agent world models, advancing the frontier of MARL research. Codes are open-sourced at …

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, but their application to long-term Earth observation analysis remains limited, primarily focusing on single-temporal or bi-temporal imagery. To address this gap, we introduce DVL-Suite, a comprehensive framework for analyzing long-term urban dynamics through remote sensing imagery. Our suite comprises 14,871 high-resolution (1.0m) multi-temporal images spanning 42 major cities in the U.S. from 2005 to 2023, organized into two components: DVL-Bench and DVL-Instruct. The DVL-Bench includes six urban understanding tasks, from fundamental change detection (pixel-level) to quantitative analyses (regional-level) and comprehensive urban narratives (scene-level), capturing diverse urban dynamics including expansion/transformation patterns, disaster assessment, and environmental challenges. We evaluate 18 state-of-the-art MLLMs and reveal their limitations in long-term temporal understanding and quantitative analysis. These challenges motivate the creation of DVL-Instruct, a specialized instruction-tuning dataset designed to enhance models' capabilities in multi-temporal Earth observation. Building upon this dataset, we develop DVLChat, a baseline model capable of both image-level question-answering and pixel-level segmentation, facilitating a comprehensive understanding of city dynamics through language interactions.

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) are widely used for regression and optimization tasks such as Bayesian optimization (BO) due to their expressiveness and principled uncertainty estimates. However, in settings with large datasets corrupted by outliers, standard GPs and their sparse approximations struggle with computational tractability and robustness. We introduce Robust Computation-aware Gaussian Process (RCaGP), a novel GP model that jointly addresses these challenges by combining a principled treatment of approximation-induced uncertainty with robust generalized Bayesian updating. The key insight is that robustness and approximation-awareness are not orthogonal but intertwined: approximations can exacerbate the impact of outliers, and mitigating one without the other is insufficient. Unlike previous work that focuses narrowly on either robustness or approximation quality, RCaGP combines both in a principled and scalable framework, thus effectively managing both outliers and computational uncertainties introduced by approximations such as low-rank matrix multiplications. Our model ensures more conservative and reliable uncertainty estimates, a property we rigorously demonstrate. Additionally, we establish a robustness property and show that the mean function is key to preserving it, motivating a tailored model selection scheme for robust mean functions. Empirical results confirm that solving these challenges jointly leads to superior performance across both clean and outlier-contaminated settings, both on regression and high-throughput Bayesian optimization benchmarks.

abstract: We present Plenodium (plenoptic medium), an effective and efficient 3D representation framework capable of jointly modeling both objects and participating media. In contrast to existing medium representations that rely solely on view-dependent modeling, our novel plenoptic medium representation incorporates both directional and positional information through spherical harmonics encoding, enabling highly accurate underwater scene reconstruction. To address the initialization challenge in degraded underwater environments, we propose the pseudo-depth Gaussian complementation to augment COLMAP-derived point clouds with robust depth priors. In addition, a depth ranking regularized loss is developed to optimize the geometry of the scene and improve the ordinal consistency of the depth maps. Extensive experiments on real-world underwater datasets demonstrate that our method achieves significant improvements in 3D reconstruction. Furthermore, we conduct a simulated dataset with ground truth and the controllable scattering medium to demonstrate the restoration capability of our method in underwater scenarios. Our code and dataset are available at https://plenodium.github.io/.

abstract: Recent interest in Multi-Agent Systems of Large Language Models (MAS LLMs) has led to an increase in frameworks leveraging multiple LLMs to tackle complex tasks. However, much of this literature appropriates the terminology of MAS without engaging with its foundational principles. In this position paper, we highlight critical discrepancies between MAS theory and current MAS LLMs implementations, focusing on four key areas: the social aspect of agency, environment design, coordination and communication protocols, and measuring emergent behaviours. Our position is that many MAS LLMs lack multi-agent characteristics such as autonomy, social interaction, and structured environments, and often rely on oversimplified, LLM-centric architectures. The field may slow down and lose traction by revisiting problems the MAS literature has already addressed. Therefore, we systematically analyse this issue and outline associated research opportunities; we advocate for better integrating established MAS concepts and more precise terminology to avoid mischaracterisation and missed opportunities.

abstract: Video large language models (video LLMs) excel at video comprehension but face significant computational inefficiency due to redundant video tokens. Existing token pruning methods offer solutions. However, approaches operating within the LLM (inner-LLM pruning), such as FastV, incur intrinsic computational overhead in shallow layers. In contrast, methods performing token pruning before the LLM (outer-LLM pruning) primarily address spatial redundancy within individual frames or limited temporal windows, neglecting the crucial global temporal dynamics and correlations across longer video sequences. This leads to sub-optimal spatio-temporal reduction and does not leverage video compressibility fully. Crucially, the synergistic potential and mutual influence of combining these strategies remain unexplored. To further reduce redundancy, we introduce HoliTom, a novel training-free holistic token merging framework. HoliTom employs outer-LLM pruning through global redundancy-aware temporal segmentation, followed by spatial-temporal merging to reduce visual tokens by over 90%, significantly alleviating the LLM's computational burden. Complementing this, we introduce a robust inner-LLM token similarity-based merging approach, designed for superior performance and compatibility with outer-LLM pruning. Evaluations demonstrate our method's promising efficiency-performance trade-off on LLaVA-OneVision-7B, reducing computational costs to 6.9% of FLOPs while maintaining 99.1% of the original performance. Furthermore, we achieve a 2.28x reduction in Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and a 1.32x …

title: OVERT: A Benchmark for Over-Refusal Evaluation on Text-to-Image Models
central_claim: OVERT is the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating over-refusal in T2I models. The central empirical claim is that over-refusal is widespread across T2I models (e.g., DALL-E-3-Web shows 51.7% avg refusal rate on benign prompts), demonstrating a strong safety-utility trade-off where models that better reject harmful prompts also tend to over-reject benign ones.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'OVERT includes 4,600 seemingly harmful but benign prompts across nine safety-related categories... Using OVERT, we evaluate several leading T2I models and find that over-refusal is a widespread issue across various categories.' Table 1 (tab:evaluation-mini) shows refusal rates for 5 T2I models across 9 categories on OVERT-mini.
mre_config: Evaluate a single T2I model's refusal rate on one category of OVERT-mini (200 prompts per category). For example: `python main.py --model_name 'stable-diffusion-3.5-large' --category 'sexual_content' --split 'mini'`. The metric is refusal rate (% of benign prompts refused). Using SD-3.5-Large locally or proprietary APIs (Imagen-3, DALL-E-3) via API keys.
agent_task: Reproduce the over-refusal evaluation on a single T2I model using OVERT-mini. Steps: (1) Clone the OVERT GitHub repo: https://github.com/yixiao-huang/OVERT; (2) Install dependencies: pip install tyro tqdm requests pillow torch diffusers numpy; (3) Configure API keys in utils/api_keys.json for desired model (imagen/dall-e/flux), or use local SD-3.5-Large without API keys; (4) Run evaluation for one category: python main.py --model_name 'stable-diffusion-3.5-large' --category 'sexual_content' --split 'mini'; (5) Check the refusal rate in eval_logs/{category}/{model_name}/eval_results_mini.json and compare to paper's Table 1 (SD-3.5-Large sexual content: 7.5% refusal rate). The MRE validates over-refusal by demonstrating that the model refuses benign prompts containing sensitive keywords like 'pornography', 'sexual content', etc.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo yixiao-huang/OVERT contains complete evaluation code: main.py (entry point with model selection, category/split options), utils/eval_utils.py (eval_model function with API calls and refusal detection), utils/stable_diffusion_utils.py (SD model loader). README shows example usage: `python main.py --model_name 'imagen-3.0-generate-002' --category 'sexual_content' --split 'mini'`. All files verified accessible via GitHub MCP.

dataset_available.evidence: OVERT dataset available in two verified locations: (1) GitHub repo data/ directory with OVERT-mini/*.json (1800 prompts, 200 per category), OVERT-full/*.json (4600 prompts), OVERT-unsafe/*.json (1785 prompts); (2) HuggingFace dataset yixiaoh/OVERT with CSV files (verified with 1.3K downloads). Both sources confirmed accessible via GitHub MCP and HuggingFace MCP tools.

weights_available.evidence: This paper does not train or release model weights. The paper evaluates existing T2I models: (1) Proprietary APIs - Imagen-3, DALL-E-3 (no weights available); (2) Open-source - SD-3.5-Large is available separately on HuggingFace (stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-large) but is not released by this paper. No custom checkpoints, adapters, or fine-tuned weights are released by the authors.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: OVERT is a custom benchmark dataset created by the authors for evaluating over-refusal in T2I models. It contains 4600 synthetic prompts across 9 safety-related categories designed to trigger over-refusal. It is not a standard widely-recognized ML benchmark like ImageNet, CIFAR-10, or COCO.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified: The paper uses proprietary APIs (Imagen-3, DALL-E-3, FLUX1.1-Pro) for evaluation rather than reported GPU-hours. For local evaluation with SD-3.5-Large on OVERT-mini (200 prompts × ~3-4 image_prompts per seed = ~700 image generations), estimated inference time is ~0.5-1 H100-hours. API-based evaluation does not consume local H100 compute. Engineering/debugging time (setup, API key configuration, troubleshooting) is additional and not included.
abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) models have achieved remarkable success in generating visual content from text inputs. Although multiple safety alignment strategies have been proposed to prevent harmful outputs, they often lead to overly cautious behavior -- rejecting even benign prompts -- a phenomenon known as $\textit{over-refusal}$ that reduces the practical utility of T2I models. Despite over-refusal having been observed in practice, there is no large-scale benchmark that systematically evaluates this phenomenon for T2I models. In this paper, we present an automatic workflow to construct synthetic evaluation data, resulting in OVERT ($\textbf{OVE}$r-$\textbf{R}$efusal evaluation on $\textbf{T}$ext-to-image models), the first large-scale benchmark for assessing over-refusal behaviors in T2I models. OVERT includes 4,600 seemingly harmful but benign prompts across nine safety-related categories, along with 1,785 genuinely harmful prompts (OVERT-unsafe) to evaluate the safety-utility trade-off. Using OVERT, we evaluate several leading T2I models and find that over-refusal is a widespread issue across various categories (Figure 1), underscoring the need for further research to enhance the safety alignment of T2I models without compromising their functionality. As a preliminary attempt to reduce over-refusal, we explore prompt rewriting; however, we find it often compromises faithfulness to the meaning of the original prompts. Finally, we demonstrate the flexibility of our generation framework in accommodating diverse safety requirements by generating customized evaluation data …

title: Autoencoding Random Forests
central_claim: RFAE can autoencode tabular data using random forests, projecting data to a latent space via diffusion maps and decoding back to the input space, achieving competitive performance with neural autoencoders on compression and reconstruction tasks.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'RFAE is competitive with the state of the art across a range of tasks including data visualization, compression, clustering, and denoising.' Table 1 shows mean distortion across 20 datasets where RFAE has best average rank (1.80) among 5 methods.
mre_config: Encode and decode Fisher's iris dataset using RFAE R package with a small RF (50 trees, k=2 latent dimensions, k=5 for kNN decoding), compute reconstruction error, compare reconstructed values to original inputs. This matches the minimal example in the RFAE package README (https://github.com/bips-hb/RFAE).
agent_task: Reproduce the RFAE autoencoding pipeline on Fisher's iris dataset: (1) Install RFAE package from https://github.com/bips-hb/RFAE using devtools::install_github('bips-hb/RFAE'); (2) Train a small RF with ranger::ranger on iris training set with num.trees=50; (3) Encode training data with encode(rf, iris[trn,], k=2); (4) Embed test samples with predict(emap, rf, iris[tst,]); (5) Decode with decode_knn(rf, emap, emb, k=5)$x_hat; (6) Compute reconstruction_error() between decoded and actual test samples. Verify decoded values approximate original inputs reasonably well, demonstrating that the RF autoencoder can compress and reconstruct tabular data.

code_available.evidence: RFAE R package available at https://github.com/bips-hb/RFAE with source code in R/ directory implementing encode(), decode_knn(), and reconstruction_error() functions. README provides working example with iris dataset. Python version also mentioned at https://github.com/binhducvu/RFAE_py.

dataset_available.evidence: Paper uses MNIST (standard benchmark at http://yann.lecun.com/exdb/mnist/) and 20 UCI datasets. Iris dataset (used in package example) is built into R. All datasets are publicly available.

weights_available.evidence: No pretrained model checkpoints are released. RFAE is a post-processing pipeline that works on any trained random forest object (RF, URF, or ARFs from ranger package), so no model weights are needed.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: MNIST is a widely recognized public benchmark for image data. UCI datasets (abalone, adult, banknote, breast cancer, etc.) are standard public benchmarks. Iris is a standard R built-in dataset.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified: The MRE uses a small RF (50 trees) on a small dataset (150 iris samples). The paper reports RFAE runtime on plpn (333 samples, 8 features) averages 3.24 seconds total. Scaling to iris (150 samples, 4 features) would be even faster. The MRE requires only CPU compute, not GPU, so H100-hours are negligible. No GPU training is needed since RFAE is a post-processing step on a pre-trained RF.
abstract: We propose a principled method for autoencoding with random forests. Our strategy builds on foundational results from nonparametric statistics and spectral graph theory to learn a low-dimensional embedding of the model that optimally represents relationships in the data. We provide exact and approximate solutions to the decoding problem via constrained optimization, split relabeling, and nearest neighbors regression. These methods effectively invert the compression pipeline, establishing a map from the embedding space back to the input space using splits learned by the ensemble's constituent trees. The resulting decoders are universally consistent under common regularity assumptions. The procedure works with supervised or unsupervised models, providing a window into conditional or joint distributions. We demonstrate various applications of this autoencoder, including powerful new tools for visualization, compression, clustering, and denoising. Experiments illustrate the ease and utility of our method in a wide range of settings, including tabular, image, and genomic data.

title: Policy Optimized Text-to-Image Pipeline Design
central_claim: FlowRL, a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework with surrogate reward modeling, generates novel ComfyUI workflows that achieve 60% HPSv2 winrate vs ComfyGen baseline and 41% unique flow generation ratio vs ComfyGen's 7%
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'we implement a two-phase training strategy: initial workflow vocabulary training followed by GRPO-based optimization.' Table 1: FlowRL achieves 60% HPSv2 winrate vs ComfyGen and 0.61 GenEval overall score matching ComfyGen. Table 3: 41% unique ratio and 1% existence in training data vs ComfyGen's 7% unique ratio and 94% existence in training data.
mre_config: Llama 3.1-8B with LoRA (rank=16) fine-tuned on prompt-flow pairs for SFT stage, ModernBert reward model trained on prompt-flow-score triplets, GRPO fine-tuning (group_size=4, lr=5e-6, 2 epochs) with ensemble of 7 reward models and CFG inference (gamma=1.5); evaluated on GenEval benchmark and CivitAI prompt test set measuring HPSv2 winrate vs ComfyGen.
agent_task: Clone GenEval repository (https://github.com/dbolya/ComfyGen_eval) for benchmark evaluation. Reconstruct FlowRL training from scratch: (1) download Llama 3.1-8B base model and implement LoRA fine-tuning with custom token encoding for ComfyUI workflows using the paper's prompt format ('>>> Prompt: {p_i} >>> Flow: {f_i}'); (2) train ModernBert reward model on prompt-flow-score triplets in format '[PROMPT] {p_i} [FLOW] {f_i}'; (3) implement GRPO fine-tuning (group_size=4, lr=5e-6, clip=0.2, KL_coef=0.2, 2 epochs) with ensemble of 7 reward models and uncertainty-aware filtering; (4) implement dual-model CFG inference (gamma=1.5); (5) generate flows, convert to ComfyUI JSON, run through ComfyUI API, and evaluate with HPSv2 and GenEval. Note: Custom training dataset must be reconstructed from public sources or obtained separately; engineering effort for encoding scheme, tokenization, flow JSON parsing is substantial.

code_available.evidence: Searched GitHub and HuggingFace for FlowRL, FlowRL, ComfyGen-RL, policy optimized workflow, arXiv 2505.21478, author names (Uri Gadot, Rinon Gal), ComfyGen, and workflow generation variants. No FlowRL code repository found. OpenReview supplement contains only FlowRL_appendix.pdf (paper PDF), no code/scripts/configs. ComfyUI (github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI) is the execution engine but not the paper's training/inference code.

dataset_available.evidence: FlowRL training requires ComfyGen's custom dataset (33 human-created flows with 2000 augmented variants, 10000 CivitAI prompts, human preference scores for ~330 flows). This custom dataset was not publicly released. The 500 CivitAI test prompts are also not released. GenEval benchmark (standard for T2I evaluation) is available at the ComfyGen_eval repository but is used for evaluation, not as the custom training data.

weights_available.evidence: No FlowRL checkpoints, LoRA adapters, or reward model weights found on HuggingFace or GitHub after searching FlowRL weights, FlowRL model, ComfyGen-RL checkpoints, and other variants.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: GenEval benchmark (github.com/dbolya/ComfyGen_eval) is a standard public benchmark for evaluating text-to-image prompt adherence, used in the paper for evaluation. However, the paper's custom ComfyGen flow dataset with human preference scores used for training is non-standard and unavailable.

h100_estimate_basis: Compute budget based on paper's reported training: SFT stage on 1 H100 for 10 hours (10 H100-hours). Reward model on 1 A100-80GB for 4 hours (1.28 H100-hours equivalent, using A100->H100 factor 0.32). GRPO fine-tuning on 8 H100 GPUs for 10 hours (80 H100-hours). MRE minimal config totals approximately 80 H100-hours. Engineering/debugging time for reconstructing the custom flow encoding, tokenization, JSON parsing, and ComfyUI API integration is additional and substantial. Custom ComfyGen flow dataset (unreleased) must be reconstructed or obtained separately.
abstract: Text-to-image generation has evolved beyond single monolithic models to complex multi-component pipelines. These combine fine-tuned generators, adapters, upscaling blocks and even editing steps, leading to significant improvements in image quality. However, their effective design requires substantial expertise. Recent approaches have shown promise in automating this process through large language models (LLMs), but they suffer from two critical limitations: extensive computational requirements from generating images with hundreds of predefined pipelines, and poor generalization beyond memorized training examples. We introduce a novel reinforcement learning-based framework that addresses these inefficiencies. Our approach first trains an ensemble of reward models capable of predicting image quality scores directly from prompt-workflow combinations, eliminating the need for costly image generation during training. We then implement a two-phase training strategy: initial workflow vocabulary training followed by GRPO-based optimization that guides the model toward higher-performing regions of the workflow space. Additionally, we incorporate a classifier-free guidance based enhancement technique that extrapolates along the path between the initial and GRPO-tuned models, further improving output quality. We validate our approach through a set of comparisons, showing that it can successfully create new flows with greater diversity and lead to superior image quality compared to existing baselines.

title: RepoMaster: Autonomous Exploration and Understanding of GitHub Repositories for Complex Task Solving
central_claim: RepoMaster achieves significantly higher task completion rates (75.92% vs 40.74% task pass rate with Claude 3.5) than OpenHands and SWE-Agent on GitTaskBench while reducing token usage by ~95% through hierarchical code analysis, core component identification, and context-aware exploration.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'Evaluated on the adjusted MLE-bench, RepoMaster achieves a 110% relative boost in valid submissions over the strongest baseline OpenHands. On our newly released GitTaskBench, RepoMaster lifts the task-pass rate from 40.7% to 62.9% while reducing token usage by 95%.' Table 2: RepoMaster with Claude 3.5 achieves 75.92% execution completion and 62.96% task pass rate vs OpenHands (53.70%, 40.74%) with 95% fewer tokens (154k vs 2883k).
mre_config: Single GitTaskBench task evaluation using RepoMaster with one LLM (e.g., GPT-4o): 1) Set up GitTaskBench via pip install; 2) Clone RepoMaster repository; 3) Configure API keys; 4) Run single task via RepoMaster: `python launcher.py --mode backend --backend-mode repository_agent` with a task prompt; 5) Run evaluation via `gittaskbench grade --taskid <taskid>` to verify task pass.
agent_task: Reproduce a single GitTaskBench task using RepoMaster: 1) Install GitTaskBench: `pip install -e .` from https://github.com/QuantaAlpha/GitTaskBench; 2) Install RepoMaster: `pip install -r requirements.txt` from https://github.com/QuantaAlpha/RepoMaster; 3) Configure API keys (OPENAI_API_KEY, SERPER_API_KEY, JINA_API_KEY) in configs/.env; 4) Clone a task repository from GitTaskBench/code_base/ to a working directory; 5) Create task prompt following examples in GitTaskBench/queries/<taskid>/query.json; 6) Run RepoMaster: `python launcher.py --mode backend --backend-mode repository_agent` with the task prompt; 7) Save output to the specified output directory; 8) Evaluate: `gittaskbench grade --taskid <taskid> --output_dir <output_path>`; 9) Verify task pass criteria are met.

code_available.evidence: RepoMaster source code verified at https://github.com/QuantaAlpha/RepoMaster with launcher.py (entry point), run.sh (launch script), src/core/, src/services/, src/utils/ modules, and configuration files. The repository contains full implementation of the agent framework including hierarchical code tree analysis, function call graph, module dependency graph, and exploration tools.

dataset_available.evidence: GitTaskBench dataset verified at https://github.com/QuantaAlpha/GitTaskBench with complete benchmark: 54 tasks across 7 domains in queries/, 18 repositories in code_base/, evaluation configs in config/, ground truth in groundtruth/, test scripts in test_scripts/, and Python evaluation package with CLI tool (`gittaskbench grade --taskid`).

weights_available.evidence: RepoMaster is an agent framework that calls LLM APIs (OpenAI, Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini). No model weights or checkpoints are required. The framework orchestrates exploration and code execution using external LLM services.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: GitTaskBench is a custom benchmark released with the paper (18 repos, 54 tasks). While the benchmark is publicly released and reproducible, it is not a widely recognized public ML benchmark like CIFAR-10, ImageNet, or MLE-Bench. MLE-R uses MLE-Bench-Lite which is based on Kaggle competitions.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified. RepoMaster is an agent framework (not a training pipeline) that calls LLM APIs. No GPU training is required for reproduction. The main cost is API calls (token usage ~154k-250k per task with Claude 3.5/GPT-4o per paper Table 2). Estimate assumes ~2 H100-hours as a conservative upper bound accounting for overhead in running the agent framework and evaluation pipeline.
abstract: The ultimate goal of code agents is to solve complex tasks autonomously. Although large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in code generation, real-world tasks typically demand full-fledged code repositories rather than simple scripts. Building such repositories from scratch remains a major challenge. Fortunately, GitHub hosts a vast, evolving collection of open-source repositories, which developers frequently reuse as modular components for complex tasks. Yet, existing frameworks like OpenHands and SWE-Agent still struggle to effectively leverage these valuable resources. Relying solely on README files provides insufficient guidance, and deeper exploration reveals two core obstacles: overwhelming information and tangled dependencies of repositories, both constrained by the limited context windows of current LLMs. To tackle these issues, we propose RepoMaster, an autonomous agent framework designed to explore and reuse GitHub repositories for solving complex tasks. For efficient understanding, RepoMaster constructs function-call graphs, module-dependency graphs, and hierarchical code trees to identify essential components, providing only identified core elements to the LLMs rather than the entire repository. During autonomous execution, it progressively explores related components using our exploration tools and prunes information to optimize context usage. Evaluated on the adjusted MLE-bench, RepoMaster achieves a 110% relative boost in valid submissions over the strongest baseline OpenHands. On our newly released GitTaskBench, RepoMaster lifts the …

title: ALTER: All-in-One Layer Pruning and Temporal Expert Routing for Efficient Diffusion Generation
central_claim: ALTER achieves same-level visual fidelity to the original 50-step Stable Diffusion v2.1 model while utilizing only 25.9% of its total MACs with just 20 inference steps and delivering a 3.64x speedup through 35% sparsity.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'ALTER achieves same-level visual fidelity to the original 50-step Stable Diffusion v2.1 model while utilizing only 25.9% of its total MACs with just 20 inference steps and delivering a 3.64x speedup through 35% sparsity.' Table 2 (tab:sdv2.1-cache-comparison): ALTER (0.65) with 20 steps achieves 3.64x speedup over 50-step SDv2.1 baseline, with FID-5K of 25.25 vs 27.29 for SDv2.1.
mre_config: Train ALTER (0.65) hypernetwork + UNet on a 0.3M subset of LAION-Aesthetics V2 (6.5+) at 512x512 for 32k steps (hypernetwork trained 2 epochs, batch size 64 on 2 A100 GPUs), then evaluate FID and CLIP score on MS-COCO 2014 validation (30k samples) at 768 resolution resized to 256 using PNDM sampler with 20 steps. Target: FID ~13.89, CLIP ~32.18.
agent_task: Reproduce the ALTER (0.65) experiment on SDv2.1: (1) Implement the ALTER framework with hypernetwork-based layer pruning masks and temporal expert routing from the paper description (Expert Generator using MLP + LayerNorm + ReLU with Gumbel-Sigmoid, Temporal Router using MLP + LayerNorm + ReLU with Gumbel-Softmax); (2) Fine-tune ALTER on a 0.3M subset of LAION-Aesthetics V2 at 512x512 for 32k steps with batch size 64 (2 A100 GPUs), using AdamW optimizer (UNet LR=1e-5, hypernetwork LR=7e-5), alternating optimization with hypernetwork trained for 2 epochs; (3) Apply knowledge distillation losses from frozen teacher SDv2.1 (output-level and feature-level); (4) Use sparsity ratio p=0.65, 10 temporal experts, Gumbel temperature 0.4, loss weights lambda_denoise=1e-4, lambda_outKD=lambda_featKD=lambda_balance=1.0, lambda_ratio=5.0; (5) Evaluate FID and CLIP on 30k MS-COCO 2014 val samples at 768→256 resolution with PNDM sampler at 20 steps. Target: FID ~13.89, CLIP ~32.18, MACs ~899.7G, Latency ~2.1s.

code_available.evidence: No GitHub repository found after exhaustive search across multiple query families: full title, acronym 'ALTER', arXiv ID '2505.21817', method keywords ('temporal expert routing', 'layer pruning diffusion'), author names (Xiaomeng Yang, Yanzhi Wang, Northeastern University), code search for 'ALTER diffusion SDv21 layer pruning temporal expert', and organization-based queries. HuggingFace search for ALTER diffusion code/repos/spaces also returned no matching results. The arXiv abstract page contains no code or project links. Paper submitted May 27, 2025 with no mention of external code release.

dataset_available.evidence: The MRE evaluation datasets MS-COCO 2014 (30k val) and CC3M (14k val) are standard public benchmarks for text-to-image generation. The paper uses these for evaluation alongside the training set (LAION-Aesthetics V2 subset) which is also publicly accessible.

weights_available.evidence: No ALTER-trained checkpoints are released. While the paper uses pretrained SDv2.1 as the starting point (available as 'stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-1' on HuggingFace), no ALTER-specific model weights, hypernetwork checkpoints, or pruned model artifacts were found on any platform after exhaustive search.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: MS-COCO 2014 validation split and Conceptual Captions 3M (CC3M) are widely recognized standard benchmarks for text-to-image generation evaluation, used extensively in diffusion model literature (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E, etc.).

h100_estimate_basis: Paper reports training on 2 A100 GPUs, global batch size 64, 32k steps with alternating bi-level optimization. Estimated wall-clock: ~8 A100-hours (2 A100 × ~4.5 hours based on SDv2.1 fine-tuning efficiency). Converting to H100: 8 × 0.32 (A100→H100 BF16 factor) ≈ 2.6 H100-hours, rounded to 4 H100-hours to account for the additional bi-level optimization overhead and engineering effort. Evaluation on 30k MS-COCO samples adds ~0.5 H100-hours. Engineering/debugging time beyond compute not included.
abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in generating high-fidelity images. However, their iterative denoising process results in significant computational overhead during inference, limiting their practical deployment in resource-constrained environments. Existing acceleration methods often adopt uniform strategies that fail to capture the temporal variations during diffusion generation, while the commonly adopted sequential pruning-then-fine-tuning strategy suffers from sub-optimality due to the misalignment between pruning decisions made on pretrained weights and the model's final parameters. To address these limitations, we introduce ALTER: All-in-One Layer Pruning and Temporal Expert Routing, a unified framework that transforms diffusion models into a mixture of efficient temporal experts. ALTER achieves a single-stage optimization that unifies layer pruning, expert routing, and model fine-tuning by employing a trainable hypernetwork, which dynamically generates layer pruning decisions and manages timestep routing to specialized, pruned expert sub-networks throughout the ongoing fine-tuning of the UNet. This unified co-optimization strategy enables significant efficiency gains while preserving high generative quality. Specifically, ALTER achieves same-level visual fidelity to the original 50-step Stable Diffusion v2.1 model while utilizing only 25.9% of its total MACs with just 20 inference steps and delivering a 3.64x speedup through 35% sparsity.

title: Align-DA: Align Score-based Atmospheric Data Assimilation with Multiple Preferences
central_claim: Align-DA uses reinforcement learning-based preference alignment (DPO) with multiple reward signals to consistently improve atmospheric data assimilation accuracy over non-aligned baselines across different observation guidance methods.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'Experiments with multiple reward signals demonstrate consistent improvements in analysis quality across different evaluation metrics and observation-guidance strategies.' Table 1 shows Align-ObsFree-M reduces MSE by 5.44% and z500 WRMSE by 7.94% over baseline; Table 3 shows Align-DPS-M reduces MSE by 2.65%.
mre_config: Single-variable (z500 WRMSE) assimilation accuracy comparison at 1% observation density between Align-DPS-M and DPS baseline. Requires: VAEformer training (80 epochs, batch 32, vit_large config), score-based diffusion training in latent space (100K iterations, batch 32, lr 1e-4), DPO fine-tuning (β=8000, batch 32, lr 1e-5, 500 steps on 4000 preference pairs), and evaluation with WRMSE metric at 1% observation density.
agent_task: Reproduce z500 WRMSE assimilation accuracy comparison at 1% observation density: (1) Register for ECMWF CDS access and download ERA5 hourly data (1979-2018) for 69 variables at 1.40625° resolution, (2) Preprocess to match paper format (128x256 grid, 13 pressure levels + 4 surface variables), (3) Train VAEformer following CRA5 paper (vit_large, 24 transformer blocks, 1024 dim, patch 4x4, lr 2e-4 with warmup, batch 32, 80 epochs), (4) Train score-based diffusion model in latent space (100K iterations, batch 32, lr 1e-4, variance-preserving SDE with cosine schedule), (5) Generate preference dataset (4000 pairs) by sampling N=32 instances and ranking by three rewards (assimilation accuracy WRMSE, 48h forecast RMSE, geostrophic balance score), (6) DPO fine-tune (β=8000, batch 32, lr 1e-5, 500 steps), (7) Evaluate DPS guidance and Align-DPS-M at 1% observation density, report z500 WRMSE improvements.

code_available.evidence: OpenReview supplement contains code files (train.py, dpo_tune.py, models/diffDA.py, store.py, datasets/era5_npy_f32.py) but all are marked binary (is_text: false) and cannot be read. No external GitHub or HuggingFace repository found after searches for 'Align-DA', 'AlignDA', 'diffDA', '2505.22008', 'CRA5', 'VAEformer', 'Fengwu', 'fengwu-ai', and 'score-based data assimilation' keywords.

dataset_available.evidence: Training config references S3 bucket 's3://era5_np_float32' for preprocessed numpy arrays (69 variables, 128x256 grid, 1979-2018), not publicly accessible. Paper requires custom preprocessing pipeline to create dataset from ECMWF ERA5. mean_std.json files show statistics but are not the actual data.

weights_available.evidence: No pre-trained model checkpoints, VAEformer weights, score-based diffusion model weights, or DPO-aligned model weights released in supplement or externally. Full pipeline requires trained checkpoints for VAEformer, diffusion model, and DPO-aligned model.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: ERA5 reanalysis from ECMWF is a standard public benchmark dataset widely used in atmospheric science. While the specific preprocessed format (69 variables, 128x256 grid, specific pressure levels) requires custom preprocessing pipeline, the underlying source data is publicly available via ECMWF CDS with registration.

h100_estimate_basis: Paper reports VAE training (80 epochs, batch 32, ~24h on 4 A100) and diffusion training (2 days on 4 A100). Total reported compute: 4 days on 4 A100. Using A100→H100 conversion (0.32x): ~61 H100-hours for core training. MRE pipeline requires additional DPO fine-tuning (~2h), Fengwu forecasting model for evaluation (8 AR steps), and custom data preprocessing. Full pipeline estimate: 192 H100-hours. Engineering time for dependency setup, data pipeline, and debugging not included.
abstract: Data assimilation (DA) aims to estimate the full state of a dynamical system by combining partial and noisy observations with a prior model forecast, commonly referred to as the background. In atmospheric applications, this problem is fundamentally ill-posed due to the sparsity of observations relative to the high-dimensional state space. Traditional methods address this challenge by simplifying background priors to regularize the solution, which are empirical and require continual tuning for application. Inspired by alignment techniques in text-to-image diffusion models, we propose Align-DA, which formulates DA as a generative process and uses reward signals to guide background priors, replacing manual tuning with data-driven alignment. Specifically, we train a score-based model in the latent space to approximate the background-conditioned prior, and align it using three complementary reward signals for DA: (1) assimilation accuracy, (2) forecast skill initialized from the assimilated state, and (3) physical adherence of the analysis fields. Experiments with multiple reward signals demonstrate consistent improvements in analysis quality across different evaluation metrics and observation-guidance strategies. These results show that preference alignment, implemented as a soft constraint, can automatically adapt complex background priors tailored to DA, offering a promising new direction for advancing the field.

title: Differentiable Generalized Sliced Wasserstein Plans
central_claim: DGSWP enables differentiable optimization of non-linear (neural network) slice projectors for sliced Wasserstein plans via Stein's lemma, achieving significantly better OT plan approximation than linear methods (min-SWGG) in 2D and being the only slicing-based method that works in high-dimensional settings.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'we reformulate min-SWGG as a bilevel optimization problem and propose a differentiable approximation scheme to efficiently identify the optimal slice, even in high-dimensional settings.' Figure 1 (xp/fig_illus.py): 8Gaussians→TwoMoons OT plan comparison showing DGSWP (NN) transport cost 13.80 vs min-SWGG 22.22 vs exact OT 13.50. Figure 4: gradient flow experiments showing DGSWP converges in high dimensions where other slicing methods fail. Table 1: CIFAR-10 FID scores where DGSWP-CFM (NN) achieves best Euler FID 3.62.
