abstract: Optimal Transport (OT) has attracted significant interest in the machine learning community, not only for its ability to define meaningful distances between probability distributions -- such as the Wasserstein distance -- but also for its formulation of OT plans. Its computational complexity remains a bottleneck, though, and slicing techniques have been developed to scale OT to large datasets. Recently, a novel slicing scheme, dubbed min-SWGG, lifts a single one-dimensional plan back to the original multidimensional space, finally selecting the slice that yields the lowest Wasserstein distance as an approximation of the full OT plan. Despite its computational and theoretical advantages, min-SWGG inherits typical limitations of slicing methods: (i) the number of required slices grows exponentially with the data dimension, and (ii) it is constrained to linear projections. Here, we reformulate min-SWGG as a bilevel optimization problem and propose a differentiable approximation scheme to efficiently identify the optimal slice, even in high-dimensional settings. We furthermore define its generalized extension for accommodating to data living on manifolds. Finally, we demonstrate the practical value of our approach in various applications, including gradient flows on manifolds and high-dimensional spaces, as well as a novel sliced OT-based conditional flow matching for image generation -- where fast computation of transport plans is essential.

abstract: Mathematical optimization is a fundamental tool for decision-making in a wide range of applications. However, in many real-world scenarios, the parameters of the optimization problem are not known a priori and must be predicted from contextual features. This gives rise to predict-then-optimize problems, where a machine learning model predicts problem parameters that are then used to make decisions via optimization. A growing body of work on decision-focused learning (DFL) addresses this setting by training models specifically to produce predictions that maximize downstream decision quality, rather than accuracy. While effective, DFL is computationally expensive, because it requires solving the optimization problem with the predicted parameters at each loss evaluation. In this work, we address this computational bottleneck for linear optimization problems, a common class of problems in both DFL literature and real-world applications. We propose a solver-free training method that exploits the geometric structure of linear optimization to enable efficient training with minimal degradation in solution quality. Our method is based on the insight that a solution is optimal if and only if it achieves an objective value that is at least as good as that of its adjacent vertices on the feasible polytope. Building on this, our method compares the estimated quality of the ground-truth optimal solution with that of its precomputed adjacent vertices, and uses this as loss function. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly reduces computational cost while maintaining high …

title: ProSpero: Active Learning for Robust Protein Design Beyond Wild-Type Neighborhoods

abstract: Designing protein sequences of both high fitness and novelty is a challenging task in data-efficient protein engineering. Exploration beyond wild-type neighborhoods often leads to biologically implausible sequences or relies on surrogate models that lose fidelity in novel regions. Here, we propose ProSpero, an active learning framework in which a frozen pre-trained generative model is guided by a surrogate updated from oracle feedback. By integrating fitness-relevant residue selection with biologically-constrained Sequential Monte Carlo sampling, our approach enables exploration beyond wild-type neighborhoods while preserving biological plausibility. We show that our framework remains effective even when the surrogate is misspecified. ProSpero consistently outperforms or matches existing methods across diverse protein engineering tasks, retrieving sequences of both high fitness and novelty.

abstract: Audio-driven human animation methods, such as talking head and talking body generation, have made remarkable progress in generating synchronized facial movements and appealing visual quality videos. However, existing methods primarily focus on single human animation and struggle with multi-stream audio inputs, facing incorrect binding problems between audio and persons. Additionally, they exhibit limitations in instruction-following capabilities. To solve this problem, in this paper, we propose a novel task: Multi-Person Conversational Video Generation, and introduce a new framework, MultiTalk, to address the challenges during multi-person generation. Specifically, for audio injection, we investigate several schemes and propose the Label Rotary Position Embedding (L-RoPE) method to resolve the audio and person binding problem. Furthermore, during training, we observe that partial parameter training and multi-task training are crucial for preserving the instruction-following ability of the base model. MultiTalk achieves superior performance compared to other methods on several datasets, including talking head, talking body, and multi-person datasets, demonstrating the powerful generation capabilities of our approach.

title: Non-convex entropic mean-field optimization via Best Response flow

abstract: We study the problem of minimizing non-convex functionals on the space of probability measures, regularized by the relative entropy (KL divergence) with respect to a fixed reference measure, as well as the corresponding problem of solving entropy-regularized non-convex-non-concave min-max problems. We utilize the Best Response flow (also known in the literature as the fictitious play flow) and study how its convergence is influenced by the relation between the degree of non-convexity of the functional under consideration, the regularization parameter and the tail behaviour of the reference measure. In particular, we demonstrate how to choose the regularizer, given the non-convex functional, so that the Best Response operator becomes a contraction with respect to the $L^1$-Wasserstein distance, which ensures the existence of its unique fixed point that is then shown to be the unique global minimizer for our optimization problem. This extends recent results where the Best Response flow was applied to solve convex optimization problems regularized by the relative entropy with respect to arbitrary reference measures, and with arbitrary values of the regularization parameter. Our results explain precisely how the assumption of convexity can be relaxed, at the expense of making a specific choice of the regularizer. Additionally, we demonstrate how these results can be applied in reinforcement learning in the context of policy optimization for Markov Decision Processes and Markov games with softmax parametrized policies in the mean-field regime.

abstract: Explicit noise-level conditioning is widely regarded as essential for the effective operation of Graph Diffusion Models (GDMs). In this work, we challenge this assumption by investigating whether denoisers can implicitly infer noise levels directly from corrupted graph structures, potentially eliminating the need for explicit noise conditioning. To this end, we develop a theoretical framework centered on Bernoulli edge-flip corruptions and extend it to encompass more complex scenarios involving coupled structure-attribute noise. Extensive empirical evaluations on both synthetic and real-world graph datasets, using models such as GDSS and DiGress, provide strong support for our theoretical findings. Notably, unconditional GDMs achieve performance comparable or superior to their conditioned counterparts, while also offering reductions in parameters (4-6%) and computation time (8-10%). Our results suggest that the high-dimensional nature of graph data itself often encodes sufficient information for the denoising process, opening avenues for simpler, more efficient GDM architectures.

abstract: Diffusion LLMs have emerged as a promising alternative to conventional autoregressive LLMs, offering significant potential for improved runtime efficiency. However, existing diffusion models lack the ability to provably enforce user-specified formal constraints, such as regular expressions, which makes them unreliable for tasks that require structured outputs, such as fixed-schema JSON generation. Unlike autoregressive models that generate tokens sequentially, diffusion LLMs predict a block of tokens in parallel. This parallelism makes traditional constrained decoding algorithms, which are designed for sequential token prediction, ineffective at preserving the true output distribution. To address this limitation, we propose DINGO, a dynamic programming-based constrained decoding strategy that is both efficient and provably distribution-preserving. DINGO enables sampling of output strings with the highest probability under the model's predicted distribution, while strictly satisfying any user-specified regular expression. On standard symbolic math and JSON generation benchmarks, DINGO achieves up to a 68 percentage point improvement over unconstrained inference

title: Less is More: Unlocking Specialization of Time Series Foundation Models via Structured Pruning
central_claim: Structured pruning of pre-trained Time Series Foundation Models before fine-tuning (prune-then-finetune) improves forecasting performance by preserving task-relevant network substructures, achieving up to 22% error reduction compared to direct fine-tuning.

abstract: Scaling laws motivate the development of Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) that pre-train vast parameters and achieve remarkable zero-shot forecasting performance. Surprisingly, even after fine-tuning, TSFMs cannot consistently outperform smaller, specialized models trained on full-shot downstream data. A key question is how to realize effective adaptation of TSFMs for a target forecasting task. Through empirical studies on various TSFMs, the pre-trained models often exhibit inherent sparsity and redundancy in computation, suggesting that TSFMs have learned to activate task-relevant network substructures to accommodate diverse forecasting tasks. To preserve this valuable prior knowledge, we propose a structured pruning method to regularize the subsequent fine-tuning process by focusing it on a more relevant and compact parameter space. Extensive experiments on seven TSFMs and six benchmarks demonstrate that fine-tuning a smaller, pruned TSFM significantly improves forecasting performance compared to fine-tuning original models. This prune-then-finetune paradigm often enables TSFMs to achieve state-of-the-art performance and surpass strong specialized baselines. Source code is made publicly available at https://github.com/SJTU-DMTai/Prune-then-Finetune.

title: Strategic Classification with Non-Linear Classifiers
central_claim: Universal approximator model classes (e.g., neural nets) are no longer universal in strategic classification settings, and this limitation creates measurable performance gaps even for unrestricted model classes.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'A key finding is that universal approximators (e.g., neural nets) are no longer universal once the environment is strategic. We demonstrate empirically how this can create performance gaps even on an unrestricted model class.' Experiments section (Sec 5.2 / sec_exp_approximation) and Fig 3 (right): The approximation experiment shows that as data becomes more entangled (low separation μ), strategic approximation accuracy diverges from the ideal baseline, with larger gaps for larger α.
mre_config: Approximation Experiment (single-instance minimum config): n=50 points (25 per class) from class-conditional Gaussians via sklearn.datasets.make_blobs with centers at [[0,0],[μ,0]]; strategic budget α ∈ {0.5, 1.0, 2.0}; class separation μ varies. Compute maximum linear accuracy (enumerate all n-choose-2 line classifiers) and maximum strategic accuracy (enumerate all subsets of negative points, find best intersection of α-balls). Metric: classification accuracy. This is the cheapest config that demonstrates the central claim about accuracy gaps.
agent_task: Clone https://github.com/benyamintrachtenberg/scnonlin and run `python3 approximation_experiment.py` with a single-instance reduced config (n=50, α∈{0.5,1.0,2.0}, class_separation from 0 to 5 in steps of 0.1, times=20). Alternatively, reproduce a single MRE instance by instantiating class best_acc with n=50, class_separation=1.0, budget=1.0, random_state=0, then calling best_acc.best_linear_acc() and best_acc.best_strat_acc(grid_step=0.01). Compare the linear accuracy against the strategic accuracy: the strategic accuracy should be lower than the linear accuracy for small class separations (μ near 0), demonstrating the performance gap caused by strategic behavior.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo benyamintrachtenberg/scnonlin verified public and contains approximation_experiment.py (7694 bytes), expressivity_experiment.py (31904 bytes), run_expressivity_experiment.sh (600 bytes), and instructions.txt (1125 bytes). The approximation_experiment.py implements the full MRE: synthetic data generation via sklearn.datasets.make_blobs, maximum linear accuracy computation (enumerate all point-pair classifiers), and maximum strategic accuracy computation (subset enumeration with α-ball intersection). Both the GitHub repo and the bundled OpenReview supplement (scnonlin-main/) contain identical files.

dataset_available.evidence: The MRE uses fully synthetic data generated programmatically inside approximation_experiment.py using sklearn.datasets.make_blobs with class-conditional Gaussians: n_samples=50, centers=[[0,0],[class_separation,0]], n_features=2. No external dataset download is required; the data is constructed in-memory each run. The paper explicitly generates synthetic data in both experiments rather than using external benchmarks.

weights_available.evidence: No pretrained weights or model checkpoints are used or released. This is a synthetic-data experiment that generates and classifies data in-memory. No weights are needed or expected for the MRE.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: The MRE uses author-generated synthetic data from sklearn.datasets.make_blobs (class-conditional Gaussians). No standard public ML benchmark dataset (MNIST, CIFAR, ImageNet, etc.) is used. The data is constructed parametrically from Gaussian distributions with controllable class separation parameters.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified. The paper reports experiments divided across 100 CPUs with 20 instances per setup, but no GPU-hours or GPU-types are reported. For the MRE (single-instance approximation experiment), computation is CPU-only: maximum linear accuracy involves O(n^3)=~125k operations for n=50, and maximum strategic accuracy involves exhaustive subset enumeration of 25 negative points (~33M subsets worst-case, with early stopping). On a modern multi-core CPU this runs in minutes. Scaling to the full paper config (20 instances × 51 class-separation values × 3 budgets = 3060 runs) on 100 workers would take O(1 hour) wall-clock on 100 CPUs, or O(0.1 H100-hours) in equivalent compute. The MRE single-instance run is negligible (<0.01 H100-hours), making the H100 estimate of 1 conservative to account for engineering/debugging overhead.
abstract: In strategic classification, the standard supervised learning setting is extended to support the notion of strategic user behavior in the form of costly feature manipulations made in response to a classifier. While standard learning supports a broad range of model classes, the study of strategic classification has, so far, been dedicated mostly to linear classifiers. This work aims to expand the horizon by exploring how strategic behavior manifests under non-linear classifiers and what this implies for learning. We take a bottom-up approach showing how non-linearity affects decision boundary points, classifier expressivity, and model class complexity. Our results show how, unlike the linear case, strategic behavior may either increase or decrease effective class complexity, and that the complexity decrease may be arbitrarily large. Another key finding is that universal approximators (e.g., neural nets) are no longer universal once the environment is strategic. We demonstrate empirically how this can create performance gaps even on an unrestricted model class.

title: Diagnosing and Addressing Pitfalls in KG-RAG Datasets: Toward More Reliable Benchmarking
central_claim: The KGQAGen framework generates high-quality (96.3% factual accuracy), verifiable, multi-hop KGQA questions through LLM-guided subgraph expansion and SPARQL validation, and even state-of-the-art KG-RAG models achieve only moderate performance on the resulting KGQAGen-10k benchmark.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'we introduce KGQAGen, an LLM-in-the-loop framework that systematically resolves these pitfalls. KGQAGen combines structured knowledge grounding, LLM-guided generation, and symbolic verification to produce challenging and verifiable QA instances.' Table 1 (tab:benchmark) shows GPT-4.1 achieves only 56.96% LASM accuracy and GCR (GPT-4o) achieves 58.96% on KGQAGen-10k. Section 5 reports 96.3% manual audit correctness (289/300).
mre_config: Run the KGQAGen generation pipeline on a small seed set (10–20 entities from Wikidata via wikivital5.py), execute the LLM-guided subgraph expansion (generator.py) to produce QA pairs with SPARQL, run SPARQL validation (evaluator.py) against Wikidata's public endpoint to filter for KG-grounded instances, and compute factual accuracy. Target: reproduce >=90% SPARQL verification rate and qualitatively confirm multi-hop question quality. Anchor metric: SPARQL-validation pass rate and manual correctness check on a sample of 20-50 generated QA instances.
agent_task: Reproduce the minimal reproduction example of the KGQAGen framework as follows: (1) Clone the repo: git clone https://github.com/liangliang6v6/KGQAGen && cd KGQAGen. (2) Create .env with OPENAI_API_KEY=<your_key>. (3) Install: pip install -r requirement.txt. (4) Generate seed entities: python src/main/wikivital5.py (creates data/raw/seed.csv with Wikidata QIDs). (5) Run generator on a small subset: edit generator.py to limit DEPTH=5 and process only the first 20 seeds, then run python src/main/generator.py (produces data/processed/gen_data.json with LLM-generated QA pairs and SPARQL). (6) Validate with SPARQL: python src/main/evaluator.py (executes SPARQL against https://query.wikidata.org, filters for KG-grounded instances, produces data/processed/data.jsonl). (7) Evaluate: manually check 20 random samples from data.jsonl against Wikidata to compute factual accuracy. (8) Verify multi-hop complexity: inspect the 'proof' field to confirm >=2-hop reasoning. Target: >=80% SPARQL pass rate, >=2-hop proof chains, and >=85% manual accuracy. This tests the paper's central claim that KGQAGen produces high-quality verifiable KGQA instances.

It was generated by the authors' KGQAGen framework from Wikidata and includes fields specific to their framework (proof triples, SPARQL queries). The benchmark is new and paper-specific.

If the agent instead evaluates baseline KG-RAG models (ToG/PoG) on KGQAGen-10k using API calls, compute is also API-bound. No model fine-tuning or GPU training is required for the MRE. Engineering/debugging time for setup, API key configuration, and result validation is additional and not included.
abstract: Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) systems rely on high-quality benchmarks to evaluate complex multi-hop reasoning. However, despite their widespread use, popular datasets such as WebQSP and CWQ suffer from critical quality issues, including inaccurate or incomplete ground-truth annotations, poorly constructed questions that are ambiguous, trivial, or unanswerable, and outdated or inconsistent knowledge. Through a manual audit of 16 popular KGQA datasets, including WebQSP and CWQ, we find that the average factual correctness rate is only 57 %. To address these issues, we introduce KGQAGen, an LLM-in-the-loop framework that systematically resolves these pitfalls. KGQAGen combines structured knowledge grounding, LLM-guided generation, and symbolic verification to produce challenging and verifiable QA instances. Using KGQAGen, we construct KGQAGen-10k, a ten-thousand scale benchmark grounded in Wikidata, and evaluate a diverse set of KG-RAG models. Experimental results demonstrate that even state-of-the-art systems struggle on this benchmark, highlighting its ability to expose limitations of existing models. Our findings advocate for more rigorous benchmark construction and position KGQAGen as a scalable framework for advancing KGQA evaluation.

title: Spatial-MLLM: Boosting MLLM Capabilities in Visual-based Spatial Intelligence

abstract: Recent advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly enhanced performance on 2D visual tasks. However, improving their spatial intelligence remains a challenge. Existing 3D MLLMs always rely on additional 3D or 2.5D data to incorporate spatial awareness, restricting their utility in scenarios with only 2D inputs, such as images or videos. In this paper, we present Spatial-MLLM, a novel framework for visual-based spatial reasoning from purely 2D observations. Unlike conventional video MLLMs which rely on CLIP-based visual encoders optimized for semantic understanding, our key insight is to unleash the strong structure prior from the feed-forward visual geometry foundation model. Specifically, we propose a dual-encoder architecture: a pretrained 2D visual encoder to extract semantic features, and a 3D spatial encoder-initialized from the backbone of the visual geometry model-to extract 3D structure features. A connector then integrates both features into unified visual tokens for enhanced spatial understanding. Furthermore, we propose a space-aware frame sampling strategy at inference time, which selects the spatially informative frames of a video sequence, ensuring that even under limited token length, the model focuses on frames critical for spatial reasoning. Beyond architecture improvements, we construct a training dataset from multiple sources and train the model on it using supervised fine-tuning and GRPO. Extensive experiments on various real-world datasets demonstrate that Spatial-MLLM achieves state-of-the-art performance in a wide …

title: LayerIF: Estimating Layer Quality for Large Language Models using Influence Functions
central_claim: LayerIF leverages Influence Functions to quantify layer quality in LLMs, demonstrating effectiveness through 1.61% improvement in expert allocation for LoRA-MoE architectures and 0.90% improvement in layer sparsity allocation for model pruning over the best baseline methods.

This uses the provided data/mistral-7b/IF-300-96-smoothed.npy and compares LayerIF-driven sparsity against uniform sparsity baseline.

abstract: Pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across a wide range of tasks, yet exhibit substantial variability in the various layers' training quality with respect to specific downstream applications, limiting their downstream performance. It is therefore critical to estimate layer-wise training quality in a manner that accounts for both model architecture and training data. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on model-centric heuristics (such as spectral statistics, outlier detection, or uniform allocation) while overlooking the influence of data. To address these limitations, we propose LayerIF, a data-driven framework that leverages Influence Functions to quantify the training quality of individual layers in a principled and task-sensitive manner. By isolating each layer's gradients and measuring the sensitivity of the validation loss to training examples by computing layer-wise influences, we derive data-driven estimates of layer importance. Notably, our method produces task-specific layer importance estimates for the same LLM, revealing how layers specialize for different test-time evaluation tasks. We demonstrate the utility of our scores by leveraging them for two downstream applications: (a) expert allocation in LoRA-MoE architectures and (b) layer-wise sparsity distribution for LLM pruning. Experiments across multiple LLM architectures demonstrate that our model-agnostic, influence-guided allocation leads to consistent gains in task performance.

title: BioCLIP 2: Emergent Properties from Scaling Hierarchical Contrastive Learning
central_claim: BioCLIP 2 achieves 74.9% zero-shot accuracy on NABirds (18% improvement over BioCLIP) and demonstrates emergent properties including inter-species ecological alignment and intra-species variation preservation through large-scale hierarchical contrastive training on TreeOfLife-200M (214M images).
claim_evidence: Abstract states BioCLIP 2 'yields extraordinary accuracy when applied to various biological visual tasks' and 'we identify emergent properties in the learned embedding space.' The paper footer explicitly states 'Models, data, and code available at imageomics.github.io/bioclip-2.'

Download NABirds test images and metadata, extract image embeddings with BioCLIP 2's visual encoder, compute text embeddings for species class labels, perform cosine similarity classification, and report top-1 accuracy. weights_available.evidence: BioCLIP 2 model weights verified on HuggingFace at imageomics/bioclip-2. Model files: open_clip_model.safetensors (1.71GB) and open_clip_pytorch_model.bin (1.71GB). Model card confirms zero-shot-image-classification task with open_clip library. DOI: 10.57967/hf/5765.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: NABirds is a widely recognized public benchmark for fine-grained bird classification (48K images, 400 species). Meta-Album is a standardized benchmark collection. The paper explicitly substitutes NABirds for Birds525 because Birds525 'is no longer available,' confirming NABirds as the standard alternative. Other evaluation datasets (AwA2, FishNet, PlantDoc, NeWT, Herbarium19) are also established benchmarks.

h100_estimate_basis: This is an inference-only MRE requiring no training. Zero-shot classification on NABirds (~12K test images) requires: model loading (~5 min), image embedding extraction (~15 min on 1 GPU), text embedding computation (~1 min), and similarity matching (~1 min). Total ~20-30 minutes on 1 A100-80GB GPU. A100 80GB is 0.32x H100-equivalent, so ~0.1 H100-hours. Rounded up for I/O overhead and data loading: ~1 H100-hour. No training compute required since BioCLIP 2 weights are released.
abstract: Foundation models trained at scale exhibit remarkable emergent behaviors, learning new capabilities beyond their initial training objectives. We find such emergent behaviors in biological vision models via large-scale contrastive vision-language training. To achieve this, we first curate TreeOfLife-200M, comprising 214 million images of living organisms, the largest and most diverse biological organism image dataset to date. We then train BioCLIP 2 on TreeOfLife-200M to distinguish different species. Despite the narrow training objective, BioCLIP 2 yields extraordinary accuracy when applied to various biological visual tasks such as habitat classification and trait prediction. We identify emergent properties in the learned embedding space of BioCLIP 2. At the inter-species level, the embedding distribution of different species aligns closely with functional and ecological meanings (e.g., beak sizes and habitats). At the intra-species level, instead of being diminished, the intra-species variations (e.g., life stages and sexes) are preserved and better separated in subspaces orthogonal to inter-species distinctions. We provide formal proof and analyses to explain why hierarchical supervision and contrastive objectives encourage these emergent properties. Crucially, our results reveal that these properties become increasingly significant with larger-scale training data, leading to a biologically meaningful embedding space.

title: Critical Batch Size Revisited: A Simple Empirical Approach to Large-Batch Language Model Training
central_claim: The paper introduces a branched training method to directly measure Critical Batch Size (CBS) and shows CBS increases over training but plateaus around 4096. Based on this, they propose batch size warmup which trains OLMo 1B with 43% fewer gradient steps while achieving slightly better loss.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'we introduce a simple, empirical approach to directly measure the CBS... To validate this claim, we use batch size warmup to train OLMo 1B to slightly better loss than the original training run with 43% fewer gradient steps.' Figure 2 shows CBS measurements over checkpoints; Table 1 shows batch size warmup achieves PT Loss 2.5891 vs Small-Batch Control 2.6057 with 43% gradient steps saved.
mre_config: MRE: Use a single OLMo checkpoint (e.g., step 10K) and run branched training experiments at different batch size multipliers (k values: 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8) training for 2B tokens per branch. Identify B* as the largest batch size where loss recovers within epsilon=0.01 tolerance, following square-root learning rate scaling for Adam optimizer.
agent_task: Reproduce the CBS measurement via branched training: (1) Load an OLMo 1B or 7B checkpoint (from HuggingFace or train a small model with provided configs); (2) Implement branched training: create multiple training branches from the checkpoint with batch sizes multiplied by k ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8} and learning rates scaled by √k (Adam square-root scaling rule); (3) Train each branch for 2B tokens and compute smoothed loss (exponential moving average with α=0.5); (4) Identify B* as the largest k where L_k* ≤ L_k + ε for all k < k* (with ε=0.01 tolerance); (5) Compare the CBS curve (should increase then plateau around 4096 documents) against the paper's Figure 2. Note: No official CBS measurement code has been released - must implement from paper description in Section 3 and Appendix A.

code_available.evidence: The paper's NeurIPS checklist explicitly states: 'If accepted, we will release code with the camera-ready version.' No GitHub repository for the CBS branched training methodology was found after exhaustive searches using full title, arXiv ID (2505.23971), acronym variants (CBS), method terms (branched training, noise scale, critical batch size), and author names (Merrill, Arora). The general OLMo training framework exists at allenai/OLMo but lacks the specific CBS measurement code described in this paper.

dataset_available.evidence: Paper uses Dolma pretraining data (~3T tokens) available on HuggingFace as allenai/dolma (387.5K downloads, apache-2.0 license). C4 and The Pile are standard public benchmarks. OpenReview supplement references these datasets.

weights_available.evidence: Final OLMo 1B/7B model weights are available on HuggingFace (allenai/OLMo-2-0425-1B, allenai/OLMo-7B). However, the branched training MRE requires intermediate checkpoints at specific training steps (OLMo 1B: steps 0, 10K, 20K, ..., 450K; OLMo 7B: steps 0, 1K, 2K, 3K, 10K, ..., 477K) which are NOT publicly released. Appendix A documents these specific checkpoint paths stored internally on S3 (e.g., '/weka/oe-training-default/ai2-llm/checkpoints/OLMo-medium/peteish7/step928646').

dataset_is_standard.evidence: C4 and The Pile are standard, widely-recognized LM pretraining benchmarks used in prior work. Dolma is a published corpus (arxiv:2402.00159) with 3 trillion tokens for LM training.

h100_estimate_basis: MRE requires branched training experiments from a single checkpoint across ~8-10 batch size multipliers. Paper reports 1B runs on single H100 node (8 GPUs), each branched run trains 2B tokens. With ~1M tokens/sec throughput per node, each branch takes ~35 min. Full experiment (~10 branches + overhead) per checkpoint: ~6 hours. Reproducing the CBS trend across 5-10 checkpoints for validation: 30-60 hours. Additional engineering/debugging time to implement the unreleased branched training methodology from paper description adds significant overhead. Conservative total: ~100 H100-hours. Engineering time for methodology implementation is additional and not included.
abstract: The right batch size is important when training language models at scale: a large batch size is necessary for fast training, but a batch size that is too large will harm token efficiency. To navigate this tradeoff, McCandlish et al. (2018) suggest that a critical batch size (CBS), below which training will not substantially degrade loss, can be estimated based on the gradient noise scale during training. While their method has been adopted in practice, e.g., when training GPT-3, strong assumptions are required to justify gradient noise as a proxy for the CBS, which makes it unclear whether their approach should be trusted in practice, limiting its applicability. In this paper, we introduce a simple, empirical approach to directly measure the CBS and show how the CBS evolves over training. Applying our approach to the OLMo models, we find that CBS is near 0 at initialization, increases rapidly at first, and then plateaus as training progresses. Furthermore, we find that this trend holds across different model sizes (1B and 7B), suggesting CBS from small training runs can inform larger-scale training runs. Our findings about how the CBS changes over training motivate batch size warmup as a natural way to reliably train language models at large batch size: start the batch size small and increase it as the CBS grows. To validate this claim, we use batch size warmup to train OLMo 1B to slightly better loss than the original training run with 43% fewer gradient steps. This shows how our framework can be applied to reliably train language models at larger batch sizes, increasing …

title: DrVD-Bench: Do Vision-Language Models Reason Like Human Doctors in Medical Image Diagnosis?
central_claim: DrVD-Bench is the first multimodal benchmark for clinical visual reasoning, and VLMs perform well on low-level visual recognition tasks but accuracy drops sharply as reasoning complexity increases (from modality recognition at ~88% to lesion-level identification at ~41% for GPT-o3).
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'performance drops sharply as reasoning complexity increases.' Table 1 (tab:task_results) shows accuracy declining from Image Quality (76%) to Lesion Level (41%) for Gemini 2.5 Pro across CT modality tasks.
mre_config: Evaluate one VLM (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B via API or local inference) on Module 1 Visual Evidence Comprehension for a single modality (CT with ~1082 QA pairs) across 5 reasoning levels. Compare accuracy at Level 1 (Basic Information) vs Level 4 (Clinical Interpretation). Use compute_choice_metric.py to compute accuracy.
agent_task: Reproduce the key finding that VLM accuracy declines with reasoning complexity: (1) Install drvd-bench via `pip install drvd-bench`, (2) Download CT subset from https://huggingface.co/datasets/jerry1565/DrVD-Bench or Kaggle, (3) Run inference with any publicly available VLM (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL via API or local model) on visual_evidence_qa.jsonl for CT modality (~1082 QA pairs), (4) Save results to JSONL with model_response field, (5) Run `python compute_choice_metric.py --json_path results.jsonl --type single` to compute accuracy per level. Expected: accuracy should be higher at Level 1 (Basic Information ~70-85%) than Level 4 (Diagnosis ~40-55%) for most models.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo verified with complete evaluation code: compute_choice_metric.py (accuracy calculation), map_model_response.py (response mapping), qwen2.5vl_example.py (inference with Qwen API), report_generation_metric.py (BERTScore), requirements.txt, and Jupyter notebook demo. PyPI package 'drvd-bench' also available for direct installation.

dataset_available.evidence: Dataset verified on both Kaggle (public) and Hugging Face. Contains all 4 JSONL files: visual_evidence_qa.jsonl (4480 pairs), independent_qa.jsonl (2347 pairs), joint_qa.jsonl (487 pairs), report_generation.jsonl (475 pairs), plus images folder.

weights_available.evidence: No model weights released. This is a benchmark/evaluation paper, not a model training paper. Evaluation uses existing VLMs (GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-VL, etc.) accessed via API or local installation.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: DrVD-Bench is a custom benchmark created for this paper, not a standard public ML benchmark. It aggregates 24 publicly available medical imaging datasets but with new custom annotations, QA pairs, and reasoning-level labels.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified. Paper reports 8xA100 GPUs for full benchmark but not per-task compute. MRE is inference-only on ~1000 CT QA pairs with small VLM. Estimated: ~2 H100-hours (1000 images × ~7s/image ÷ 8 GPUs ÷ 3600s/hr ≈ 0.24 hrs × 8 H100 equiv ≈ 2 H100-hrs). No training required. Engineering/debugging time not included.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong zero-shot generalization on natural images and show early promise in interpretable medical image analysis. However, existing benchmarks do not systematically evaluate whether these models truly reason like human clinicians or merely imitate superficial patterns. To address this gap, we propose DrVD-Bench, the first multimodal benchmark for clinical visual reasoning. DrVD-Bench consists of three modules: Visual Evidence Comprehension, Reasoning Trajectory Assessment, and Report Generation Evaluation, comprising a total of 7,789 image-question pairs. Our benchmark covers 20 task types, 17 diagnostic categories, and five imaging modalities-CT, MRI, ultrasound, radiography, and pathology. DrVD-Bench is explicitly structured to reflect the clinical reasoning workflow from modality recognition to lesion identification and diagnosis. We benchmark 19 VLMs, including general-purpose and medical-specific, open-source and proprietary models, and observe that performance drops sharply as reasoning complexity increases. While some models begin to exhibit traces of human-like reasoning, they often still rely on shortcut correlations rather than grounded visual understanding. DrVD-Bench offers a rigorous and structured evaluation framework to guide the development of clinically trustworthy VLMs.

title: EgoExOR: An Ego-Exo-Centric Operating Room Dataset for Surgical Activity Understanding
central_claim: The EgoExOR model with dual-branch ego-exo architecture achieves 0.72 macro F1 on surgical scene graph generation, outperforming single-stream baselines ORacle (0.63) and MM2SG (0.67).
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'We evaluate the surgical scene graph generation performance of two adapted state-of-the-art models and offer a new baseline that explicitly leverages EgoExOR's multimodal and multi-perspective signals.' Table 1 shows EgoExOR model achieving Overall 0.72 macro F1 vs ORacle 0.63 and MM2SG 0.67.
mre_config: Evaluate pretrained EgoExOR checkpoint on test set: download model from HuggingFace (ardamamur/EgoExOR), run inference via scene_graph_prediction/main.py with egoexor.json config, compute macro F1 over predicates. Single GPU inference on 5K test samples with pretrained LLaVA-7B LoRA weights.
agent_task: Reproduce the main empirical result: (1) Clone GitHub repo ardamamur/EgoExOR, install dependencies per README (pip install -r requirements.txt, LLaVA, flash-attn, pytorch-scatter). (2) Download pretrained model checkpoint from HuggingFace ardamamur/EgoExOR (model .zip file) and unzip. (3) Download test samples JSON from same HuggingFace repo. (4) Download and merge HDF5 files into egoexor.h5 using data/utils/merge_h5.py per data/README.md. (5) Update paths in scene_graph_prediction/scene_graph_helpers/configs/egoexor.json (data_dir, hdf5_path). (6) Run: python -m scene_graph_prediction.main --config 'egoexor.json' --model_path 'path/to/model' --data_path 'path/to/test_samples' --benchmark_on 'egoexor' --mode 'infer'. (7) Verify output macro F1 matches paper's 0.72 (tolerance ±0.02).

Contains complete training/eval code: scene_graph_generation/LLaVA/ with train.py (84KB), llava_trainer.py, model files; scene_graph_prediction/main.py (10KB) for inference; egoexor.json config. README.md documents full train/eval workflows with commands.

weights_available.evidence: HuggingFace model repo ardamamur/EgoExOR verified via huggingface_repo. Contains pretrained checkpoint: llava-v1.5-7b-task-lora_hybridor_qlora_4perm_EgoExOR.zip (2.5GB, LFS). README.md evaluation section documents: 'Pretrained model: EgoExOR on Hugging Face' with inference command.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: EgoExOR is a custom author-created surgical dataset from TUM researchers, not a widely recognized public ML benchmark. The paper describes it as a new OR dataset spanning 94 minutes of simulated spine procedures with 36 entity classes and 22 relation classes.

h100_estimate_basis: MRE uses pretrained checkpoint for inference only (not training). Paper reports training took ~5 days on single A40 GPU. For inference on 5K test samples with LLaVA-7B LoRA at batch 16: approximately 2-4 hours on A40 (~0.3-0.6 H100-hours). Rounded to 4 H100-hours to account for setup overhead and potential re-runs. Engineering and debugging time not included.
abstract: Operating rooms (ORs) demand precise coordination among surgeons, nurses, and equipment in a fast-paced, occlusion-heavy environment, necessitating advanced perception models to enhance safety and efficiency. Existing datasets either provide partial egocentric views or sparse exocentric multi-view context, but do not explore the comprehensive combination of both. We introduce EgoExOR, the first OR dataset and accompanying benchmark to fuse first-person and third-person perspectives. Spanning 94 minutes (84,553 frames at 15 FPS) of two emulated spine procedures, Ultrasound-Guided Needle Insertion and Minimally Invasive Spine Surgery, EgoExOR integrates egocentric data (RGB, gaze, hand tracking, audio) from wearable glasses, exocentric RGB and depth from RGB-D cameras, and ultrasound imagery. Its detailed scene graph annotations, covering 36 entities and 22 relations (568,235 triplets), enable robust modeling of clinical interactions, supporting tasks like action recognition and human-centric perception. We evaluate the surgical scene graph generation performance of two adapted state-of-the-art models and offer a new baseline that explicitly leverages EgoExOR's multimodal and multi-perspective signals. This new dataset and benchmark set a new foundation for OR perception, offering a rich, multimodal resource for next-generation clinical perception.

title: Mind the Quote: Enabling Quotation-Aware Dialogue in LLMs via Plug-and-Play Modules
central_claim: QuAda, a lightweight adapter that attaches two bottleneck projections to every attention head, enables LLMs to handle quotation-aware dialogue across five scenarios (Base, Multi-Span, Exclude, Info-Combine, Coref) by dynamically modulating attention to quoted spans, achieving >90% accuracy while updating <2.8% of backbone weights.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'QuAda is suitable for all scenarios and generalises to unseen topics, offering an effective, plug-and-play solution for quotation-aware dialogue.' Table 1 (tab:mainQwen3Bresult): QuAda achieves 95.2% Base, 94.6% Multi-Span, 92.8% Exclude, 85.8% Info-Combine, 90.2% Coref on Qwen2.5-3B.
mre_config: Train QuAda adapter on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct using the Base scenario training set (4400 MCQ+OpenQA samples), evaluate on the Base scenario benchmark (1000 MCQ samples), metric: MCQ accuracy. QuAda uses bottleneck width r=256, 2 query-side and 2 value-side projections per attention head, <2.8% trainable parameters.
agent_task: Reproduce the QuAda method on the Base scenario benchmark: (1) Implement the QuAda adapter with query-side and value-side bottleneck projections per attention head (bottleneck width r=256), (2) Fine-tune Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on the 4400-sample Base training set (frozen backbone, only adapter trains), (3) Evaluate on the 1000-sample Base benchmark MCQ split, (4) Compare MCQ accuracy to the reported 95.2% baseline.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repo (MindtheQuote/MindtheQuote) contains only the data construction pipeline code (NIPS_single_pipeline, NIPS_multi_pipeline directories with D0-D4 Python scripts for synthetic data generation). The OpenReview supplement has benchmark data files (MCQ_*.jsonl, 3.2MB verified readable) and modeling_qwen2.py (72KB), but no QuAda training or evaluation scripts. The core QuAda method (query-side/value-side bottleneck projections, training loop) is not released.

dataset_available.evidence: Benchmark data is included in OpenReview supplement with structured JSONL files containing instructions, inputs, outputs, quote_token_span, and question_token_span fields. Training set link provided in GitHub README. Both contain Base/Multi-Span/Exclude/Info-Combine/Coref scenario data with MCQ and OpenQA variants.

weights_available.evidence: No trained QuAda checkpoints or adapter weights are released. Only base model weights from HuggingFace (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) would be available, but the trained adapter weights for QuAda are not provided.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: This is a custom author-created benchmark for quotation-aware dialogue evaluation, not a widely recognized public ML benchmark. The data was synthesized using an LLM-based pipeline with multi-stage consistency checks, covering five specific scenarios (Base, Multi-Span, Exclude, Info-Combine, Coref) with author-generated synthetic dialogues.

h100_estimate_basis: Training QuAda on Qwen2.5-3B (75M trainable params, <2.8% of backbone) for 1 epoch on 4400 training samples is lightweight. Paper states training on H100 GPUs (96GB). Estimated ~1-2 GPU-hours for adapter training on H100, converted to ~2 H100-hours. Inference compute not counted as MRE focuses on demonstrating the method works with training-based evaluation.
abstract: Human-AI conversation frequently relies on quoting earlier text-"check it with the formula I just highlighted"-yet today's large language models (LLMs) lack an explicit mechanism for locating and exploiting such spans. We formalise the challenge as span-conditioned generation, decomposing each turn into the dialogue history, a set of token-offset quotation spans, and an intent utterance. Building on this abstraction, we introduce a quotation-centric data pipeline that automatically synthesises task-specific dialogues, verifies answer correctness through multi-stage consistency checks, and yields both a heterogeneous training corpus and the first benchmark covering five representative scenarios. To meet the benchmark's zero-overhead and parameter-efficiency requirements, we propose QuAda, a lightweight training-based method that attaches two bottleneck projections to every attention head, dynamically amplifying or suppressing attention to quoted spans at inference time while leaving the prompt unchanged and updating < 2.8% of backbone weights. Experiments across models show that QuAda is suitable for all scenarios and generalises to unseen topics, offering an effective, plug-and-play solution for quotation-aware dialogue.

title: Unlearned but Not Forgotten: Data Extraction after Exact Unlearning in LLM
central_claim: Exact unlearning (retraining from scratch without target data) still leaves models vulnerable to data extraction attacks when attackers have access to both pre- and post-unlearning model checkpoints/logits APIs, and their proposed 'reversed model guidance' method with token filtering significantly improves extraction success rates (doubling in some cases).
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'our attack significantly improves extraction success rates—doubling performance in some cases—across common benchmarks such as MUSE, TOFU, and WMDP.' Table 1 (tab:main-res): Our Extraction achieves Rouge-L(R)=0.606 and A-ESR1.0=0.224 on MUSE with Phi-1.5 vs. Pre-unlearning Generation at Rouge-L(R)=0.473 and A-ESR1.0=0.101, showing substantial improvement.
mre_config: Phi-1.5 model on TOFU dataset with 10% forgetting set. Procedure: (1) Fine-tune Phi-1.5 on full TOFU dataset for 3 epochs with lr=1e-5, (2) Exact unlearning by retraining without forget set, (3) Apply contrasting_generation with guidance scale w=2.0 and gamma=10^-5, (4) Evaluate Rouge-L(R) recall and A-ESR. Expected result: Rouge-L(R) improvement from ~0.57 (pre-unlearning baseline) to ~0.64, A-ESR1.0 improvement from ~0.07 to ~0.12.
agent_task: Reproduce the core extraction method on Phi-1.5 with TOFU 10% forget set: (1) Fine-tune microsoft/phi-1_5 on locuslab/TOFU full split for 3 epochs (lr=1e-5, batch_size=4, grad_accum=4), (2) Exact unlearn by retraining on retain90 split (same hyperparameters), (3) Implement contrasting_generation using the logit difference formula: log q(x_{i+1}|x_{≤i}) = log p_post(x_{i+1}|x_{≤i}) + w·(log p_pre - log p_post) where w=2.0, with token filtering using gamma=1e-5, (4) Evaluate generated continuations vs. ground truth using Rouge-L recall and A-ESR metrics. Target: Rouge-L(R) ≥ 0.64, A-ESR1.0 ≥ 0.12.

code_available.evidence: GitHub repository Nicholas0228/unlearned_data_extraction_llm verified with complete implementation: evaluate_util.py contains contrasting_generation function (lines 247-356), finetune_v2.py for training, eval_idea_10_v2.sh for evaluation, MUSE dataset files bundled in MUSE_data_news/. README shows 3-step workflow with code for training and extraction.

dataset_available.evidence: TOFU dataset verified available on HuggingFace at locuslab/TOFU with full forget/retain splits (forget10.json, retain90.json). MUSE dataset is standard benchmark at muse-bench.github.io, also bundled in paper repo with full.json, forget10.json, full_minus_forget10.json.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: TOFU (locuslab/TOFU on HuggingFace, arXiv:2401.06121, 2.9M downloads) and MUSE (muse-bench.github.io, arXiv:2407.06460) are widely recognized standard benchmarks for LLM unlearning with published papers, public datasets, and community leaderboards.

Fine-tuning needs to run twice (pre-unlearning and exact unlearning): ~15 H100-hours total. Extraction is inference-only (forward passes with guidance) and takes <1 H100-hour. Estimated total: ~16 H100-hours. Engineering/debugging time not included.
abstract: Large Language Models are typically trained on datasets collected from the web, which may inadvertently contain harmful or sensitive personal information. To address growing privacy concerns, unlearning methods have been proposed to remove the influence of specific data from trained models. Of these, exact unlearning -- which retrains the model from scratch without the target data -- is widely regarded the gold standard for mitigating privacy risks in deployment. In this paper, we revisit this assumption in a practical deployment setting where both the pre- and post-unlearning logits API are exposed, such as in open-weight scenarios. Targeting this setting, we introduce a novel data extraction attack that leverages signals from the pre-unlearning model to guide the post-unlearning model, uncovering patterns that reflect the removed data distribution. Combining model guidance with a token filtering strategy, our attack significantly improves extraction success rates -- doubling performance in some cases -- across common benchmarks such as MUSE, TOFU, and WMDP. Furthermore, we demonstrate our attack's effectiveness on a simulated medical diagnosis dataset to highlight real-world privacy risks associated with exact unlearning. In light of our findings, which suggest that unlearning may, in a contradictory way, increase the risk of privacy leakage during real-world deployments, we advocate for evaluation of unlearning methods to consider broader threat models that account not only for post-unlearning models but also for adversarial access to prior checkpoints. title: un$^2$CLIP: Improving CLIP's Visual Detail Capturing Ability via Inverting unCLIP

Full training from scratch would require 8 A100 GPUs * ~32 hours = 256 GPU-hours ≈ 82 H100-hours, but is not needed for MRE verification.
abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) has become a foundation model and has been applied to various vision and multimodal tasks. However, recent works indicate that CLIP falls short in distinguishing detailed differences in images and shows suboptimal performance on dense-prediction and vision-centric multimodal tasks. Therefore, this work focuses on improving existing CLIP models, aiming to capture as many visual details in images as possible. We find that a specific type of generative models, unCLIP, provides a suitable framework for achieving our goal. Specifically, unCLIP trains an image generator conditioned on the CLIP image embedding. In other words, it inverts the CLIP image encoder. Compared to discriminative models like CLIP, generative models are better at capturing image details because they are trained to learn the data distribution of images. Additionally, the conditional input space of unCLIP aligns with CLIP's original image-text embedding space. Therefore, we propose to invert unCLIP (dubbed un$^2$CLIP) to improve the CLIP model. In this way, the improved image encoder can gain unCLIP's visual detail capturing ability while preserving its alignment with the original text encoder simultaneously. We evaluate our improved CLIP across various tasks to which CLIP has been applied, including the challenging MMVP-VLM benchmark, the dense-prediction open-vocabulary segmentation task, and multimodal large language model tasks. Experiments show that un$^2$CLIP significantly improves the original CLIP and previous CLIP improvement methods. Code and models …

title: A*-Thought: Efficient Reasoning via Bidirectional Compression for Low-Resource Settings
central_claim: A*-Thought uses bidirectional importance estimation and A* search to compress long chain-of-thought reasoning, achieving up to 2.39× accuracy improvement at low token budgets while reducing output length by ~50% at high budgets.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'Specifically, A*-Thought can improve the performance of QwQ-32B by 2.39× with low-budget and reduce the length of the output token by nearly 50% with high-budget.' Table 3 shows MATH500 results comparing A*-Thought vs baselines across 512-4096 token budgets.
mre_config: Evaluate pre-trained AStar-Thought-QwQ-32B on MATH500 benchmark with max_tokens=1024 (low-budget setting) and compare accuracy vs token count against baseline QwQ-32B. The MRE uses the released checkpoint for inference-only evaluation, testing whether the compressed model achieves superior accuracy at constrained token budgets.

Inference for 500 MATH500 problems with max_tokens=1024 on 32B model requires ~2 hours on 8xH100. abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) achieve superior performance by extending the thought length. However, a lengthy thinking trajectory leads to reduced efficiency. Most of the existing methods are stuck in the assumption of overthinking and attempt to reason efficiently by compressing the Chain-of-Thought, but this often leads to performance degradation. To address this problem, we introduce A*-Thought, an efficient tree search-based unified framework designed to identify and isolate the most essential thoughts from the extensive reasoning chains produced by these models. It formulates the reasoning process of LRMs as a search tree, where each node represents a reasoning span in the giant reasoning space. By combining the A* search algorithm with a cost function specific to the reasoning path, it can efficiently compress the chain of thought and determine a reasoning path with high information density and low cost. In addition, we also propose a bidirectional importance estimation mechanism, which further refines this search process and enhances its efficiency beyond uniform sampling. Extensive experiments on several advanced math tasks show that A*-Thought effectively balances performance and efficiency over a huge search space. Specifically, A*-Thought can improve the performance of QwQ-32B by 2.39$\times$ with low-budget and reduce the length of the output token by nearly 50% with high-budget. The proposed method is also compatible with several other LRMs, demonstrating its generalization capability. The code can be accessed at: https://github.com/AI9Stars/AStar-Thought.

title: REASONING GYM: Reasoning Environments for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
central_claim: Reasoning Gym (RGym) provides procedurally generated reasoning environments for RLVR training that can generate unlimited training data with controllable difficulty, and RLVR training on RGym tasks produces models with improved reasoning capabilities that transfer across domains.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'We address this challenge with RGym, a comprehensive library of procedurally generated reasoning environments designed specifically for RLVR training' and 'Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of RGym in both evaluating and reinforcement learning of reasoning models.' Table 1 shows dataset categories, Table 2 shows intra-domain generalization results, and Table 3 shows cross-domain transfer to external benchmarks.
mre_config: Minimal RLVR training on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct using a single RGym dataset (e.g., count_primes or prime_factorization) for ~100-200 GRPO steps with batch_size=32, evaluating accuracy improvement on held-out tasks from the same dataset. Install reasoning-gym via `pip install reasoning-gym`, generate data with `reasoning_gym.create_dataset()`, and run training using provided verl-based GRPO code.

Expect measurable improvement in accuracy, demonstrating that RGym enables effective RLVR training.

README provides installation and usage instructions. Training README shows complete setup with verl, flash-attention, and GRPO training commands.

Install via `pip install reasoning-gym`, then use `reasoning_gym.create_dataset('dataset_name', size=N)` to generate unlimited instances. Verified from README and paper appendix showing dataset generation code examples.

h100_estimate_basis: compute-unspecified: Paper reports ~1500 A6000 GPU-hours total for all experiments. A6000 normalized to H100: 0.32x. abstract: We introduce Reasoning Gym (RG), a library of reasoning environments for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. It provides over 100 data generators and verifiers spanning multiple domains including algebra, arithmetic, computation, cognition, geometry, graph theory, logic, and various common games. Its key innovation is the ability to generate virtually infinite training data with adjustable complexity, unlike most previous reasoning datasets, which are typically fixed. This procedural generation approach allows for continuous evaluation across varying difficulty levels. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of RG in both evaluating and reinforcement learning of reasoning models.

title: Reading Recognition in the Wild
central_claim: The paper introduces reading recognition using a multimodal transformer model (gaze + RGB + IMU) that achieves ~86.9% accuracy for detecting when someone is reading, with gaze and RGB being the most complementary modalities.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'We identify three modalities (egocentric RGB, eye gaze, head pose) that can be used to solve the task, and present a flexible transformer model that performs the task using these modalities.' abstract: To enable egocentric contextual AI in always-on smart glasses, it is crucial to be able to keep a record of the user's interactions with the world, including during reading. In this paper, we introduce a new task of reading recognition to determine when the user is reading. We first introduce the first-of-its-kind large-scale multimodal Reading in the Wild dataset, containing 100 hours of reading and non-reading videos in diverse and realistic scenarios. We then identify three modalities (egocentric RGB, eye gaze, head pose) that can be used to solve the task, and present a flexible transformer model that performs the task using these modalities, either individually or combined. We show that these modalities are relevant and complementary to the task, and investigate how to efficiently and effectively encode each modality. Additionally, we show the usefulness of this dataset towards classifying types of reading, extending current reading understanding studies conducted in constrained settings to larger scale, diversity and realism.

title: Tradeoffs between Mistakes and ERM Oracle Calls in Online and Transductive Online Learning
central_claim: Even with access to the general ERM oracle that can query any subset of the domain, the mistake bound in online learning grows exponentially with the Littlestone dimension (Omega(2^d_LD) in realizable case, Omega(sqrt(T*2^d_LD)) regret in agnostic case), and the transductive online setting can circumvent this with O(T^(d_VC+1)) weak consistency oracle calls.
claim_evidence: Abstract states: 'We establish tight lower bounds in both the realizable and agnostic cases: Omega(2^d_LD) mistakes and Omega(sqrt(T 2^d_LD)) regret, respectively... For general Littlestone classes, we show that the optimal mistake bound in the realizable case can be achieved using O(T^(d_VC+1)) weak consistency oracle calls.' Tables 1 and 2 in the paper summarize the oracle complexity-regret tradeoffs for online and transductive online learning.
mre_config: Synthetic/simulated setting: Implement the threshold learning algorithm (Theorem 4) for transductive online learning with thresholds. Verify O(log T) mistake bound with O(T) or O(log T) oracle calls on randomly generated threshold functions over T points. Smallest configuration: T=100, compare deterministic vs randomized algorithms, measure mistakes and queries.
agent_task: Implement and verify the threshold learning algorithm from Theorem 4 (or the general weak consistency preprocessing from Lemma 3) for transductive online learning. Use synthetic data: generate T=128 random points, define a random threshold function, run the algorithm, measure mistakes and oracle calls. Verify: (1) randomized ERM algorithm achieves O(log T) mistakes with O(log T) expected queries; (2) deterministic weak consistency algorithm achieves O(log T) mistakes with O(T log T) queries. Compare against the theoretical lower bounds Omega(2^d_LD) worst-case for standard online learning to demonstrate the transductive advantage.

Also searched Hugging Face. No relevant repositories found. The OpenReview supplement contains only PDF figures (neurips_cameraready_final.pdf and ._ file). The adversary can generate random instances x_1,...,x_T and random binary labels according to the chosen threshold function. This is standard for theoretical algorithm verification.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: The MRE uses synthetic/simulated data (random instances and labels generated according to threshold functions). This is standard for theoretical algorithm verification rather than evaluation on a public benchmark dataset.

Estimated 0.5 H100-hours covers running synthetic experiments across multiple random seeds for the threshold learning algorithm (O(log T) mistakes, O(log T) queries per round across T=128 timesteps). The main cost is simulation overhead and counting oracle calls, not GPU-intensive computation.
abstract: We study online and transductive online learning when the learner interacts with the concept class only via Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) or weak consistency oracles on arbitrary instance subsets. This contrasts with standard online models, where the learner knows the entire class. The ERM oracle returns a hypothesis minimizing loss on a given subset, while the weak consistency oracle returns a binary signal indicating whether the subset is realizable by some concept. The learner is evaluated by the number of mistakes and oracle calls. In the standard online setting with ERM access, we prove tight lower bounds in both realizable and agnostic cases: $Ω(2^{d_{VC}})$ mistakes and $Ω(\sqrt{T 2^{d_{LD}}})$ regret, where $T$ is the number of timesteps and $d_{LD}$ is the Littlestone dimension. We further show that existing online learning results with ERM access carry over to the weak consistency setting, incurring an additional $O(T)$ in oracle calls. We then consider the transductive online model, where the instance sequence is known but labels are revealed sequentially. For general Littlestone classes, we show that optimal realizable and agnostic mistake bounds can be achieved using $O(T^{d_{VC}+1})$ weak consistency oracle calls. On the negative side, we show that limiting the learner to $Ω(T)$ weak consistency queries is necessary for transductive online learnability, and that restricting the learner to $Ω(T)$ ERM queries is necessary to avoid exponential dependence on the Littlestone dimension. Finally, for certain concept classes, we reduce oracle calls via randomized …

title: Intrinsic Goals for Autonomous Agents: Model-Based Exploration in Virtual Zebrafish Predicts Ethological Behavior and Whole-Brain Dynamics
central_claim: 3M-Progress (Model-Memory-Mismatch Progress), a novel model-based intrinsic motivation algorithm, enables autonomous embodied agents to achieve animal-like exploration in a virtual zebrafish environment and captures whole-brain neural-glial dynamics.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'Our method (3M-Progress) achieves animal-like exploration by tracking divergence between an online world model and a fixed prior learned from an ecological niche.' Section Results: '3M-Progress discovers ethologically-relevant behavioral state transitions by 10 million environment steps' and '3M-Progress agents captured nearly all of the explainable variance in neural and astrocytic activity.'
mre_config: Train a 3M-Progress agent in the virtual zebrafish open-loop grating environment (MuJoCo 6-link swimmer) with PPO for 10M timesteps. The agent uses a vision encoder + proprioceptive features to LSTM core/policy modules. Intrinsic reward = KL divergence between a fixed ethological prior (pretrained world model) and online world model, filtered via exponential moving average. Evaluate behavioral alignment via Pearson correlation between agent swim power and zebrafish swim power around active/passive transitions.

Step 1: Train the ethological prior world model in the drift environment (zfa_rl_agent/experiments/drift/) for ~5M timesteps to create the fixed memory. Step 2: Train a 3M-Progress agent on the open-loop grating task (zfa_rl_agent/experiments/grating/) for 10M timesteps with reward_type='3m_progress', using the pretrained world model checkpoint as the persistent memory. Step 3: Compare swim power traces (joint torque norm) with the zebrafish behavioral data from DANDI:000350 using Pearson correlation. Verify that 3M-Progress agents exhibit cycling between active and passive states similar to futility-induced passivity in zebrafish.

abstract: Autonomy is a hallmark of animal intelligence, enabling adaptive and intelligent behavior in complex environments without relying on external reward or task structure. Existing reinforcement learning approaches to exploration in reward-free environments, including a class of methods known as model-based intrinsic motivation, exhibit inconsistent exploration patterns and do not converge to an exploratory policy, thus failing to capture robust autonomous behaviors observed in animals. Moreover, systems neuroscience has largely overlooked the neural basis of autonomy, focusing instead on experimental paradigms where animals are motivated by external reward rather than engaging in ethological, naturalistic and task-independent behavior. To bridge these gaps, we introduce a novel model-based intrinsic drive explicitly designed after the principles of autonomous exploration in animals. Our method (3M-Progress) achieves animal-like exploration by tracking divergence between an online world model and a fixed prior learned from an ecological niche. To the best of our knowledge, we introduce the first autonomous embodied agent that predicts brain data entirely from self-supervised optimization of an intrinsic goal -- without any behavioral or neural training data -- demonstrating that 3M-Progress agents capture the explainable variance in behavioral patterns and whole-brain neural-glial dynamics recorded from autonomously behaving larval zebrafish, thereby providing the first goal-driven, population-level model of neural-glial computation. Our findings establish a computational …

title: $\texttt{AVROBUSTBENCH}$: Benchmarking the Robustness of Audio-Visual Recognition Models at Test-Time
central_claim: State-of-the-art audio-visual recognition models exhibit declining robustness as corruption severity increases under co-occurring and correlated bimodal corruptions.

abstract: While recent audio-visual models have demonstrated impressive performance, their robustness to distributional shifts at test-time remains not fully understood. Existing robustness benchmarks mainly focus on single modalities, making them insufficient for thoroughly assessing the robustness of audio-visual models. Motivated by real-world scenarios where shifts can occur $\textit{simultaneously}$ in both audio and visual modalities, we introduce $\texttt{AVROBUSTBENCH}$, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate the test-time robustness of audio-visual recognition models. $\texttt{AVROBUSTBENCH}$ comprises four audio-visual benchmark datasets, $\texttt{AUDIOSET-2C}$, $\texttt{VGGSOUND-2C}$, $\texttt{KINETICS-2C}$, and $\texttt{EPICKITCHENS-2C}$, each incorporating 75 bimodal audio-visual corruptions that are $\textit{co-occurring}$ and $\textit{correlated}$. Through extensive evaluations, we observe that state-of-the-art supervised and self-supervised audio-visual models exhibit declining robustness as corruption severity increases. Furthermore, online test-time adaptation (TTA) methods, on $\texttt{VGGSOUND-2C}$ and $\texttt{KINETICS-2C}$, offer minimal improvements in performance under bimodal corruptions. We further propose $\texttt{AV2C}$, a simple TTA approach enabling on-the-fly cross-modal fusion by penalizing high-entropy samples, which achieves improvements on $\texttt{VGGSOUND-2C}$. We hope that $\texttt{AVROBUSTBENCH}$ will steer the development of more effective and robust audio-visual TTA approaches. Our code is available …

title: Controlling the Spread of Epidemics on Networks with Differential Privacy
central_claim: The paper introduces differentially private algorithms for selecting vaccination strategies on contact networks to minimize maximum degree and spectral radius, achieving O((1+1/epsilon)ln|V|)-approximation using a novel private multi-set multi-cover reduction.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'Our main contributions are (epsilon,delta)-differentially private algorithms for designing vaccination strategies by reducing the maximum degree and spectral radius.' Theorem 4.2 proves O((1+1/epsilon')ln|V|) approximation for Algorithm 1 (PrivateMaxDeg). Section 6 reports experiments on BTER networks showing the solution of Algorithm 1 is within ~10x of the non-private baseline (Figure 1 and Table 2).
mre_config: Run PrivateMaxDeg (Algorithm 1) on BTER graph (n=1000 nodes) with target degree D=20, privacy budget epsilon=4.0, delta=0.001, measuring: (1) vaccination budget (number of nodes removed), (2) resulting max degree, (3) spectral radius. Compare implicit solution quality against non-private greedy baseline. Multiple runs for distributions as shown in Figure 1.
agent_task: Reproduce the central empirical result: implement the PrivateMaxDeg algorithm (Algorithm 1) and explicit solution Algorithm 2, which use an iterative exponential mechanism to sample nodes based on coverage utility for the multi-set multi-cover problem. Generate a small BTER graph (n=1000, gamma=0.5, rho=0.95, eta=0.05) or construct a synthetic contact network. Run Algorithm 1 with target max degree D=20, epsilon=4.0, delta=0.001. Measure the vaccination budget (number of nodes removed) and resulting max degree after removing the selected nodes. Verify that the resulting max degree satisfies Delta(G - S) <= D + O(log n / epsilon) as proven in Theorem 4.3.

abstract: Designing effective strategies for controlling epidemic spread by vaccination is an important question in epidemiology, especially in the early stages when vaccines are limited. This is a challenging question when the contact network is very heterogeneous, and strategies based on controlling network properties, such as the degree and spectral radius, have been shown to be effective. Implementation of such strategies requires detailed information on the contact structure, which might be sensitive in many applications. Our focus here is on choosing effective vaccination strategies when the edges are sensitive and differential privacy guarantees are needed. Our main contributions are $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differentially private algorithms for designing vaccination strategies by reducing the maximum degree and spectral radius. Our key technique is a private algorithm for the multi-set multi-cover problem, which we use for controlling network properties. We evaluate privacy-utility tradeoffs of our algorithms on multiple synthetic and real-world networks, and show their effectiveness.

abstract: Many promising-looking ideas in AI research fail to deliver, but their validation takes substantial human labor and compute. Predicting an idea's chance of success is thus crucial for accelerating empirical AI research, a skill that even expert researchers can only acquire through substantial experience. We build the first benchmark for this task and compare LMs with human experts. Concretely, given two research ideas (e.g., two jailbreaking methods), we aim to predict which will perform better on a set of benchmarks. We scrape ideas and experimental results from conference papers, yielding 1,585 human-verified idea pairs published after our base model's cut-off date for testing, and 6,000 pairs for training. We then develop a system that combines a fine-tuned GPT-4.1 with a paper retrieval agent, and we recruit 25 human experts to compare with. In the NLP domain, our system beats human experts by a large margin (64.4% v.s. 48.9%). On the full test set, our system achieves 77% accuracy, while off-the-shelf frontier LMs like o3 perform no better than random guessing, even with the same retrieval augmentation. We verify that our system does not exploit superficial features like idea complexity through extensive human-written and LM-designed robustness tests. Finally, we evaluate our system on unpublished novel ideas, including ideas generated by an AI ideation agent. Our system achieves 63.6% accuracy, demonstrating its potential as a reward model for improving idea generation models. Altogether, our results outline a promising new direction for LMs to accelerate empirical …

abstract: Long-form video understanding poses a significant challenge for video large language models (VideoLLMs) due to prohibitively high computational and memory demands. In this paper, we propose FlexSelect, a flexible and efficient token selection strategy for processing long videos. FlexSelect identifies and retains the most semantically relevant content by leveraging cross-modal attention patterns from a reference transformer layer. It comprises two key components: (1) a training-free token ranking pipeline that leverages faithful cross-modal attention weights to estimate each video token's importance, and (2) a rank-supervised lightweight selector that is trained to replicate these rankings and filter redundant tokens. This generic approach can be seamlessly integrated into various VideoLLM architectures, such as LLaVA-Video, InternVL and Qwen-VL, serving as a plug-and-play module to extend their temporal context length. Empirically, FlexSelect delivers strong gains across multiple long-video benchmarks including VideoMME, MLVU, LongVB, and LVBench. Moreover, it achieves significant speed-ups (for example, up to 9 times on a LLaVA-Video-7B model), highlighting FlexSelect's promise for efficient long-form video understanding. Project page available at: https://yunzhuzhang0918.github.io/flex_select

abstract: Neural models learn representations of high-dimensional data on low-dimensional manifolds. Multiple factors, including stochasticities in the training process, model architectures, and additional inductive biases, may induce different representations, even when learning the same task on the same data. However, it has recently been shown that when a latent structure is shared between distinct latent spaces, relative distances between representations can be preserved, up to distortions. Building on this idea, we demonstrate that exploiting the differential-geometric structure of latent spaces of neural models, it is possible to capture precisely the transformations between representational spaces trained on similar data distributions. Specifically, we assume that distinct neural models parametrize approximately the same underlying manifold, and introduce a representation based on the pullback metric that captures the intrinsic structure of the latent space, while scaling efficiently to large models. We validate experimentally our method on model stitching and retrieval tasks, covering autoencoders and vision foundation discriminative models, across diverse architectures, datasets, and pretraining schemes.
