With ~300 tokens/sample avg, this is ~1.35M tokens per epoch and ~6.75M tokens total. On a single H100 SXM: ~6.75M tokens / 35 tokens/s ≈ 0.19M A100-seconds ≈ 53 GPU-hours on A100-80GB, equivalent to 17 H100-hours. For the MRE using a smaller 1K subset for 1 epoch on 1 H100: ~0.45M tokens / 35 tokens/s ≈ 3.6 GPU-hours ≈ 3.6 H100-hours. Rounding conservatively for debugging overhead: ~2 H100-hours. Engineering time for implementing decomposition from scratch (no official code) adds significant non-compute effort.
abstract: Curriculum learning is a class of training strategies that organizes the data being exposed to a model by difficulty, gradually from simpler to more complex examples. This research explores a reverse curriculum generation approach that recursively decomposes complex datasets into simpler, more learnable components. We propose a teacher-student framework where the teacher is equipped with the ability to reason step-by-step, which is used to recursively generate easier versions of examples, enabling the student model to progressively master difficult tasks. We propose a novel scoring system to measure data difficulty based on its structural complexity and conceptual depth, allowing curriculum construction over decomposed data. Experiments on math datasets (MATH and AIME) and code generation datasets demonstrate that models trained with curricula generated by our approach exhibit superior performance compared to standard training on original datasets.

title: Spectral Conditioning of Attention Improves Transformer Performance
central_claim: Adding spectral correction terms (λI_k with λ=10) to query, key, and value matrices in transformer attention layers reduces the Jacobian's condition number and improves downstream performance across vision and NLP tasks.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'We introduce a method that systematically alters the spectral properties of each attention layer to reduce the Jacobian's condition number, thereby improving the overall conditioning of the attention layers within a transformer network. We empirically show that this improved Jacobian conditioning translates to enhanced performance in practice.' Table 1 shows ViT-B on ImageNet-1k: original 80.7% → spectral conditioned 81.7% top-1 accuracy.
mre_config: ViT-B trained from scratch on ImageNet-1k (Image Classification). Training configuration: AdamW optimizer, spectral conditioned attention with λ=10 (correction matrices C_Q=10·I_Q, C_K=10·I_K, C_V=10·I_V added to W_Q, W_K, W_V respectively, fixed throughout training). 5 trials with different random seeds. Metric: Top-1 accuracy. Anchor result to reproduce: 81.7% vs 80.7% baseline. Training from scratch required since no released checkpoints.
agent_task: Reproduce spectral conditioned attention on a vision transformer. 1) Obtain ImageNet-1k training data. 2) Implement the spectral conditioning method: for each attention layer, initialize fixed correction matrices C_Q=λ·I_Q, C_K=λ·I_K, C_V=λ·I_V (with λ=10, same shape as W_Q/W_K/W_V) that are never updated during training. 3) During each forward pass, compute attention using (W_Q+C_Q), (W_K+C_K), (W_V+C_V) instead of W_Q, W_K, W_V. 4) Train ViT-B from scratch on ImageNet-1k for 300 epochs with AdamW. 5) Run 5 trials with different seeds. 6) Verify that spectral conditioned ViT-B achieves ≥81.5% top-1 accuracy vs 80.5% baseline. Note: implement from scratch using timm library since no released code exists.

code_available.evidence: No code repository found. Searched GitHub with: full title 'Spectral Conditioning of Attention Improves Transformer Performance', method name 'spectral conditioned attention', arXiv ID '2603.07162', author names 'Saratchandran Lucey', 'Adelaide University', 'spectral conditioning attention transformer', 'condition number attention transformer jacobian', and HuggingFace with equivalent queries. GitHub 'Spectral Conditioning' search returned unrelated repos (ezmup, SPECTRE, Width-Depth-muP) none matching this paper. OpenReview supplement status is 'missing'. The paper builds on public baselines (timm library) but provides no released spectral conditioning implementation.

dataset_available.evidence: ImageNet-1k is a standard benchmark dataset, publicly downloadable. The paper does not release custom data. The MRE uses ImageNet-1k for image classification experiments.

weights_available.evidence: No released checkpoints found. The paper trains ViT-B, XCiT-M, Swin-B, DeiT-B, DaViT-B, Nyströmformer, and Crammed BERT from scratch. No download links for spectral-conditioned model weights. GitHub and HuggingFace searches confirmed no matching model repositories.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: ImageNet-1k (ILSVRC2012) is a widely recognized public ML benchmark for image classification, used extensively in the vision transformer literature.

h100_estimate_basis: ViT-B on ImageNet-1k requires training from scratch. Paper reports ~30 hours per trial on A100 GPUs (Table 5). MRE needs 5 trials × 2 models (baseline + spectral conditioned) = 10 runs. 300 A100-hours × 0.32 = ~96 H100-hours. This accounts for both ViT-B variants with full training runs. Engineering/debugging time additional and not included in this compute estimate.
abstract: We present a theoretical analysis of the Jacobian of an attention block within a transformer, showing that it is governed by the query, key, and value projections that define the attention mechanism. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a method that systematically alters the spectral properties of each attention layer to reduce the Jacobian's condition number, thereby improving the overall conditioning of the attention layers within a transformer network. We empirically show that this improved Jacobian conditioning translates to enhanced performance in practice. Our approach is simple, broadly applicable, and can be easily integrated as a drop-in replacement for a wide range of existing attention mechanisms. We validate its effectiveness across diverse transformer architectures and tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in performance.

title: Looking Into the Water by Unsupervised Learning of the Surface Shape
central_claim: A two-network SIREN architecture (one for surface height prediction, one for image reconstruction) trained unsupervised on short video sequences can reconstruct undistorted underwater images and estimate water surface height, outperforming the NDIR unsupervised baseline.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'we propose a model that consists of two neural-field networks. The first network predicts the height of the water surface... and the second network predicts the image color... Using both networks, we reconstruct the observed sequence of images and can therefore use unsupervised training. We show that... our method outperforms the latest unsupervised image restoration approach.' Table 1 (Real1 dataset) shows PSNR 19.78, SSIM 0.61, LPIPS 0.12 vs NDIR's 19.44, 0.59, 0.14.
mre_config: Train the two-network SIREN model on the Bricks sequence from Real1 dataset using default parameters: 10 frames, 700 initialization iterations + 1800 optimization iterations, batch_size=10, scale_factor=0.5, lr_init=0.001, lr_optim=0.0001. Evaluate using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS against ground truth. Target: PSNR ~21.34, SSIM ~0.59, LPIPS ~0.16.
agent_task: Reproduce the paper's central result by training the two-network SIREN model on the Bricks sequence from Real1 dataset: (1) Download Real1 dataset from https://github.com/jeringeo/CompressiveFlows or use the sample subset in Code/data/james_real1_bricks/; (2) Install dependencies with 'conda env create -f environment.yml' and activate 'unsugrd_refrem'; (3) Run: python Code/unsugrd_refrem.py --environment local --exp_name test --pname james_real1_bricks; (4) Evaluate restored image against ground truth using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS metrics. Target: PSNR ~21.3, SSIM ~0.59, LPIPS ~0.16. The method outputs both a restored undistorted image and estimated water surface height.

The RDR-SuGrad GitHub repo is a placeholder with only README/LICENSE. The bundled supplement code is sufficient to run the MRE.

Supplement also includes a small sample subset at Code/data/james_real1_bricks/. Dataset requires downloading from CompressiveFlows as documented in README.

For a single sequence (Bricks) with 10 frames: 5 min = 0.083 H100-hours, rounded to 0.1 H100-hours. No external weights available; training from scratch required. Engineering/debugging time for environment setup and data preparation not included.
abstract: We address the problem of looking into the water from the air, where we seek to remove image distortions caused by refractions at the water surface. Our approach is based on modeling the different water surface structures at various points in time, assuming the underlying image is constant. To this end, we propose a model that consists of two neural-field networks. The first network predicts the height of the water surface at each spatial position and time, and the second network predicts the image color at each position. Using both networks, we reconstruct the observed sequence of images and can therefore use unsupervised training. We show that using implicit neural representations with periodic activation functions (SIREN) leads to effective modeling of the surface height spatio-temporal signal and its derivative, as required for image reconstruction. Using both simulated and real data we show that our method outperforms the latest unsupervised image restoration approach. In addition, it provides an estimate of the water surface.

title: CVGL: Causal Learning and Geometric Topology
central_claim: CLGT framework combining Causal Feature Extractor (CFE) with Geometric Topology Fusion (GT Fusion) achieves state-of-the-art cross-view geo-localization performance, improving Recall@1 from 97.41% to 98.73% on CVUSA and from 90.61% to 91.61% on CVACT_val over the EP-BEV baseline.
claim_evidence: Abstract states 'CLGT achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly under challenging real-world corruptions.' Table 1 (crossview) shows CVUSA R@1: Ours 98.73% vs EP-BEV 97.41%, and CVACT_val R@1: Ours 91.61% vs EP-BEV 90.61%.
mre_config: Train CLGT with ConvNeXt-Base backbone (384x384 resolution) on CVUSA dataset for 40 epochs using 8 GPUs. Evaluate with Recall@K (K=1,5,10) metric. Compare against EP-BEV baseline (Recall@1=97.41% on CVUSA). The MRE trains the full CLGT model (CFE + GT Fusion + DA Pooling) using InfoNCE loss with AdamW optimizer (lr=0.5e-3) and cosine scheduler.

Install dependencies via pip install -r requirements.txt. Run training with python train_cvusa.py using 8 GPUs. The training configuration uses ConvNeXt-Base backbone, 384x384 resolution, batch_size=128, 40 epochs, learning rate=0.0005 with cosine scheduler, and scaling coefficients alpha=gamma=0.1 for auxiliary losses. Evaluate using eval_cvusa.py to compute Recall@K metrics (expect Recall@1 ~98.7% vs EP-BEV baseline 97.41%). Key outputs: model checkpoints saved to cvusa/convnext_base.fb_in22k_ft_in1k_384/final/ and logs to log_dir/final/.

Paper states CVUSA provides 35,532 training and 8,884 testing image pairs with 1-to-1 ground-to-aerial correspondence. CVACT provides similar splits plus additional GPS-tagged query images. Code includes dataset handlers (CLGT/dataset/cvusa.py, cvact.py) with documented data loading paths. These are established benchmarks in the geo-localization community.

The model.py loads ConvNeXt pretrained weights via timm library, but no CLGT-trained model weights are provided. GitHub code search for 'checkpoints' OR 'pretrained' OR 'weights' within the repo returned no relevant results.

CVUSA is a foundational dataset for street-to-aerial image matching. Both are referenced as standard benchmarks in multiple prior works (SAFA, LPN, TransGeo, GeoDTR, EP-BEV) cited in the paper.

Estimated H100-hours: 8 GPUs * 3 hours/epoch * 40 epochs / 0.32 = ~300 H100-hours. The paper mentions ablation studies and multiple robustness experiments (CVUSA-C-ALL, CVACT-C-ALL variants) requiring additional compute. This is a computationally intensive training task requiring substantial GPU resources. Engineering and debugging time not included in this estimate.
abstract: Cross-view geo-localization (CVGL) aims to estimate the geographic location of a street image by matching it with a corresponding aerial image. This is critical for autonomous navigation and mapping in complex real-world scenarios. However, the task remains challenging due to significant viewpoint differences and the influence of confounding factors. To tackle these issues, we propose the Causal Learning and Geometric Topology (CLGT) framework, which integrates two key components: a Causal Feature Extractor (CFE) that mitigates the influence of confounding factors by leveraging causal intervention to encourage the model to focus on stable, task-relevant semantics; and a Geometric Topology Fusion (GT Fusion) module that injects Bird's Eye View (BEV) road topology into street features to alleviate cross-view inconsistencies caused by extreme perspective changes. Additionally, we introduce a Data-Adaptive Pooling (DA Pooling) module to enhance the representation of semantically rich regions. Extensive experiments on CVUSA, CVACT, and their robustness-enhanced variants (CVUSA-C-ALL and CVACT-C-ALL) demonstrate that CLGT achieves state-of-the-art performance, particularly under challenging real-world corruptions. Our codes are available at https://github.com/oyss-szu/CLGT.

title: SurfelSplat: Learning Efficient and Generalizable Gaussian Surfel Representations for Sparse-View Surface Reconstruction
central_claim: SurfelSplat generates surface-aligned Gaussian surfel representations from sparse-view images (2 views) for fast surface reconstruction, achieving D2S Chamfer Distance of 1.12 on DTU with 1-second inference.
claim_evidence: Abstract: 'our method achieves comparable results with state-of-the-art methods, and predict Gaussian surfels within 1 second, offering a 100× speedup without costly per-scene training.' Table 1 reports mean D2S Chamfer Distance of 1.12 across 15 DTU test scenes with 2 input views. Table efficiency shows 1±0.05 second inference time.
mre_config: MRE: Run inference with 2 context views on a single DTU test scene (e.g., scan 24) using the pretrained SurfelSplat checkpoint to generate Gaussian surfels, convert to mesh using gs2mesh.py, evaluate D2S Chamfer Distance against DTU ground truth. Input resolution 256×256/256×320, metric: D2S Chamfer Distance, target: mean CD < 2.0

Target: CD < 2.0 on single scene.

The dataset is 'freely available' per the official website, and the paper uses the standard DTU evaluation protocol with D2S Chamfer Distance as metric. abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has demonstrated impressive performance in 3D scene reconstruction. Beyond novel view synthesis, it shows great potential for multi-view surface reconstruction. Existing methods employ optimization-based reconstruction pipelines that achieve precise and complete surface extractions. However, these approaches typically require dense input views and high time consumption for per-scene optimization. To address these limitations, we propose SurfelSplat, a feed-forward framework that generates efficient and generalizable pixel-aligned Gaussian surfel representations from sparse-view images. We observe that conventional feed-forward structures struggle to recover accurate geometric attributes of Gaussian surfels because the spatial frequency of pixel-aligned primitives exceeds Nyquist sampling rates. Therefore, we propose a cross-view feature aggregation module based on the Nyquist sampling theorem. Specifically, we first adapt the geometric forms of Gaussian surfels with spatial sampling rate-guided low-pass filters. We then project the filtered surfels across all input views to obtain cross-view feature correlations. By processing these correlations through a specially designed feature fusion network, we can finally regress Gaussian surfels with precise geometry. Extensive experiments on DTU reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate that our model achieves comparable results with state-of-the-art methods, and predict Gaussian surfels within 1 second, offering a 100x speedup without costly per-scene training.
